Tea a ld Sir Andrew Clarke. For years, whenever my Customers have asked me for a Mild Tea, I have advised the Pure. old Fashioned China which I keep, and the advice has been appreciated. It is very satisfactory to them that much an eminent authority as Sir Andrew Clarke, the London Physician, corroborates opinion. Here is an extract from an interesting lecture, delivered by Sir Andrew the other day, to the Students of the London Hospital : "Tea is a blessed beverage. Ido not know what I should do without it. But there is tea and tea, and one of the teas I have in my mind is the representation of all that is physiologically wicked. Igo about town a good deal holding consulta- tions here and there, and about five o'clock, when I get into apiece, the lady of the house will say to me : 'Sir Andrew, you look tired, do let me give you a cup of tea.' I say ' thank you very much. But the tea has stood for half-an-hour, and she remarks, 'I know you do you not like it strong, Sir Andrew, and she then pours about a tablespoonful of the tea into a cup and fills thecup up with water. Now I call it positive cruelty to give tea like that to anybody and I hope you, gentlemen, will always set your face against it. Tea, to be useful, should be first of an Black China Tea ; the Indian Tea which is being cultivated has beeoflle so powerful in its effects upon the nerves system that a cup of it taken early in the morning, as many do, so disorders the nervous system that those who take it actually get into a state of tea intoxication, and It produces a form of nervous disturbance, which is most painful to witness. If you want to have, either for yourselves or for your patients, tea which will not Injure and which will refresh, get Black China Tea, putting in the right measure—the old fashioned teaspooaful for each person and one for the blessed pot. Then pour on briskly boiling water, and within five minutes you must pour it Off again, or it will become wicked instead of good." - -

Such Is Sir Andrew Clarke's opinion and advise. A few words of warning, however, are necessary to those who have for gotten what this old fashioned ea is like. The colour of the tea after it is brewed will be found tube much paler than that now in use, and the taste may not be acceptable at first owing to its apparent insipidness ; but it its use is persisted In, it will very soon be bound to be much moresultable for the system, and if, in a week to two after its use, a 'trial is again made of the kind now in ordinary use, you will wonder however you could have been using it,and you will endorse Sir Andrew's statement.

DEsoanrxs inflamed by genius, abruptly broke all his friendly connections, hired an obscure house in are unfrequented corner of Paris and applied himself to study during two years, unknown to his acquaintances.

div.head: "CAPITAL" CHAT.
div.p: "CAPITAL" CHAT.

Miss Chaplin, the well-known sculptress, is the fortunate recipient of an order from the _Queen. Her Majesty has two Spanish bullocks in the park at Osborne,which are singularly beautiful creatures, with enormous horns, and she desires to have them modelled as a group.

Sir Arthur Sullivan is about to take a pretty villa in the vicinity of Monte Carlo, not very far from the Villa Guilla, which he rented last season during his severe illness. At present he is staying at the Grand, and doing very well at the gaming tables. He is much thinner than formerly, but is in excellent spirits.

Mr. W. H. Rideing, editor of the "North American Review," secured two Gladstone articles during his recent visit. One by himself has already appeared in the " North American Review.' Another, by Mrs. Drew, will be the feature of the next number of the" Youths Companion," a Boston magazine controlled by Mr. Rideing. The article will treat of Mr. Gladstone's methods of work.

The Duke of Newcastle is twenty-eight years old, and is of studious and artistic tastes. Nothing he enjoyes more than taking" snapshots" with his camera. He devours literature, and is far better acquainted with it than his sporting neighbour, the Duke of Portland. The Duchess of Newcastle is passionately fond of dogs, and drives a four-in- hand with great skill.

Several valuable appointments at the colonial bar are waiting to be filled up. The tirincipal are the Attorney-Generalship of Ceylon, worth £l,lOO a year; the Attorney-Generalship and a judgeship in Trinidad, each figuring cut to £l,OOO per annum; and the Receiver-Generalship in the same island, valued at .eBOO a year. The list is likely soon to be swelled by a judgeship in the Straits Settlements, salary £1,300, which it is expected that Mr. Justice Wood, now on his way home, will decide to resign, after bolding it for many years.

The Duchess of Albany, accompanied by her children, will pass the winter months at the Villa Nevada; Cannes. The villa is charmingly situated, and within easy distance of the picturesque little chapel where a beautiful memorial is erected in memory of the late duke. M. and Mdme. de ,Falbe have already arrived and taken up their abode in their sumptuous winter residence known as Villa Valetta-Californie. Amongst the other arrivald this month are the Grand Due Alexis, Sir Charles Murray, the Grand Due and Duchesse Michel of Russia, and the Marquis of Grouchy.

Cardinal Lavigerie, who died last Saturday in Algiers, was a splendid specimen in the nineteenth century of the soldier-priest. For thirty years he waged, with all the zeal of a Crusader, an incessant warfare with the Arabs in command of slave cara- vans. He visited England in MSS, and addressed a vast meeting in London, describing in impassioned language the horrors of the slave trade, and exhibi- ting whips, thongs, goads and fetters used by the Arabs on the slaves employed by them to carry ivory from the interior of Africa to the coast.

Bishop Anson, formerly rector of Woolwich, who has lately resigned the See of Qu'Appelle,Canada, has been appointed Master of St. John's Hospital, Litchfield, where he is to succeed Bishop Bromby. At present his lordship, having given up his bish- opric, is making a tour to the United States before returning to England. Bishop Anson, who was born in 1840, is the son of the first Earl of Litch- field, and is a bachelor. He is by no means a bad preacher, but excels as a worker. and is of a rather retiring disposition. He left Woolwich nine years ago to go as a missionary to the North-West Terri- tory, and was consecrated a year or two afterwards first Bishop of Qu'Appelle,where he soon gathered around him a band of earnest clergymen and other Church workers.

The Rev.. Hugh MacSorley, of Sc. Paul's, Totten- ham, who was found dead in bed on Saturday morn- ing, was in many respects a remarkable man. His career at Trinity College, Dublin, was a very brilliant one, and to the last he retained his math- ematical and classical attainments. His fierce Protestantism " was not an index of character, for with his family and among his friends he was one of the pleasantest and wittiest of men. lie did yeonian's service to the cause of education and served many years upon the Tottenham School Board. His chutch services were of Calvinistic, severity, and the" black gown " was sacred to him. He leaves few of his school of thought among the London clergy.

As a rule, lima agents are not of literary tastes, but Jir. Gilbert Murray, who for the lest twenty- flur years has been agent on the estates of succes- sive Earls of Harrington, is a notable exception. There is hardly an agricultural paper one tikes up nowadays but has a practical letter or article over his familiar signature. Mr. Murray now and then dips into the reviews as well; and his various speeches on agricultural topics are perused with , more interest than, perhaps, those of any other ' member ef the profe.sion. He is descended from a long line of tenant farmers, and few men have had better opportunities of acquiring a practical know- rledie of agriculture. White-btFted, whit C-bearded, me iiim-sized, with sparkling eyes an& a- kind; thoughtful, and pleasing face, Mr. Murray has en- deared himself to many besides the numerous Elvaston tenantry, with whom he has been so long associated.

" The quiet limit of the , world," where M. de Lesseps passes his old age, far from the excitements of politics and trade, is.the little town of Vatan, in elf department of Indre. A drowsy old-world place it is. surrounded by a beautiful plain, and with a history that dates back to the fifth century. It possesses some remains of ruined towers and walls, and a flue old church, the wood-carvings and colored ghiss of which have given to Vatan any interest it may have for the tourist. The house of M. de Lesseps is known as the Chateau de la Chesney, and is situated at a little distance from the town. It has a park on the one side of it. Agnes Sorel once resided here, and an image qf that fair lady is one of the ornaments in M. de Lesseps' boudoir. The house has been considerably enlarged at different periods so that it might accommodate a numerous family and still more numerous friends.

Mr. Nathaniel Clayton, whose seat for the Hex- ham Division of Northumberland was on Wednesday declared void, is an elderly gentleman of precise habits. He practised as a solicitor for many years in Newcastle-on-Tyne, but retired from business two years ago on succeeding to the enormous for- tune of his eccentric uncle, John Clayton, who was Town Clerk of Newcastle for about half-a-century. This fortune included estates of about twenty-five thousand acres in Northumberland, as well as nearly three quarters of a million sterling. The Chesters, where the garden party that excited .Mr. Justice ,Cave's displeasure took place, is dpeltituated on fi North Tyne, with some of the nestito an remains in the neighbourhood. Mr. Clayton is a better an- tiquary than he is a politician.

The Mr, James Edgcome, whose name fig* ured on Tuesday so prominently in the correspondence with the Rome secretary relative to Trafalgar- square, is the life and soul of the "Fair Trade League," which was practically of his inception. 140 t only has he organised the league, but for a long while he edited the "Ftur. Trade Journal," which has now become a thing of the past. As the chief secretarial officer he takes a large part in the regu- lar weekly reunions at the clubrooms, and inasmuch as opponents are welcome thereto, for the purpose of discussion, there is just the prospect of the mem- bers of the league learning more about free trade than they have ever been privileged to learn before.

Mr. Edgcome is an elder brother of Treeve Edg- come (the barrister), who, it will he remembered, n,uccessf ully contested as a Gladstonian the En- field division of Middlesex, in 1886,in opposition to Viscount Folkestone,the present Earl Radnor. The two brothers are as opposite in politics as the poles, and it was on that occasion that Mr. "Fair Trade" Edgcome opposed the candidature of his brother by speaking from the Tory platform in favour of his lordship.

Clumber House, where the Duke and Duchess of 1 Newcastle gave a grand ball on Tuesday night, one of the three principal houses of the Dukeries, was built by the second duke in 1770, and is one of the most magnificent, albeit comfortable, of " stately homes of England." It is in the classic style, and along the principal front, which abuts on a lake of eighty-seven acres,runs a delicate lonic col- onnade, whilst classic statues and sculptures adorn the beautiful pleasure gardens that border the lake on each side of the house. In the centre of the terrace is a fountain, cut from one solid piece of marble, and weighing fifty tons, which was brought

div.head: EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 3, 1892 lONIE,
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 3, 1892 lONIE,

from Italy, and is a noble example of southern art. Inside the house is a veritable treasure-store, for though the great fire of 1879, which wrecked twenty rooms, destroyed many pictures and articles of vertu, others have taken their place; the present duke, like his predecessors, being an enlightened patron of art. The pictures in the state dining- room (a magnificent apartment that will accom- modate one hundred and fifty guests) alone, com- prising instances of Bnyders,Largan,and Zuccaretti, are valued at £25,000.

the second-class billiard room was received with much enthusiasm. He thereupon addressed a few remarks to those present. He observed that as a Conservative he should always deal with matters in a Conservative way. (Hear, hear.) He thanked those present for their hearty congratulations. Subsequently a meeting was held in the first class billiard room, Councillor Heaton in the chair,and Councillor Hill and Councillor Shaw supporting him. The Chairman remarked that Mr. Shaw had won by a majority of 152. They had never had such a majority before except in the case of Mr. Hill, who at one time was beaten, and then tried again and won. They bad had a very low. poll ; people had been very hrisewarsnls voting, but he was very pleased indeed that the Con- servatives had returned their candidate. Although the Tories of Warrington were very slow, and did not take the part they ought to do when they had the opportu- nity, still if they would work in the way they could do they would make Warrington in the future a good Tory town as it had always been since he came to it. (Ap- plause.) He thanked the voters of the ward for having returned Mr. Shaw ; and in returning him they had returned a very good man to the Council. Ae the Chair- man of the Board of Guardians he (Mr. Heaton) had had two or three years' experience of Mr. Shaw, sitting under him. He found he was a very useful man, and if they were inclined to let anything slip, he reminded them all, and would be heard. (Hear, hear.) That was a very great qualification. He liked a man to express his opinions. He was a proper man to have in the Council. Councillor Hill then spoke. Ho expressed the opinion that St. John's Ward would always prove a Conservative ward, if properly worked, though it had been for about ten years handed over to the Liberal party.—Mr. Roberts then addressed the meet- ing. He believed that Mr. Shaw was a man who would not sit in the Council with his tongue tied, but that he would express his opinion for the benefit of the ratepayers. Councillor Shaw expressed the pride he felt at being placed in the p )sition he had achieved, and drew comparisons between his own claims and those of Mr. Mounfield on the electors. He declared himself a work- man's friend,andasserted that he supported the principle ot the payment of standard wages, and said he did not I believe in the maxim of employing one lad to one man— (applause)—but, as lie had always done since he became an employer, in having one or two apprentices to Bto 10 men. He claimed that the Conservatives had had a glorious victorv,and that he had been honestly returned. They had had, he said, a fair and honest conflict ; lie had seen nothing wrong on the Radical side, and there had been nothing wrong on that of the Conservatives.— A vote of thanks to the Chairi?lan concluded the pro- ceedings.

div.head: ST. JOHN'S WARD ELECTION.
div.p: ST. JOHN'S WARD ELECTION.

The polling in connection with the election for the municipal representation of St. John's Ward, commenced at eight o'clock on Monday morning, in the Clubroom, John-st. The candidates were Mr. Joseph blounfield, Liberal, builder, 60, Manchester- road; Mr. Wm. James Shaw, Conservative, plumber and painter. 89, Dallam-lane ; Mr. William Diggle, Independent, gentleman, 19, Wellington-at.; and Mr. Johh Patrick Byrne, Irish Labour candidate, insurance agent, 145, Mersey-st. The presiding officers at the polling stations were Messrs. W. H. Woodcock. C. H. Unsworth, aud F. W. Walker; and the polling clerks were Messrs. H. D. Longdin, F. W. Howard, and S. Wellhead. The personation agents were—for the Liberals, Messrs. J. Maguire. J. C. Clayton, and C. Littleworth ; and for the Conser- vatives, Messrs. R. Kean, R. Brierley, and Barnes. The election was characterised by elements which imparted to it abundant interest. There was not only the struggle between the Liberal and Conservative partisans to give flavour to it, but there was also the somewhat unique feature in it of the appearance of a ' man whose candidature was representative alike of Irish Nationalism and of the labour cause. Then there was the candidature of Mr. Wm Diggle, who as the indefatigable interviewer of the local magistrates, and by lecturing and the like, has made himself, in his own peculiar fashion, indelibly associated with the agitation against the intercepting depots and other cog- nate institutions which be denounces as nuisances. His appeal to the constituency gave an additional colouring of interest to the contest,by enduing it with something of the aspect of pleasantry. It is curious to notice on what diversified issues the candidates have appealed to their constituents. Mr. Shaw • suddenly disclosed himself as allied with Mr. Diggle. so far as the objects of his some- what eccentric sanitary crusade are concerned, for in his address be described the intercepting depots, to the rate- payers, as an" abominable" thing "so improperly and cruelly planted in your midst," and declared his inten- tion of becoming an uncompromising opponent of their continuance. He advocated also all Corporation con- tracts being given to Warrington men who pay the proper standard rate of wages, and he posed as a trades unionist. 'Mr. Byrne in his addrus struck a sensitive chord in the public mind by impeach- ing the Sanitary Committee as having greatly in- creased the smallpox epidemic by the planting of temporary hospitals among the houses of the workers. He also expressed himself in 'favour of the removal of the intercepting depots and he denounced the 'pail' system. 'Mr. Msunfield informed his constituents that he would be in favour of closing the depots if necessary , for the health of the district. There were minor matters , mentioned in the addresses, but, we have contented ourselves with recapitulating the principal points in them.

• The polling was but dull until the. usual time for the first advent in force of voters, the dinner hour, when , the workmen made their appearance in large numbers. All the candidates were seen about the poll during the day, Mr. Diggle being prominently to the fore and ever ready to engnge in a bout of " chaff " with those who felt disposed to be Satirical at his expense, or to enter into speculative discussion as to hisown chances,though, he declared emphatically that if defeated this time the electors might be assured that he would never claim their suffrages again. He was subjected to consider- able raillery during the day by various women, with whom he seemed delighted to exchange badinage, and he seemed to imagine that he bad made a favourable impression on the female part of the constituency in the course of a desultory and informal sort of canvass he had made among them ; and counted much upon the support be declared he had been promised. Mr. Diggle relied on his own unaided individuality in his contest, for unlike the other candidates he had neither commit- tee rooms nor cards, and his candidature was singularly free from the conventional inethods of procedure. The polling concluded at eight o'clock, and the ballot •boxes were then conveyed to the Town nail where shortly before nine o'clock the result of the voting was declared by Alderman Sutton, returning officer. About 200 people had collected on the pathway in front of the steps, but the scene was not characterised by any dis- play of enthusiasm. The following was the official de- claration :

SHAW (C) MOUNFIELD (L) BYRNE (Labour) DIGGLE (I) The announcement of Mr. Shaw's triumph was received with cheering, but a loud peal of laughter soundfld forth as the number for Mr. Diggle was called out. AT THE LIBERAL CLUB.

After the declaration of --p7AI-; snumber of Liberals adjourned to the Liberal Club in Bewsey-street. But no formal speeches were made. The subject ef Mr. Mounfield's defeat was discussed, and it wail pretty well decided that the election had not been a fair test of the ward. Mr. Mounfield had done very little if any can- vassing, and there was a number of close upon 400 per- sons who did not vote at all. It was said at the club that most of those 400 persons, who were of both politi- cal creeds, refrained from voting. Some refused to con- nect themselves with the election because they con- sidered it was the outcome of a violated compromise. Others refused to vote because they considered an elec- tion at this period was both unwise and dangerous, and unfair to the town in its present state with regard to smallpox. . MEETING OS IRISHMEN.

On Sunday afternoon a " mass "meeting of Irishmen was held in the League Hall, 01.1(3rd-street, in support of the Labour candidates, Mr. John P. Byrne. There was a large attendance. Mr. D. Donnellan presided, and in the course of a very lengthy speech, in which he severely criticized the conduct of the Liberal party to the Irishmen of Warrington, moved the following resolution Resolved, that we, the Irishmen of Warrington, hoar with indignation of a so-called meeting of Irishmen held in the Brick-street School to support the candidature of Mr. Mounfield. We repudiate the right of some ha lf-a- dozen Irishmen to claim the said meeting as being a representative one, and, further, we pledge ourselves by every legal means in our power to support the candida- ture of Mr. John Patrick Byrne at the coming election." (Applause.) He asked if he, as an Irishman, was free to exercise his rights in the coming contest, or was he not free ? He denied the right before God of any man to dictate to them. He was a member of neither the Liberal nor Conservative Club, but he had signed his name in the register of the National League. (Applause.) He joined it as a Nationalist, and to further the cause of Ireland in every way he could. He denied the truth of the statement that the Liberals of Warring- ton had been loyal to local Irishmen •, he denied it with all the power God had given him. He had been 21 years in Warrington, but the Liberal party bad never tried ta do justice to the Irish vote. Irishmen had been called together periodically at the heels of the Liberals to sup- port them at elections in-coanection with the Board of Guardians and the Town Council, but had it ever entered into the minds of the Liberals that the Irishmen of Warrington, of whick there were a large number, were entitled to be represented municipally? It appeared that Irishmen were simply and solely created by the God of nature to follow the Liberals and be at their call when- ever they were wanted. (Applause.) Mr. Merinos( seconded the resolution, which was supported by Messrslianuraz CALLAGHAN and KILDUFF, and carried with only two dissentients:

Mr. BYRN]. (the candidate) then said he appeared be- fore the audience as an Irish Labour candidate, and he was at least as capable as the other candidates. He stood before them as a workingman. He had always had to work for his living, and if elected, and justice was thus done to him by his fellow countrymen in the ward, he would be returned at the head of the pelt on Monday next. (Applause.) Judging from the promises he had received from his English friends, and if his fellow- countrymen did their duty, he would be the winning candidate. Be had no personal interest to serve. Re- ferring to his address to the burgesses, he said he had framed it himself, that it was a good effort for a work- ingman, and would compare favourably with the addresses which had been issued by Messrs. Shaw and Mounfield. If elected he" should stand in the Council Chamber on his back irrespective of political parties." Alluding to the recent Parliamentary election, Mr. Byrne said two gentlemen .sere in communication with the Liberal party—Mr. McDougall, flour merchant, of Man- chester, and Dr. Houston. The claims of each were put before the Liberal party. Mr. McDougall agreed to pro- vide a certain portion of the expenses; Dr. Houston agreed to" pay the whole ling,' and the result was that Dr. Houston was preferred to Mr. McDougall, because he would put his hands deeper into his pockets. (Laughter.) It cost the doctor £1,700. Why was Dr. Houston brought to Warrington ? The Liberal party knew they were not going to carry the seat with him ; indeed, a certain Town Councillor admitted " they could not carry him, but that they were bound to have a candidate." Alluding to the meeting in support of the candidature of Mr. Mounfield, Mr. Byrne expressed his surprise that any Irishman would willingly lend his name to such a fiasco. Mr. Arthur H. Lee refused to contest the ward because he was opposed to politics in the Council Chamber, and so was he. To fight these contests politically meant that the interests of the working-men classes were ignored. He had no personal interest to serve, but if Mr. Shaw was elected he would be placed on the Watch Committee. - . . . _
- A vote of thanks to the ChAirman brought the meet- ing to a close.___ _
AT THE CONSERVATIVE CLUB.
After the declaration of the result, Mr. Shaw pro- ceeded to the Conservative Club, and on his entering

div.head: GERMAN IDEAL EMPLOYER OF LABOUR.
div.p: A GERMAN IDEAL EMPLOYER OF LABOUR.
HERR IT. FREESE, OF BERLIN.

Industral conciliation is the order of the day. Employers of labour are waking up to the necessity and the advantages of letting the most complete harmony possible reign among the great factors of production, and have instituted councils of arbitra- tion to settle such little disputes as arise from time to time in large establishments, but which, when neglected or ignored, place social peace in peril. Under a variety of names, these councils all make it their business to allow the working personnel of an industrial establishment to take part in the administration of the enterprise, Delegates are nominated by the workmen, and though their co-operation is more extensive in some factories than in others, they have generally a voice in each questions as hours of labour, wages supervision of apprentices, etc., while the tenhnical and commer- cial guidance of the enterprise rests with the employers alone. A recent number of the .Reforme Social e gave an account of the economic and social institutions of M. Brandts, at Miitichen-Gladbach, and more recently still, M. Julien Weiler explained his ideas of industrial conciliation and the results obtained at Mariemont-Bascoup. In the Rs:forme Sociale of October 16, Dr. Ernest Dubois describes the window-blind factory of Herr H. Freese at Berlin, with branch works at Ham- burg, Leipzig, and Breslau, there being about 200 workmen engaged in the four establishments. Here the Council of Conciliation or the representation of the workmen (ArbeitervertrOtung) has been in ex- istence since 1884, but it was reorganised in 1890. It consists of fifteen members, four of whom are nominated by the director and the others by the workmen. All the workmen are electors, and they are eligible after six months' service in the factory. The elections take place at the beginning of every year. Last year the chief nominated a woman- worker to sit on the Council, and this year the workmen followed up the new departare by elect- ing members from both sexes. The Council meets compulsorily once a quarter, and at other times at the summons of the chief or the workmen, to discuss the general interests of the factory and the concerns of the workmen, to settle disputes between workers, inflict fines, give advice in cases of complaint, discuss wages and the hours of labour, itsc. At the close of each meeting any workman may be admitted to make known his grievances—in a wcrd, the thousands of little in- cidents which concern him and his life in the factory never have the chance of engendering re- volts and other serious difficulties, for the frank ' explanation and the prompt solution dispel them at the outset.

The general regulations of the factory have been drafted by the employer and the representatives of the workmen. The working day is fixed at nine hours—six to five in summer,and seven to half-past six in winter, with two hours and two hours and a half tor rest,except in rare cases provided for in the constitution. The workmen have rejected the eight hours' day. As soon as a change is proposed either by the manager or the workmen, it must receive common consent Lefore it can become law. Most of the work is piece-work. A very curious point is the wage-tariff, which is fixed for two years in each department, always, of course, by common consent. During that period the contract- ing parties can make no change, and if no other proposition is accepted in the six weeks before the end of the term, the tariff continues in force for another period of two years. "It was after full consideration of the matter that I decided on the two years," says Herr Freese ; " it is running some risk, hut if I give up my right of reducing wages for two years, my workmen, on the other hand, understand that they can ask for no increase during the same period, and we have thus a certain term of tranquillity 'assured us. I have never had a strike, and that is worth a good deal. The tariffs, moreover, are arranged on terms ex- tremely clear and fair for both parties, and I have not yet had occasion to repent my decision." i Herr Freese, it should be added, s a firm believer in the principle of profit-sharing, which he has also introduced into his establishments: Last year two per cent, of the net profits was distributed among all the workmen, no matter how long or how short a time they had been in his employ, and the sum paid to each wa3 in proportion to the wages he was receiving.

THE HOUSE AND LAND INVESI3IENT TRUST. AN INDEBTEDNESS OF £1,692,439. A meeting of the creditors and shareholders 'of the House and Land Investment Trust, Limited, was held in London, on Thursday, under the presidency of Mr. C. J. Stewart, official receiver and provisional liquidator, who in his statement of affairs said there was an unsecured indebtedness to 17,000 depositors to the amount of £1.892,439. The reserve fund was set down in the books at £36,000, hut there was nothing to represent that fund. The debenture loans stood at £103,500,and the debenture holders took possession of all the property in September. After going into further detail as to the bad prospect, Mr. Stewart said that nothing should be covered up by a voluntary liquidation or reconstruction. The facts were such that he wouftl produce his report to the court:at the earliest:possible moment,in order:tolsecure the public examination of all the officials of the Society, and expose the modes adopted of dealing with the money of the class who were encouraged to invest on the ground of prudence and thrift. Mr. J. S. Balfour, M.P., one of the directors,:who was received with oppro- brious language by some of those present, said he felt the disaster keenly, by which the whole current of his life had been changed. He would do all in his power to assist the provisional liquidator to realise all the pro- perty. A provisional committee was appointed.

div.head: PRIDE OF THE MILL.
div.p: PRIDE OF THE MILL.
A THRILLING LOVE STORY
BY LAURA JEAN LIBBEY.
CIIA.PTER XXXIV. "GREAT GOD! THE MA.DRIAGE MUST BE STOPPED."

riNa.l ti. strangeou bliclal party ever seen. So thought tlie good old minister, as he watched them advancing slowly up the aisle—the bridegroom so dark and stern, the bride-elect pale as death, and the shabbily dressed man and woman following in the rear.

Asa usual thing, the faces of brides were smiling and joyous. There was love-light in their eyes and happiness in their hearts, and the manner in which they clung to their lovers' arms, as they timidly approached the altar, was a caress in itself. This one held coldly aloof, and the beautiful, sad dark eyes seemed heavy with unshed tears. "Yes, verily, a strange bridal party," muttered the minister, thoughtfully. "Nothing can save me now," thought bole, drearily. "I shall leave this place the wife of a man I abhor. This is but the beginning of the horrible future." In the centre of the dim old church lonic came to a sudden halt.

"Before we step to the altar, I have a request to make of you, Frank Lyons," she said, slowly. He started uneasily. "I say, if what you ask be within my power, I promise beforehand to grant it." Before explaining the thrilling event that trans- pired, we must go back a little to the cause that occasioned it.

The sound of the carriage wheels had scarcely died away in the distance ere William Rlalcohn, the boat-builder's son, came slowly up the street. "I knew he was a rascal," 14e muttered to himself, "and of the deepest dye. I told mother so, but she could not believe it. ' Fine feathers make fine birds,' they say." Entering the house, he threw himself down in his favourite arm chair to smoke and think.
"He is the greatest villain that ever went un- hung," he muttered; "but for ITER sake, because he is a relative of hers, I will not expose him. I knew I could not be mistaken. HE IS THE SAME MAN."
An hour or more had elapsed ere, by the merest chance, his eye fell upon the letter his mother had left for him on the table. _ _ .

"A letter for me, and in mother's handwriting I" he murmured. "How strange I No doubt it is a reminder of some gift she is wanting me to buy; for, now that I remember it, to-morrow is her birth- day." With a good-humoured smile on his honest, face, the young man broke the seal. As he glanced over the contents of the letter the smile died from his face, and an exclamation of horror broke from his lips. Glancing over his shoulder, we will read it with him, dear reader. It ran as follows: MY DEAR SON,--I am out of patience waiting for you to return. As it is unusual for you to find your father and me both gone from home, I write to let you know where we are going. I fancy it will be a surprise to you. It appears that I was mistaken in believing the gentleman (Mr. Lyons, she calls him) to be a relative of Miss Lawrence. He is neither kith nor kin. Imagine my great amazement when Miss lone called me to her room, and said, very abruptly : "I am going to marry the gentleman who called hers this morning, Mrs. Mal- colm. The ceremony is to take place in the old church at the cross-roads at four this afternoon I should liks: to have you and your husband—your son, too, if he will —accompany me to witness the marriage." Somehow I cannot think she is marrying the gentle- man for love, for there were tears in her eyes as she turned away. If you arrive after we have left you might come on to the church, if you like, seeing thit you are invited by the young lady; but mind, William, if you do come you are to weal' your Sunday best. You will find your clothes all laid out in your room. I—"

William Malcolm neycr finished that letter. With a mighty cry he sprang to his feet. Glancing up at che clock ticking merrily on the wall, he saw that it wanted twenty minutes to four. "My God !" he cried. "I would not be in time to save her! But I can try—yes, with Heaven's help I can try! " Hurrying up to the stable, he led out Akbar with an alacrity that fairly astounded that easy-going old animal, and harnessed him, springing quickly into the saddle. One cut with his whip sent him fairly flying down the road. It was ten good miles to the church indicated in his mother's lettei. He knew of a route he could take across lots, which would save Irm at least half of the distance, he therefore turned his horse's head in that direction, riding at a break neck speed, as though a human life de- pended on it. One or two farmers, jogging along at a easy rate in their waggons, looked after the flying horseman in amazement. One called back to him:
"Look alive there, stranger, there's danger ahead; they are repairing the road just beyond the curve." But William Malcolm never heard—never heeded them.

At last, through the trees, afar off yet, he beheld I the steeple of the old church. "Heaven grant that I may be in time," he cried, hoarsely, urging his horse to greater speed; but the animal was already exhausted far beyond his en- durance. It will never be known just how it happened —whether old Akbar grew frightened at the shower of apple blossoms the wind blew over the road, or ' whether he stumbled on the rocky road—suddenly he shied and reared, and the next moment he was galloping riderless down the road. For long hours William Malcolm lay white, rigid, unconscious, in the long grass by the roadside, Slowly the hands of time moved • the sun sank in me west—the dusk or night crept on and sautes Into darkness; slowly, one by one, the golden. hearted stars came out and fixed themselves in the blue heavens—still the rigid figure lay motionless under the waving trees. Was he dead, or dying? Only the night-wind sobbing a requiem over him could have answered. It so happened that this was the particular night on which Arthur Rochester had bidden farewell to his home for ever. .
It Was his intention to take the outgoing steamer for Europe, but interests which he had at Cornwall requiring his attention, he was obliged to go on there.

At the depot he had taken a carriage, and was driving along the lonely country road, when a low moan, seemingly coming from a clump of adjacent bushes to the right, fell distinctly upon his ear. Mr. Rochester drew rein and listened. Again the sound was repeated. Hastily springing from his buggy, he secured his horse, and searched carefully in tile vicinity from whence the sound proceeded. He was soon rewarded by finding the body of a man lying under the trees. By the faint gleam of the stars he could see that the man's face was covered with blood, which flowed through a small wound on his temple. It was but the work of a moment to lift him into thc buggy, and catching up the reins again, Arthur drove in headlong haste to the village, that he might have medical attention as as soon as possible. He found Dr. Willard at home, and the young man was conveyed quickly into his office. "Ah 1 I understand how it came about," said the doctor. "This accounts for the horse that came riderless into the village early this afternoon. The animal threw him, no doubt. Parties are out now in search of the man who rode him." Dr. Willard looked grave when he examined the wound. "Directly on the temple," he said. "That's very bad. If he lives, ten to ore it will leave him a lunatic—a case for some asylum, poor fellow 1" The wound was soon dressed. Then the effects of the opiate which had been administered began to wear away. "Where am I ?" asked William Malcolm at length, struggling up to a sitting posture, looking in bewilderment around him. "How came I here ?"

"Oh, I remember I" he cried out, in horror. "I was going to stop the marriage, My horse stum- bled and threw me. Great God; I may be too late! Do not attempt to detain me 1" he cried, as the doctor held him back. "I must go!" "As I feared," said the doctor. "The man is raving crazy. Their hallucinations always take some strange form." "Re seems particularly sane," replied Arthur Rochester. "They all aeens 007 replied the doctor, dryly. "Ton will see for Yourself presently that he will havaa perfect mania on the subject of stopping marriages." "I should not wonder a bit if his sweetheart had jilted him, poor fellow!" CuiPTER xxxv.
" I bEMAND AN ANSWER..
Mbar RO.olloster loon took his leavG.
in vain William Malcolm protested that he was perfectly able to resume his journey when he found himself alone with the doctor.
"Certainly, you shall go very soon," replied Dr. Willard; but, to Malcolm's intense surprise, he s.bw him quietly turn the key in the lock. "May I inquire what that action was for 2" asked Malcolm.

"You may inquire, certainly, my good fellow," replied the doctor, with a good-humoured laugh. "Will you answer me 7 " demanded Malcolm. "That is quite another matter," laughed the doctor. Young Malcolm, when he was aroused to intense anger, was a man to be dreaded. Even the doctor was amazed at the tempestuous rage into which he flew at this answer. " Quite as mad as a March hare," he concluded. •

"Open that door I" cried Malcolm, springing for- ward, all unmindful of the pain in his head, and attempting to take the key from him by main force. "Every moment you are keeping me here is precious." "Exactly," replied the doctor; "but, really, I see no help for it. Stay here you must for the present." "I will not 1" cried Malcolm, grasping a chair, and in the intense excitement of the moment, fired to the very brink of madness at being thus re- tarded, he brought it down with full force upon the doctor's head, crying, hoarsely: "How will you open that door " Stung to fierce rage, the doctor turned and grappled with him, and in his weak state, Malcolm was soon overcome.

" I shall pay you well for that blow, my fine fellow 1" cried the doctor, furiously. "I was in- tending to send you to the hospital; but now I shall send you where you belong—to the asylum. I fancy you will become the straight-jacket into which you will be placed." . .
Smarting under the severe pain of the blow, Dr. Willard made out the certificate consigning Mal- colm to the asylum at once, and hastily summoned his assiatants to execute the order.

The truth must be gtated here and now. Although Dr. Willard was an impulsive man, he was neverthe- less an honest one. He was firmly imbued with the belief that the man before him was insane, and a danger to the community at large, and that it was an imperative duty to see him put in confine- ment at the earliest possible moment. The attendants soon appeared, and raving and cursing in one breath, and pleading in the next, poor Malcolm was hurried away from the office, and into a coach standing before the door; and ere the day broke he found himself an inmate of the asylum on Blackwell's Island. All in vain he told his story, pleading with those about him to find out for themselves whether he spoke truthfully or falsely. No one replied. Who would take the trouble to investigate the story that fell from a supposed maniac's lips? All night long Malcolm paced his narrow room despite the pain in his head, crying aloud to Heaven that his hands were tied. Ile could have saved poor Tonle Lawrence from a marriage that would prove the bitterest curse, but now it was beyond his power. All night long he listened to the frightful sounds about him, murmuring, in a horrible whisper, that- ho was not mad now, but he soon should be amid these surroundings. . .

The next ruornlng Arthur Rochester, chancing to pass the doctor's office, stopped for a moment to learn how his patient of the night before pro- gressed, and was amazed to learn that he had been so summarily disposed of. "I cannot believe that the poor fellow is insane, Doctor," he said, thoughtfully. "It seems quite incredible."

"You would have believed it had you been here when he attempted to murder me with that chair," he responded, dryly. "I have never seen a more desperate lunatic at large." All that day the conviction haunted Arthur Rochester that, for once in his life, the shrewd doctor was in error.

The subject so weighed upon Arthur's heart—he could not tell why—that he found himself wonder- ing if he ought not to take a trip over to the asylum and satisfy oimself. At last he went. To his surprise Malcolm knew him at once; still, he must not make that the test of the young man's sanity, "You are the gentleman who found me lying- by the roadside yesterday," he said, with deep emotion. "Yes," replied Arthur Rochester, kindly. __ _ -•

"'Would to Heaven you bad left me there to die rather than have saved me.for such a fate as this! I beg you, in all calmness, to listen to me, sir. I am not a madman, as you think me; I am as sane as yourself." As he listened, somehow the young man's words carried conviction with them to Arthur Rochester's heart that he was speaking the solemn truth. Many a man had been wrongfully thrust into a felon's cell, when he was innocent, by force of cir- cumstances; many a man had been confined in a madhouse by injustice and foul wrong, who was perfectly sane; had dragged out a miserable life, and had died there, all forgotten by the great bust- ling world outside, leaving vengeance to Heaven. Arthur thought of this as he gazed into the clear, earnest eyes of the young man standing before him.

"I admit I was under great mental excitement when the dootor sought to restrain me." he said, sadly, "and po man ever had more cause to be. t could have saved a woman from destruction, but fate took it out of my hands." "There! Do not look at me incredulously. I mean those words. I could have saved a woman from the cruelest of futures. It is too late now. Her doom has been sealed ere this."

"In what way 7" asked Arthur, curiously. "By marriage with the wickedest man that ever went unhung. I knew that which would have sent him to the gallows; bat the knowledge that she was to wed this man came to me too late. Will you hear the story, sir?" "Yes," replied Arthur, compelled by some im- pulse, for which he could not wholly account, to listen. "To begin with," replied Malcolm, "I am the son of Peter Malcolm, the boat-maker, and live in the little village of K—, up the Harlem River. "One night, some six weeks since, father and I were out with some of the new boats, when looking ahead, scarcely three feet in front of us, I beheld something dark in the water, as I looked it instantly disappeared only to reappear a moment later a little further off; then, to my amazement, I saw a woman's face. "In an instant I bad flung off my coat and sprung to the rescue. "We took her home—father and I—and there she lay, for long weeks, hovering between life and death. My mother's constant watchful care saved her, I often think.

, She was young and lovely, sir. I am but a rough fellow, sir, and I cannot find words to tell you what she was like. Her face was pretty as a white rose, and her lips and delicately rounded cheeks like scarlet blossoms. And those eyes I Ah, , they were like soft, bright stars. 'Do you wonder that I learned to love her, sir, with all the passionate depths of my heart—that , the whole world seemed ce;,tred in her smile, and the world's frown in her sadness 7 "1 had never thought much about love. I never knew it could change a man so completely that even ; to himself he seemed a different being. , "I worshipped her from afar, sir, content to stand near and look at her as if she were some divine being. I—l—would have given ray life for her. " I began to dread the day when she should have recovered sufficiently—to—to leave us. I would not think of that dark hour. "But I should not tell you my story, sir," he said, sadly. "How could it interest you 1' "It does interest me," responded Arthur, earnestly. "I— Pray go on." "When consciousness came to her, and my mother told her how I had rescued her, she sent for me. "'You have saved my life,' she said, holding out her little white hand to me. • Oh, pray forgive me for saying it was a cruel kindness. I wish I had died in the cold, dark waters!" (To be continued).
RUNCORN COMMISSIONERS AND THE WATERWORKS.

A special meeting of Runcorn Board of Improve- ment Commissioners was held on Monday in regard to the proposed purchase of the Runcorn Water- works. Mr. F. Wiswall presided, and there were present Messrs. P. Speakman, W. Fisher, S. Taylor, R. Abel, W. llankinson, E. W. Humphreys, T. Lea, D. Bisbrown, J. Meadowcroft, J. W. Lightburn, H. Coward, P. Smith, J. Pritchard, F. A. Lake (110 r clerk), E. Marshall (secretary), and M. Barker (surveyor). The Chairman said it was a formal meeting, in eon- formity with the Act of Parliament, to ratify what they had already done. Mr. Fisher moved the following resolution :__"TM application be made t 3 Parliament in the session of 1895, for a bill to provide for the purchase,by the Runcorn Im- provement Comthissionors, compulsorily by agreement. of the undertaking of the Runcorn, Weston, and Halton Waterworks Company for the winding and dissolution of the Company, the exteneion of powers for the 10061 government of the district, the amendment of Acts, and for other purposes. That the costs, charges, and expenses, preliminary and incidental to the applying f"." promoting and passing such Bill into an Act shall be charged upon the General District rats." Mr. P. Speakman seconded the motion. The Chairman said he had met Mr. Newton, and been ver the ground from Norton to Runcorn reservoir. Mr- Newton took notes all the time. Everything they found confirmed what he himself told the members at the Com- mittee meeting. Nothing arose out of the inspection all far as it went, to upset any of their calculations. 31r. Newton would not commit himself to any report because it was only a preliminary visit,and he was determined to. give every matter careful consideration. At his next visit. Mr. Newton would go down the well to the bottom. Be would have to provide himself with a flannel suit, and everything preparatory for that work. He would also take a sample of the mains, and do whatever he thougro fit and necessary to satisfy himself and the Board tlsat they were safe and right. A discussion took ?lace as to the instructions given t° the engineer, Mr. Newton, and the accountant, Mr. Tun- stall, and the Law Clerk said they had been instructed in the terms of the resolutions passed at the last meeting- A suggestion was made that it would be an advantagf if both gentlemen had an interview with the Parliamen- tary Committee.—The Law Clerk said this could be easily arranged.—The resolution was carried unani- mously. The Board members were invited to meet Mr. Tunstall next morning.—Mr. Taylor took no part in the proceedings.

div.head: BOY WAS RIGHT ABOUT THAT SHIP.
div.p: THE BOY WAS RIGHT ABOUT THAT SHIP.
" .31-amnta, see ! there's a ship," cried the child, calling his mother's attention to the masts and spars of a veeee which snowed over the tops of the trees. •

We were on the top of a tram passing through Green- wich, and a ship ought always to he possible in that marine neighbourhood. When we got near enough bo. see through the trees, we perceived that what the boy saw was indeed a ship, but not a floating ship. It was only a vessel fixed bodily in the ground in front of some building that looked like a hospital—a ship away out of its element, indifferent to wind or wave ; just a curio - city, nothing more. "Mamma," said the boy thoufully, I should think that ship would just hate $ whers there is4't am/ vizier. The little chap had clear intuition, he follow-ea the scent with nose in the air. Anything or anybody ought to just hate" to be useless and out of place," and yet this is exactly where most of us too often are. Take one of the commonest of all examples, read it, and tell us if you are as quick as the boy who was to draw the right moral. _ _

" I, Frederick Fisher, of 63, Lidget Hill, Lowtown, Fudsey, near Leeds, do solemnly and sincerely declare as follows : Up to being seventeen years of age (1875), I was strong and healthy. At this time I began to ieel tired, languid, weak, and had great pain at rny stomach. I had a foul taste in the mouth, my tongue was lihe a piece of brown leather, and my month was covered with thick, slimy phlegm, and I was constantly spitting up a thin watery fluid. My appetite was poor, and what I ate seemed to turn to wind, and I had great pain across the stomach, which made mu press my sides to try and relieve the pain. I had frequent attacks of billious sickness. I would go to bed fairly well and in the morn- ing would be so sick that I could not raise my head from the pillow, and for twelve hours at a time would lie prostrate. I would vomit dreadfully, throwing up a quantity of green fluid, and on one occasion I vomited something hard, like solid yolk of egg, which made think it was gall stones. " So violent were these attacks that it has taken two persons to hold my head and support me, and I would afterwards break into a sweat all over me. The attacks became so frequent that I began to lose flesh and got so weak that I could not walk across the floor, and had difficulty in getting upstairs. Getting weaker and weaker as time went on, the debility led to curvature of the spine, for before my illness I was as straight as way' one. I saw a doctor, who gave me medicines, but I got no better. He said : can't say what will be the end, the complaint has been a long time cooling and will be a long time going away.' In 1878 I attended as outdoor ta patient at the Leeds Infirmary for sis% weeks, and again in 1880 I was a patient at the same hospital. The doctors there gave me medicines, but I got little better. They seemed puzzled with icy ease, and would not say what was the matter with me. Better and worse, in a half-dead, half-alive, state, I dragged on until 1883, and was constantly leaving my work, so reduced had I be- come. I lost all hope of ever getting better, and ge" up taking medicine, for I had lost all faith in it. One day my mother persuaded me to try Mother Seigel's Curative Syrup, and she got me a bottle. After taking this medicine for a week I felt quite a new man, and by ccntinuing with it I was able to get back to Inv work. and by taking the Syrup occasionally I have been able to follow my employment. I conscientiously believe that Seigel's Syrup ha,s been the means of saving otY life, and I wish others to know of the bepefit I have re- ceived from it. My mother, who has been a greet sufferer with her lwad for many years, has found the greatest benefit from the Syrup. "If by publishing this statement it will help other sufferers, the Proprietors are .:at liberty to make whatever use they may think fit of this declaration. " And I make this solemn declaration, conscientiously believing the same to be true. By N irtue of the pro- visions of the Statutory Declaration Act, 1836 (5 and t William IV., c. 62). (Signed) " FREDERICK FISHER." " Declared at Leeds aforesaid, this ) twenty-third day of April, One Thousand Eight Hundred and Ninety-one, before me, (Signed) " ALF. COOKE, J.P., "..11avor of the Borough of Leeds." Then we have the case of a lady who says she once felt (to use her own words) "as if I wanted my stays ripped off." She meant that so great was the pain in the stomach and the sense of tightness or oppresion at her sides that she could scarcely breathe. She goes on to say that she could drink nothing but warm water, and every morsel of food site ate gave her great pain. In hope ot abating this she was poulticed with mustard and linseed, which did no good to speak of. She went through several weeks in that way, "anti then," she says, "I thought I'd try a dose out of my mother's bottle." It seems that the elder lady had suffered troro weakness and debility for three years, and the °DIY thing that helped her was the contents of that bottle, and of other bottles like it—namely, Mother Seigel's Syrup. Well, the daughter tried it also, and adds: " The effect was wonderful, for alter the first few doses all pain left me, my food agreed with me, and after it week licould hardly get enough to eat so well did feel." The lady is Miss Ellen Orme, of 73, Berry-St., hoeth.‘, near Liverpool. Dear, dear ! How much that ship in the big yard at Greenwich resembles the thousands of men and women who are more or less good for nothing because of illness: the great fleet of human ships stuck in the mud or tied up in the docks. The value of Seigel's Syrup is that it enables them to put to sea and sail.

div.p: TO WARRINGTON FROM
A WARRINGTON BOY'S SAD END.
DEATH IN A FIELD.

On Thursday last week, the 12 year old son of Mr. Wm. Richardson, of Philip-st., Winwick-road, was sent to school, and afterwards took a stroll which proved to be a fatal one for him. He was but a delicate boy with a fresh complexion, and light hair, and he wore a black jacket and a pair of corduroy trousers. He left school and is sup- posed to have made his way towards Runcorn., What his wanderings were for three days no one knows. But on Sunday the boy was found dead in a field, belonging to Mr. Clement Baguley, Manor Farm, Norton. From the information obtained by the police it would appear that Wm. Bossoms, teamsman, Norton, saw the deceased and another boy coming out of a ditch in a field at eight o'clock on Friday morning. He asked them what they were doing there, and received tne answer that they had been sleeping there all night and that they were starved. The big boy accompanying the deceased was crying. He told them to go home, and they said they belonged to Longford-st , but did not name the town. At 10.20 on Sunday morning Alexan- der Simpkin,labourer,Runcorn,whilst on the canal side at Norton, saw the deceased in a field, and gave in forma- tion to the police. P.C. Fryer, stationed at Halton, re- moved the body to Norton Lodge, to await an inquest There were no marks of violence thereon. The facts were reported to the Coroner, Mr. J. E. Worsley. The body was identified on Monday as that of the son of William Richardson, 1, Philip-it., off Bluecoat-et., Winwick-road Warrington. The boy went to school on Thursday,and then seems to have wandered off with a companion named Nicholson,who is said to have left him in a field at Norton. Deceased was exceedingly backward for his years, and was scarcely able to express his wants. The parents had searched for him without success.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF GUARDIANS.

Mr, J. Mclntyre presided over the fortnightly meeting held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday, when there were present the Rev. J. W. N. Tanner, the Rev. Dr. Gastaldi, Messrs. J. Knowles, FL E. Heywood, E. Aaron, J. Baguley, W. Pickering, J. Whitlow, J. Brandreth, W. Turner, T. Lewis, W. Wilkinson, J. M. Williams, S. Taylor, T. Les, J. W. Baguley, T. Baxter, C.C., J. Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk.)

div.head: -RECLAIMING TEER TRAMP.
div.p: -RECLAIMING TEER TRAMP.

A letter was read from Miss Barnett, of Cheltenham, asking the Guardians if they would accept a library and scripture wall cards for the tramps' department at the Workhouse, on behalf of the Tramps' Mission. All the books are of a strictly religious and non-controverial character, and would incline the tramps to lead better and nobler lives, and induce them to work honestly and SO frequent the casual wards no longer.

div.head: SALARIES OF OFFICIALS.
div.p: SALARIES OF OFFICIALS.

The following resolution had been forwarded by the Slcaford Union :—" That Boards of Guardians may be invested with power to reduce as well as augment the salaries of their officers, with the consent of the Local Government Board, but without the consent of their pfficers, The Sleaford Guardians invited the co-opera- tion of Runcorn Gurrdians in obtaining these powers.— Mr. Whitlow moved that a similar resolution be adopted and forwarded to the Loca 1 Government Board.—Mr. Lea seconded,—Carried.

div.head: COUNTY RATH.
div.p: THE COUNTY RATH.

Mr. _Reginald Potts, clerk of Cheshire County Council, informing the Guardians that the Council had ordered the following rates to be levied for the half year ending March 1893:—County rate 24d, in the £, and General Police rate of a penny in the L.—The Clerk said the County rats was the same as last half-year, and the police rate laqt half-year was of a penny in the L.

div.head: REDUCTION OF QUALIFICATION FOR GUARDIANS.
div.p: REDUCTION OF QUALIFICATION FOR GUARDIANS.

A letter from the Local Government Board was read stating that they had had under consideration the qual- ification of the elective guardians of the poor of the several unions and separate parishes in England and Wales in which the Guardians are elected under the general law. The Board had deemed it expedient that the amount of the qualification in each of the unions and separate parishes referred to should be fixed at an annual rateable value of £5, and they had issued an order accordingly.—The Clerk said the present qualifica- tion was £2s.—Dr. Gastaldi said according to popula- tion Runcorn ought to have a larger representation on the Board. Mr. Whitlow : I don't know. We have trouble enough with those that do come.

div.head: RELIBVIEG OFFICER.
div.p: THE RELIBVIEG OFFICER.
The Local Government Board wrote sanctioning the appointment of Mr. Thomas Cooke to the office of relieving officer for the Runcorn district at a salary of £lOO per annum.
TRH ASYLUM DISPUTE.

Mr. A. Hornby, clerk of the County Asylum, Chester, wrote stating that the Committee directed him to point out that any inconvenience consequent upon the trans- fer of patients to Parkside would be oily temporary, as it had been decided to at once enlarge the County Asylum. With respect to the maintenance of such patients the Committee regretted they had no power to reaoup Boards of Guardians the extra cost of conveyance to and maintenance in Parkside Asylum of the county patients from this district. The Committee had already been surcharged b 7 the Government auditor in respect of payments made in 1890 and 1891, with reference to patients transferred to the Macclesfield Asylum from their institution.
THR BALLOT FOR GUARDIANS RUCTIONS.

" Ilyeres, 17th, November, 189 g. Dear Sir, —I am in receipt of your favour of the 7th inst. containidg a copy of the resolution of your Board ia favour of the adoption of the ballot in the election of Guardians. I shall at all times be happy to support the prayer of your petition to the Local Government Board, and trust that no long time will elapse before an Act of Parliament is passed carrying out your wishes. Yours faithfully, Rum T. BRUNNII.—John Ashton, Esq."

FINANCE. Mr. Brandreth presented the report of the Finance Committee.—The balance in the treasurer's hands was £3 403 7s. 10d., out of which accounts amounting to £258 Os, 11d., including outdoor relief of £l3O, and £B7 Oa. 11d., repayment of principal and interest on Work- house loan, were payable, reducing the debt to £1,375 10s. Bd.—Passed. PROPOSED INFECTIOITS DISEASES HOSPITAL. Mr. Williams stated that the sub-committee elected to deal with the question of providing an infectious disease hospital had held a meeting that morning, and had un- animously decided that it was desirable to erect such an institution for the benefit of the whole union. It was proposed to place a hospital, capable of accommodating six male and six female patients, on the spare land at Dutton Workhouse; and that it be built on similar lines to the hospital at Runcorn, which had received the approval of the Local Government Board, but with such additions as modern requirements might suggest. At Runcorn hospital there was no mortuary, and it was intended to add that convenience to the Union Hospital. There would also be a caretaker's house attached to the main building, and it was suggested that Mr. Farring- ton, the sanitary inspector, should reside there. The Bub-Committee had also resolved that two local archi- tects should be requested to furnish plans and specific- ations for a suitable building, and that those be sub- mitted to the Committee at a meeting to be held a fortnight hence.—Mr. Dansey, the Government inspec- tor, said it would be useless passing such a resolution, as the Local Government Board would not sanction the Guardians building a hospital ; it was not part of their work, except so far as regarded the inmates of the house. It was a matter solely for the Rural Sanitary Authority, and the Guardians could make arrangements with that Authority for the reception of their patients in the hospital.—The subject was thereupon referred to the Sanitary Authority.

div.head: EXAMINER, SATETBDAY, DECEMBER 3 1892.
div.p: THE EXAMINER, SATETBDAY, DECEMBER 3 1892.
DARKEST ENGLAND.
MEETING AT EARLESTOWN,

On Monday evening, a public meeting in aid of General Booth's "Darkest England" scheme, was held in the Wesleyan schoolroom, Earlestown. Dr. Valentine presided, and in addition to several members of the Salvation Army, there were present on the platform, Staff-Captain J. B. Elmslie, of Aberdeen, who attended to give a description of the aims and objects of the scheme. Dr. Valentine said lie was glad he had acceded to the request of the deputation which waited upon him, to ask him to preside over the meeting. He had read the pamphlets which had been given to him, and he thought they should take them as true, and he was sure it gave a good account of the scheme, which was endeavouring tolescue from poverty the submerged portion of our population. Staff-Captain Elinslie, said some of their " Darkest England" meetings had been composed of a rather critical company, but, as far as he could judge, he thought he was amongst people of kindred feeling, who were all interested in the good work. He, with others, had visited from door to door, the needy poor, and had come in contact with a large number of their fellow-people, houseless and homeless, and what they wanted was food to eat, and work to do. They said let us have none of your preaching, let us have something to do, and it was through this that General Booth thought something should be done to alleviate the sufferings of the poor. He was justified in trying some scheme; in trying to meet the demands of the great surging mass. There were some millions of our fellow creatures, men and women, who were prepared and willing to work, and no work for them to do, and, he maintained, General Booth was justified in appealing to humanity for some way out of the great dark, to find them something to do, and yet people said he had no business to do it. Every right thinking person would join in commending General Booth for finding work for the unemployed. There were 10,000 people out of work that night, in the city of Londen, almost houseless and homeless. Speaking of the appeal now being made for further help, he alluded to the fact that people said why not wait until the report of the Investigation Committee had been issued. He asked were they to wait for the report before they did anything P They must in justice deal just now with the immediate wanta, and appeal to the country, report or no report, in order to do what they could to allay the distress. (Applanse.) The report could not be anything but satisfactory : they had nothing to fear, nothing to conceal. General Booth was no rogue : he had never had in hit hands a single farthing of the money subscribed for the " Dark- est England Scheme." General Booth asked for £lOO,OOO to invest in a scheme that would alleviate the suffer- ings of a certain number of people, that would obviate the necessity of sleeping on the embankment, and under archways, and also for stopping the asking for charity to assist the needs of the body; and the country he was glad to say responded at once te the noble ap- peal. General Booth said if they would give him £lOO,OOO, and £30,000 a year, he would show them a plan, by which, in a few years, there would not be a homeless man or woman in the length or breadth of the British Isles. The shelters in the City Colony were the first shelters they had to grapple with, and he was glad to say they had provided shelter for over a million poople who were homeless. They had eight of these shelters in the City of London, which were capable of sheltering something like 4,000 people every night in the week. In connection with these they had food depots, where they had to manufacture the food supply of these houseless people, and the charge for supper, lodging, and breakfast was 3d. per night,and if they had not the money to pay for their board, they were allowed to chop a cer- tain quantity of sticks, sufficient to pay for it, thus giving the men an oppertunity of earning their own bread by the sweat of their brow. Some people had said that their shelters were not clean ; there was never a bigger falsehood told, and it was very unfair for people to say that the shelters were not clean. Be was quite prepared to sit down, and take his meals on the floor of any shelter in London. There were seven workshops attached to the shelter, which were occupied by all con- ditions of men and women. In their workshop they had been able to give employment to something like 5,000 people who were out of work, and during the 21 months, these people had earned £64,162, and it had only cost £3,516. During the 21 months they had re- reived 23,159 applications from unemployed peeple, and had found employment for 10,000. The criminal classes had also received attention, and into their rescue homes they had received 3,422 girls from oft the streets of the city of London, many of them the most degraded, and some extremely young. Out of that number 2,917 had gone out during the 21 months to earn their own living in honest respectable paths. Many had been restored to their parents, and some very few had gone back, but in calculating the percentage that had been made good, 76 girls out of every 100 were respectable, and doing well. It had cost £58,000 to acquire and eetahlieh the Colonies in London and the provinces, and, considering the number of people they had given work to, and made to earn their own bread, and the thousands of women they had reclaimed, he considered it had been done remarkably cheap, and if the scheme had done nothing more than set before the country an object lesson, it had done more than General Booth ever ex- pected to do. The speaker concluded his remarks with an urgent appeal on behalf of the scheme. A vote of thanks to the Chairman terminated the proceedings.

BUT NO "SWEET WILLIAM 1"

Aw'll sing a twothry gardenia' chants, On luvly pumpums an' chrysants, Potmarjoram an' pollyants, But no " Sweet William !" We hed a grand an' gradely show, Wi' yallo tulups aw aglow, An' collyfleawrs ez white ez Brow, But no " Sweet William !" We'd pratoes that wur set i' March, Rom full o' meyliness an' starch, That nare made anny bally warch, But no "Sweet William!' Fine apricots wi' rosy cheeks, • Such ez a duke or marquis seeks ; Beside sum grand shilots an' leeks, But no" Sweet William I " We'd pears—they caw'd urn jargonelles— Sweet peyse and canterbury bells, An' orkids, reg'lar tip-top swells, But no " Sweat William Good sage an' onions not too strung, Fer stain' genders owd er yung, An' sparrowgrass full three foote lung, But no " Sweet William I " We'd fost rate trees o' gause an' furze, Wi' plants fer climbin' reaund front durs, An' cowcumbers—rale • Billingers ! ' But no "Sweet William " Grand cabbitches, both white an' red, An' turnups—(Swades)—so it wur said, Ma big ez Sanger's lion's yed I But no "Sweet William!" Eh, lads that wur an awful miss, It railly spoilt eaur neet o' bliss, Wen th' good owd Cheermon mutter't this— " We'n no Sweet William 1" Ile blamed the weather in a tone— Summut betwixt a sigh an' groan— That batter% th' hardest i'tle New Lone, An stopp'd th' "Sweet William I" Wile "Tommy" he wur mitch upset; An, like that horseball an' that Vet, He's sadly trubblet even yet, Witheaut "Sweet William !" SHOCKING CRUELTY.
