div.head: WARRINGTON INDEPENDENT ORDER
div.p: WARRINGTON INDEPENDENT ORDER
OF ODDFE LLOWS.

INITIAPEON OF THE MAYOR. An important and interesting event connected with Warrington Odd fellowship occurred on Mon- day evening at the R-iebuck Hotel, Bridge-st.,when his Worship the Mayor (Alderman Greenall), was initiated as an honorary member of the " Admiral Nelson " lodge. In response to the invitation of the presiding officer of the lodge, a large number of visiting members were present ; in fact we might say that the assembly was representative of the district. For amongst those present we noticed,be- sides the usual lodge officers,Prov. G.M. F. Webster, P.P.G.M. Richardson, P.P.G.M. Norbury, P.P.G.M. Massey, P.P.G.M. J. T. Perry, P.P.G.M. G. Perry, P.P.G.M. Beswick, P.G. P. Mather, P.G. A. Boyle, P.G. W. Bolton, P.G. J. Mather, P.G. W. Mayers, P.G. Barnett (Cadishead), P.G. Fanshawe, P.G. E. Reddish, P.G. J. 11. Sherlock, P.G. Smith, P.G. Dagnall, &c. After the transaction of the ordinary business, a most enjoyable programme was gone through.—N.G. F. J. Whittle proposed the first toast,that of " The Queen and Royal Family," after which P.G. C. Bonehill rendered a song in capital style.—P.P.G.M. Richardson next in- troduced his Worship, who was initiated into the first secrets of Oddfellowship by Pro. G.M. F. Webster.—P.G. Reddish having sung" Alice, where art thou P " was loudly applauded.—Prov. G.M.F. Webster asked the members to join with him in drinking " Health and happinness to our nowly-elected brother." He was proud of the fact that during his term of office he had had the honour of initiating into their order two such esteemed and prominent townsmen as Mr. Greenall and Mr. Pierpoint kwhose initiation, as our readers are aware, took place a few weeks ago). He was sure that if his Worship only exhibited the same energy and interest in Oddfellowship that he did in affairs of the town, they would hays a very valuable member indeed. (Applause.) He was a mem- ber of a family which was intimately connected with Warrington,and he hardly need say that Sir Gilbert Greenall was a member of their Unity. _ . .

After another song by P.G. J. H. Sherlock, Bro. GREENALL rose to respond. He said he could not find words to express himself as he wished. As they knew, his ancestors had been members of the society, and he thought that by following in their footsteps he was only taking up a good precedent. He looked upon it as a great compliment to be allowed to join them in the bonds of their brotherhood, and trusted that he should prove himself worthy of it. His Worship re- marked that politics, he was glad to see, were not al- lowed to disturb their harmony, and said that during his first year of mayoralty, which had just ended, he had endeavoured to the best of his ability, to keep politics in the background in the Council Chamber, and although they had had a very hotly contested election, he did not think anyone would say that he had thrust his opinions forward. (Applause.) He went OR to speak of the benefits of friendly societies, and concluded by thanking one and all most heartily for the kind man- ner ia which they had received him amongst them.

The Chairman-then called on Bro. Waltgr Booth for a song " Let me like a soldier fall," for which he was loudly applauded. The toast of the "Manchester Unity and Board of Directors," caine next, and was submitted by P.G. FANSHAVIN. 'He coupled with it the name of P.P.G.M. J. Emson.—P.G.'s E. Reddish and J. H. Sherlock fol- lowed with a duet,at the conclusion of which the Chair- man announced that the Mayor was obliged to leave, owing to another engagement. P.P.G.M. Joinv ExsoN (corresponding secretary of the district), is responding, expressed his regret that the Mayor had been called away,and said he felt very highly the honour conferred on the Admiral Nelson Lodge in having had the privilege of initiating their worthy chief magistrate.

THE POSITION OF TUB ORD'S. Bro. Emson said on the Ist January, 1892, the unity consisted of 463 districts, comprising 4,954 lodges, and having an aggregate of 695,687 members, showing an increase of 22.614 members on the previous year. On the same date the capital of these lodges (Sick and Funeral Funds only) amounted to £6,981,339 10s., to which he would add the District Funeral Funds, £224,604 10s. id,, or a capital of £7,209,944, shewing an average of £lO 10s. id. per member, and an increase of capital during 1891 of £181,600 Is. 9d. In addition to these funds there were the widows' and orphans' societies, with a capital of £408,991 9s. 3d. ; past grand lodges, £8,753 19s. sd. ; juvenile societies, £70,949 Os 9d.; management funds of lodges, £103,609 14s. 6d. ; man- agement funds of districts, £4,379 ; and benevolent and other funds. £37,831 4s. 3d. ; making a grand total of the capital of the society and its auxiliaries of £7,844,462 Bs. 3d.

div.head: RICEIPTS.
div.p: RICEIPTS.

The amount received for contributions during the year 1891 was £757,535 15s. 10d., showing an increase of £21,220 7s. 10d. There was received for interest dur- ing the same period on the invested capital £266,929 3s. 4d. This gave an average rate of interest of £3 18s. lop. per cent., and was equal to an annual contri- bution of 7s. 11d, per member. An increase was thus shown on the interest account of £9,507 15s. sd. The amount of contributions received under the head of members of other lodges amounted to £37,739 15s. 3d.
PAYMENTS.

During the year 1891, there was paid the sum of £635,535 7s. Yd. to members for sick benefits, being an average payment of 18s. 6d. per member, according to the returns received. The net expenditure on funeral benefits was £151,405 18s. 4d., being a sum equal to 4e. 41d. per member.

_ _ A ARTROSPIECT. During eighteen years (1874 to 1891 inclusive) there has been received by the Manchester Unity the large sum of £14,476,152 14s. ed. for contributions and in- terest, viz. : For contributions, £10,897,838 is. 9d.; for interest, £3,578,314 12s. 9d. ; and that during the same period there had been paid by the Unity for sick benefit £8,222,974 6s. Bd., and for funeral benefits, £2,120,196 13s. 3d.; or a total benefit outlay of £10,344,170 19s. 11d. Although the society had expended during the past eighteen years the very large sum of £10,344,170 19 is. 11d. n sick and funeral benefits, the capital of the sick and funeral funds of lodges and dis- tricts had increased by the sum of £.3,797,446. Refer- ring to the Board of Directors, Bro. Emson endorsed P. G. Fanshawe's remarks, and said that although it would be rather invidious to mention any particular member of the Board, he could not let the present oppor- tunity pass without expressing what the Order owed to their admirable Secretary, Bro: Thomas Collins. He ' thanked them sincerely for coupling his name with the toast. After a humorous song by P.G.F. J. Emson, who had to oblige with an encore, P.P.G.M. Massey pro- posed the toast of the " Warrington District, and Prov. G.M.P. Webster acknowledged the toast, and said that he did not think that he had anything new to tell them, but would quote a few figures to show that although Oddfellowship was not going forward by leaps and bound* in the Warrington district, it was at least doing good solid work. lie said that during the nine years ended December 31st, 1891, the total receipts were £12,742, and the payments £12,044 • whilst the present worth of the district was over £lo:ooo.—After songs by P.G.'s Panshawe end Reddish, P.G. Barnett proposed " The Admiral Nelson Lodge," and P.P.G.M. Massey followed with ene of his Lancashire dialect reci- tations, and was succeeded by Bro. Whittle, N.G. of the Lodge, said it had given him great pleasure to see so many members of other branches present that night. He said no doubt the attendance would have been larger still, if it had not been for the epidemic which was still amongst there. The toast of the visiting brethren having been ably proposed by P.G. C. Bonehlll, and responded to by P.G. Mather, a hearty vote of thanks was accorded to the Chairman, Mr. George Riley, who presided at the piano, and all those who had in any way contributed to the evening's entertainment, a very pleasant meet- ing terminating with the singing of the National Anthem.

div.head: ALLEGATIONS AGAINST A 111011 BAILIFF. ACTION FOR SLANDER.
div.p: ALLEGATIONS AGAINST A 111011 BAILIFF. ACTION FOR SLANDER.

In the Nisi Prius Court at the Manchester Assizes on Tuesday, a case of slander was tried arising out of the recent Parliamentary election at Ashton-under-Lyne. The plaintiff was Mr. W. A. Hyde, chief clerk and high bailiff of the Ashton County Court, and alderman of the borough ; and the defendant, Mr. W. Hamer, is also a member of the Town Council. The slander was con- tained in a speech made by the defendant, who was one of the supporters of the Liberal candidate, in the course of which he stated that a man "occupying a high and responsible position in the counsels of the Conservative party" was making an attempt to prevent Liberals from voting by issuing warrants for their arrest for aebt. This statement was based upon a declaration made by a man named Garner, formerly a bailiff, who had been dischargcd by the plaintiff. Garner alleged that he had refused to execute warrants for the arrest of several persons who were Liberal voters which had 11 been issued from the Ashton County Court at the time of the election. The plaintiff said he had no doubt that the charge was meant to refer to him, and Judge Hughes, the Mayor of Ashton, and other witnesses also said that having read the speech and Garner's declara- tion they had come to the conclusion that the plaintiff was the person referred to. For the defence Garner re- peated the statement he had made in his declaratian,and evidence was given to show that in a batch of warrants issued there were five against Liberals. The jury found a verdict for the plaintiff, and awarded him £l4O dam- ages.

div.head: WIDNES CONSERVATIVF CLUB.
div.p: WIDNES CONSERVATIVF CLUB.

On Monday evening the annual meet:ll of the Conservative Club, was held in the assembly room. Mr. R. Lewis presided, and he was supported on the platform by Mr. S. Upward (treasurer), and Mr. J. Treacy (secretary). Amongst those present were —Messrs. W. T. Husband, J. W. White, W. S. Callen- der, W. Oakden, T. Knowles, J. Palmer, T. Atherton Jun., R. Eastwood, T. Baron, C. Kenyon, T. Thomas, and S. Whitfield. It appeared from the balance sheet, which was read by Mr. Upward that the income for the past year was £315 10s. bid., the principal items in which were—Balance from previous year, £47 15s. Clid. ; subscriptions, £B7 3s. ; donations, Mr. T. C. Edwards Moss, £lO (two years) ; Mr. J. S. Gilliat, M P. £5 ; Lord Cranborue, £5 ; billiards, £95; cards £4 ss. 7d. ; sale of refreshments, £lBO 7s. Sid. ; (less accounts paid for ditto, £157 2s. 30.) ; hire of rooms, £3B. The expenditure included the amount paid to the Club Buildings Committee balance from previous year £47 15s. &id., on account of present year £77 4s. 50., and other items brought the amount up to £274 Os 70. leaving a balance in hand of £4l 9s. 11d. The Chairman, in moving the adoption of the balance sheet, which he thought on the whole was satisfactory, remarked that the club would have been better off by £8 but for the deficit which had to be paid off in connec- tion with the demonstration which was held in honour of Lord Cross. Their receipts had been augmented con- siderably by donations, which amounted to about £2O, against nothing in the previous year. It would, there- fore, appear that their subscription list was falling off, and that was really so, for they had about 50 members less this year than the previous one. He hoped each mem- ber would do his best to keep up the roll of membership. The receipts from the billard tables had increased from 193 last year to Zie this, but the sale of refreshments had decreased from £232 to £lBO, which is supposed showed an improved moral tone of the members. Mr. Oakden asked if an explanation could be given for the falling off of the members. Mr. Eastwood thought the Committee were responsible for not provid- ing more amusements. The balance sheet was adopted. The following officers were-re-elected :—President, Lord Cross ; vice-presidents, Lord Cranborne, Messrs. J. S. Gilliatt, M.P., C. E. Barlow, J. I. Blackburiae, Major Cross, Sir Gilbert Greenall, Messrs. Hornby Lewis, G.W. Moss, G. Pilkington, J.P., L. Pilkington, W. Pilkington, T. C. Edwards—Moss, J. H. Stocke, C. B. Toiler, H.R.D. Willis, C.C., and Mr. Stapleton Bretherton, J.P. The following were elected a committee :—Messrs. T. Baron, W. B. Callender, J. C. Crawford, G. H. Davies, W. Dwerryhouse,W. T. Husband, C. T. Kenyon, T.Knewles, J. Palmer, G. Sayce, S. Upward, H. White, J. White, J. W. White, Dr. Allen, T. H. Thomas, R. Eastwood, T. Easton, R. Lewis, F. Parr, J. P. Kershaw Whitfield,C.ll. Watson, and W. E. Oakden.—Mr. J. Treacy was re- elected secretary on the same terms as last year, and Mr. Upward was elected treasurer.—Mr. Thomas asked if something could not be done to improve matters with regard to municipal elections, &c.—Mr. White suggested that a sub-committee be appointed to look into the matter.—The Chairman thought there ought to be some organisation distinct from that club, as they had no funds they could devote to that object. It was a ques- tion for the burgesses.—The matter was left for future consideration.

div.head: WORCESTER PETITION.-EXTRAORDINARY EVIDENCE.
div.p: THE WORCESTER PETITION.-EXTRA- ORDINARY EVIDENCE.

,1 The hearing of the Worcester election petition began ' on Tuesday, before Baron Pollock and Mr. Justice Wills. The petitioners, two voters, seek to get the election of the Hon. George Allsopp, the Conservative member, declared void, mainly on the grounds of treating and bribery. Mr. Bosanquet, Q C., for the petitioners, held that Mr. Allsopp's sub-agents had been guilty of corrupt practices, for they had provided " tree singsongs," treated voters to supper and drink, and distributed money among the electors. Some remarkable evidence was given. In the petition it is stated that treating took place at no fewer than forty-two public-houses ; and some of the witnesses admitted that they had had free drink, that they had tossed for half-crowns with the landlords and won, and that they had in tavern and cottage on the polling-day received various sums for recording their votes. The price per man was higher in the morning than in the evening, when the quotation was only 3s. 6d. Two voters beckoned into a house found a man standing in front of the fire. Be had 7s. In readiness, 3s. 6d. in each hand. They received the stoney, and where shown out the back way. The trial of the Worcester petition was continued on Wednesday. Extraordinary evidence was given. On the polling-day there was "a free tap," and some of the witnesses confessed that they got so drunk that they did not know what really took place. Others admitted that they received various sums for their votes, and that they were liberally treated as public-houses, one landlord showing a cheque which he had received " to divide " among the electors who called at the inn. Edward Bowen, a Conservative canvasser, who did not deny that he was one of the "swells "of the party, said he had often" stood treat "at football, cricket, and other g*herings, but he had done this in the way of a " stir- rup-cup, and with no thought of influencing the elec- tion.

div.head: OLDHAM MURDER.
div.p: THE OLDHAM MURDER.
MELLOR SENTENCED TO DEATH.

At the Manchester Assizes on Monday, Joseph Mellor, an overlooker in an Oldham mill, was indicted for the murder of his wife, Mary Jane Mellor. According to the evidence, the prisoner and the deceased lived together for some years before they were actually ' married. On the 3rd September last the woman die- appeared, and it was given out by the prisoner that she was en a visit to her mother, who was sick. On the 19th October the police found the body of the woman in the cellar of the house which she and Joseph Mellor had occupied. The body was shockingly mutilated. Mellor was at once arrested, and his reply to the charge was to the effect that the deceased woman was not his wife. In the course of the evidence it transpired that for more than a year before the tragedy Mellor had been courting a young reeler at the mill at which he worked, and that a marriage had been arranged for Christmas next. Mellor was sentenced to death at the Manchester Assizes on Tuesday. In support of the prosecution, evidence was called to show that the prisoner had en- tered into an engagement to marry another woman at Christmas, that he had repeatedly explained the dis- appearance of his wife by making statements to the neighbours which had been proved to be false, that he had posted letters to himself with the object of induc ing people to believe that they were from his absent wife, and that his clothing as well as other articles be- longing to him were stained with blood. For the defence Mr. Cottingham pleaded that the case, resting as it did on purely circumstantial evidence which did not even satisfactorily prove the identity of the body, was too weak to warrant a conviction. After considering the evidence for ten minutes the jury found the prisoner guilty. Before sentence of death was passed upon him, Mellor made a statement to the effect that three-parts of the evidence was false. Without referring to the other weapons which had been suggested as the instru- ments of the murdsr, he strongly denied that one of them—a at iron—had any stains of blood on it. If he were to be hanged that minute, he said, he could swear to their being no blood on the flat-iron.

div.head: ANARCHISTS IN TRAFALGAR SQUARE.
div.p: ANARCHISTS IN TRAFALGAR SQUARE.

Notwithstanding that the Anarchist groups of London had on Saturday abandoned their intention to hold a meeting in Trafalgar-square on Sunday, in order to pro- test against the proposed extradition of their somrade Francois, accused of complicity with Ravachol in the various dynamite outrages in Paris, the square was in the afternoon crowded with people expecting to witness I a demonstration. There was a small nuraber of Anar- chists and Social Democrats present, and also a large I contingent of foreigners, but the majority of the people present had been attracted to the square merely from motives of curiosity. The police were present in formid- able strength, and refused to allow the delivery of any speech. Louise Michel wanted to speak, but the police intercepted her. Despite the viligance of the police there were one or two hasty addresses. One speaker, a Frenchman, stated to a small audience by which he was surrounded that if any harm resulted from the extradi- tion of Francois Londoners would hear of the matter in a forcible and revolutionary way. The police behaved with great tact and forbearance, but the crowd, which at on* time numbered several thousands, did not disperse till dusk.

div.head: PANAMA INQUIRY.
div.p: THE PANAMA INQUIRY.
EXTRAORDINARY ALLEGATIONS.

At the Panama Canal inquiry on Wednesday it was elicited that no fewer than 28 cheques for an aggregate sum of four million francs had been paid by the late Baron de Reinach on behalf of the Company to persons whose names his agent refused to disclose; and evidence was also given that the expenditure on advertising had exceeded 20,000,000 francs. In consequence of the evi- dence given on Wednesday the Vice President of the 'Committee forwarded a request to the Minister of Justice to have the cheques seized.

div.head: T-HE OFFICIALS OF THE LOCAL BOARD.
div.p: T-HE OFFICIALS OF THE LOCAL BOARD.

Alderman Sadler moved a resolution to the effect that the officials and servants formerly in the employ of the Local Board and now in the service of the Corporation be retained and continued in their several offices upon the same terms and subject to like conditions as they held their former offices with the old Local Board.

Councillor G. I. Neil seconded the motion.—Alderman Williamson asked if there was not some provision in the Charter in regard to this matter. Could they make any objection to any of Use servants being taken over ?—The Mayor : I presume you can.—Councillor Shores said the Charter provided an alternative—if the Council did not pass this resolution the officers of the Board would be- come entitled to compensation equal to two years' salary. —Alderman Williamson said it was well to have this thing explained. They would have to continue the old servants, or have new hands raw to the work, which would not be desirable. It was a mistake that each member had not a copy of the Charter so that they would be in possession of valuable information.—The Town Clerk said the printed charters were exhausted. He had,however, a copy, and he quoted from the scheme the clause bearing upon the compensation to officers, if they were not transferred to the Corporation. It appeared that the amount was left to the discretion of I My Lords Commissioners.—Alderman Williamson : I am quite satisfied. I only wish the Council to know the I circumstances under which we take the officials over. I It would be necessary for us to expend a large amount ' et ratepayers' money, in order to discard any of them.— The Mayor: The present officials have proved them- selves efficient so far, and it will be an advantage to this Council to take them over. (Hear, hear.) The motion was carried unanimously.

div.head: STANDING ORDERS AND BOROUGH ARMS..
div.p: STANDING ORDERS AND BOROUGH ARMS..
The drawing up of—St—auding Orders, the adoption of a design for the Borough Arms, and the provision of a Corporate seal were referred to the General Purposes Committee.

div.head: OFFICIAL VISIT TO CHURCH.
div.p: OFFICIAL VISIT TO CHURCH.

The Mayor said he intended to attend St.Paurs Church on Sunday neat, the 4th December. The minister, the Rev. G. H. Garrett, informed him that service would be at half-past ten in the morning, and he (the Mayor) would be glad of the attendance of any Councillors or Aldermen who felt inclined to go to church with him on that morning. It was entirely optional whether any member or all members attended this service. Alderman Wareing said he was much obliged for the kind invita- tion, and he hoped to be able to avail himself of it. (Hear, hear.) The Mayor said it would he convenient if the members met him at the Town Hall at ten o'clock.

div.head: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY . AUTHORITY.
div.p: RUNCORN RURAL SANITARY . AUTHORITY.

The fortnightly meeting was held at Dutton Workhouse on Tuesday. Mr. J. Mclntyre presided, and there were present Messrs. J. Knowles, H. E. Heywood, E. Aaron, J. Baguley, W. Pickering, J. Whitlow, J. Brandreth, W. Turner, T. Lewis, W. Wilkinson, J. M. Williams, Rev. J. W. N. Tanner; J. Ashton (clerk), and G. Ashton (deputy clerk).

„ APPLETON PAROCHIAL COMMITTEE. The minutes of the Appleton Parochial Committee contained a resolution that instructions be given to Mr. Percy Silcock to proceed with the preparation of his estimate and details of scheme for the extension of the sewerage works at Stockton Heath, by connecting the same with ths syphon under the Ship Canal at Twenty Step Bridge.—The Committee had under consideration the outbreak of smallpox, and it was resolved that the consideration of providing accomrnoderation for cases of smallpox be deferred,s.nd that it he an instruction to the medical officer of health that he at once inform the Clerk of any cases notified to him, and that the Clerk thereupon convene a special meeting of the Committee. —The minutes were adopted.

THE VEHICULAR BRIDGE ACROSS THE MERSEY. The Committee appointed to consider the communica- tion of the Runcorn Board of Commissioners, who stated that they had agreed to contribute £30,000 towards the cost ef constructing the Bridge, on the assumpton that the Rural Sanitary Authority would provide a portion of that amount, had held a meeting, but consideration of the subject was deferred.
SMALLPDX The Sanitary Inspector (Mr. Farrington) stated that there were no fresh cases of smallpox in the Authority's district, and the disease was on the decline in Warring- ton.

div.head: GIVING A DEBTOIt A "PICK-ME-UP:
div.p: GIVING A DEBTOIt A "PICK-ME-UP:
TWELVE YEARS' PENAL SERVITUDE.

At Lincoln Assizes, on Tuesday, Alexander Morgan, fishmonger, was indicted for the murder of Tom Morley, milkman, of Gainaborough. Morley owed the prisoner money, and it was alleged that Morgan, incensed be- cause he could not get the sum due to him, stealthily placed strychnine in the niian's drink and poisoned him. The evidence occupied two days. For the defence it was ' contended that Morgan had no intention of murder; that be gave Morley the poison as a " pick-me-up " to sharpen his appetite. The jury returned a verdict of "Manslaughter," and Mr. Jurtice Kennedy, who said there really was no evidence of motive, sentenced the prisoner to twelve years' penal servitude.

div.head: BLACKBURN ATROCITY.
div.p: THE BLACKBURN ATROCITY.
DUCKWORTH BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.

Cross Duc.kworth, —1;1;71s charged with the brutal murder of a little girl named Alice Barnes at Witton, near Blackburn, was taken before the magistrates at the County Police Court at Blackburn on Monday. A large number of witnesses ware called, who swore more or less positively that the prisoner was seen near the scene of the murder, and others stated that they afterwards saw him rushing through the streets, his clothing covered with mud. The case for the prosecution had not been completed when the Court adjourned. ha the examina- tion of Cross Duckworth, at Blackburn, on Tuesday, evi- dence was called to show that the prisoner was near the scene of the murder before and after the crime was com- mitted, and that the impression of a boot-mark found on the soft ground where the struggle appears to have taken place, corresponds exactly with the sole of ?. boot found in his house, and that handkerchiefs similar to that with which the girl was suffocated, were found in his house. The prisoner pleaded not guilty,but reserved his defence. He was committed to take his trial at the Liverpool Assizes.

MEDICAL lALL, ABERDARE, WALES.
THE LARKHILL BURGLARY.
THE PRISONERS wAla THEIR MONEY BACK.

At Liverpool on Monday Thomas Wilson and James Gatten, suspected of being concerned in the Longford Hall burglary, were charged with breaking into the resi- dence of Mr. A. Jones at Larkhill, and stealing £lOO worth of property, chiefly jewellery, belonging to Com- mander Neilson, a guest. The men, it is alleged, are connected with a gang of London burglars who have been ranging Yorkshire and Lancashire and entering country houses by means of ladders while the occupiers were at dinner. The prisoners on their expedition to Larkhill were disturbed by a policeman, who pulled the ladder away and succeeded in arresting them, though they pelted him with furniture. When asked by the magistrates if they had anything to say, the prisoners thought it unfair that their money, necessary for their defence, should have been taken by the police. It was pointed out that the bench was uncertain whether the money found upon them was their own or the proceeds of the burglary, and it was suggested that they should make application for it to the Judge. The prisoners thought that an application then would be rather too late, and were of opinion that the decision of the mag- istrates placed them in a hole.

div.head: CANADA AND "INDEPENDENCE."
div.p: CANADA AND "INDEPENDENCE."

Mr. Mercier, the ex-Premier of Quebec, who was recently tried and acquitted on a charge of dealing improperly with the public funds, has set on foot an agitation for obtaining the independence of Canada. A largeiy attended meeting held at Montreal on Monday night declared in favour of "independence." The President of the French Conservative Club declared in favour of the maintenance of the colonial connection. Delegates from Toronto advocated the political union of Canada with the United States.

div.head: ELECTION PETITIONS.
div.p: THE ELECTION PETITIONS.
ANOTHER SEAT DECLARER VOID.

The trial of the Fiexham election petition concluded on Tuesday. The petitioners sought to get the seat declared void on the ground that Mr. N. G Clayton, the Conservative member, had been guilty of corrupt and illegal practices. Further evidence was called, and the witnesses, examined by council on behalf of the public Prosecutor, admitted that they had given away dinner tickets to benefit the Conservative cause. Mr. Justice Cave in giving judgment strongly condemned Mr. Clayton for hie zarelessness with regard to money no-Ea- ten during the election, said that he had through his agent been guilty of corrupt and illegal practices, and that the seat must be declared void. It would be their duty to schedule Mr. Batey for corrupt and illegal prac- tices, and Mr. Edward Taite and Mr. John Emmerson for corrupt practices. Mr. Justice Willirms concurred, and condemned social gatherings in connection with political associations as pernicious in their influence on voters. The petitioners and the Public Prosecutor were granted costs. •

div.head: FOOTBALL FATALITY.
div.p: FOOTBALL FATALITY.

The Rev. G. U. Knight, late scholar of Selwyn Col- lege, Cambridge, and assistant master at Bronasgrove School, died on Sunday morning from the results of a kick accidentally received whilst playing for the Broms- grove Rugby Football Club against Worcester at Wor- cester on Saturday. In the course of the game Mr. Knight was kicked in the region of the ear, but attached no importance to the injury and went on playing. On Sunday morning he was found dead in bed.

div.head: QUALIFICATION FOR GUARDIAN&
div.p: THE QUALIFICATION FOR GUARDIAN&
REDUC noN TO £.5.

The Local Government Board 17-1-;;;e made an order fixing an annual rateable value of not less than ZS as the rating qualification for Guardians of the Poor in England and Wales. Under the system hitherto exist- ing the qualification varied in different unions. By status it could be no higher than an annual rateable value of £4O, and in some unions it was fixed at that figure ; but in others, for no apparent reason, it was £3O £25, £2O, £l5, and £lO, while it is possible that in a few it was £5. It was found that in some of the poorest perishes the highest qualifications was imposed, while the lowest prevailed in some of the richest ; and as these anomalies could be cured by administrative order, Mr. Fowler has availed himself of his powers to make the qualification uniform.

Conciliation SOME people may have forgotten all in about the Labour Commission ap- Trade Disputes. pointed by the late Government, so great is the obscurity in which it has, for the most part, pursue,4 its own labours. But a fairly diligent perusal of the daily newspaper will show that it still exists, and, indeed, pretty regularly holds a "sitting.' At times evidence which is both interesting and useful is given by one or other of the witnesses who come forward for ex— amination. Of this description was the explana- tion given on Tuesday, by Mr. S. BOULTOK, a timber merchant, of London, relative to the ! formation and working of the London Board of Conciliation. This Board was, it ! seems, formed on the initiative of the London ! Chamber of Commerce, and it consists of twelve members of that Chamber, twelve workingmen who represent as many groups of trades and in- dustries, a delegate from the London County Council (Sir JOHN LUBBOCK), and a Parliamentary representative of labour (Mr. FENWICK). The Board commenced its work with a representation of twenty-five Trades Unions ; in a month they were forty and now there are over sixty. It is claimed that already the Board has done a Con- siderable amount of very useful work. It has been the medium by which many disputes have been compromised or settled while yet in ;heir initial stage, and before any great amount cf ft - tion had been engendered between employer and employed. In a dispute as to wages or piecework, affecting the Amalgamated French Polishers, arbitration was accepted, Mr. BouLroN,Mr. Arnold FORSTER, and Sir John LUBBOCK acting as arbitra- tors. Then, again, a similar course was taken in settling a number of questions in dispute among watermen and lightermen of the River Thames, and in this instance the arbitrators were three workmen and three employers. Of course, in all these cases it depended upon the parties concerned whether or not they accepted the arbitrators, decisions, but the awards had been honourably observed on both sides. Mr. BOULTON, indeed, did not approve of compulsion. As he very justly observed, you cannot compel five hundred men to work against their will. The nearest approach to compulsion that exists is,it appearsin Nova Scotia, where the workers on becoming parties ,o arbitration are bound to deposit a fortnights wages, and the employers an equal amount, which is " confiscated " if the award is not faithfully observed. We are farther told, that voluntary arbitration Boards are established in New Zealand and New South Wales, and in the United Kingdom have been adopted in the towns of Liverpool, Wolverhampton, Aberdeen, Bristol, Birmingham, Bradford, Edinburgh, Leeds, Gloucester, Hull, Cardiff, Dundee, Nottingham, Glasgow, Manchester, Worcester, Exeter, Ply- Wrexham, and Wakefield. In mouth, Cork, France, there is a reovemeat to give legislative sanction to similar methods of dealing with in- dustrial controversies. A Bill is before the French Legislature for the establishment of a Board of A rbitration, but even in this case it is proposed to leave the carrying out of the awards to the honour of the parties concerned.

HURST to the Warrington Alder- manic bench is over, and it has proved an object lesson both to the Liberal party in the Borough and to the ratepaycv: in general. In Mr. MOUNFIELD the Liberals had an excellent candidate—not a mere "showman," but an honest, capable, hard- working, practical business man—ono who has rendered many years of yeoman service to the

Liberal cause in the town and neighbourhood, a "stalwart" who could always be relied upon, and who would certainly be of very good service to the ratepayers of the town if—as we sincerely hope he soon will be—elected to the Town Council. The division in the ranks of the Liberal party, while most deplorable, should net be taken too seriously. To the honour of the Irish electors, we believe it may be safely said that the majority of • them surported the Liberal candidate on Monday. If the Liberals of St. John's Ward will only pull themselves to- gether, they may easily, and at the earliest oppor- tunity, reverse the decision of a few days ago, and they will be most remiss in their duty to them- selves and the party generally if they fail in this respect. But what of the action of the Tory party? What about the compromise? Time was when the Tory party boasted that, individu- ally and collectively, they were " men of honour." It looks as though the "honour" of Warrington Tories in electioneering matters had ceased to be even a "pious opinion." We know that the Tory agent denies that it was part of the "compromise" that the Liberals should have a walk over in the event of a bye-election resulting from the election of Aldermen P But will Alder- man WRIGHT and Alderman Surron also deny it? We think not, and while we admit that their posi- tion has been a difficult one, at the same time they were bound to carry out the terms of agree- ment into which they voluntarily entered. What a howl of indignation there would have been from the Tory press, platform, and Club, if the Liberals had committed such a gross breach of faith. Tricks and dodges of this nature may stiliceed for a., time, but, sooner or later, the party whose leaders, while publicly disavowing all responsibil- ity, yet privately wink at them, will reap such a " whirlwind " of public distrust and contempt as will cripple their power for further evil. There is yet another aspect to this election. What is the result to the town of the recent contest? If any revival of the sad epidemic should follow upon the exposure in a crowded street of Persons still visibly suffering from smallpox, then undoubtedly the whole responsibility will be at the door of the Tories.

The London County Council on Tuesday resolved upon a course of action which is almost sure to bring into prominence a subject of great importance, not only to the metropolis but to all large towns and growing centres of population. _ _ .

On the motion of Mr. STUART, M.P.,and by sixty- six votes to twenty-one, a resolution was passed declaring that the most equitable method of secur- ing the relief of occupying rateilkyers is by the taxation of the ground values of London, and that it was necessary to take immediate action to that end in the next session of Parliament. The Lon- don County Council, when its Bill comes before Parliament, will have an irressistible case if the result is to depend upon argument. Ground values seem to be above all other sources of profit the mostsuitable for municipal taxation. Almost the whole of the value—which is sometimes of enormous magnitude—is given to the ground by the growth of population and industry, and what, therefore; can be said against the taxing of it for the benefit of the community P And if the London County Council is permitted to tap such a source of i ticome there can certainly be nothing said againist the Corporation of Warrington, or of any othei town, having the same right.

THE Hexham election petition has resulted in the unseating of another Tory member of Parlia- ment. The result of the late election in the Hexham division of Northumberland was a sur- prise, seeing how pronounced had been the Liberal majorities at previous contests. But the evidence given before the judges at Newcastle explains much. The Tory candidate, Mr. CLAYTON, was an extremely wealthy man—a millionaire, or very near it—and his generosity in a political direction, and through the gentleman who was his election agent, was quite extraordinary—in fact it was of such a kind that only a millionaire in search of Parliamentary honours could very well afford to indulge it. It was, at all events, of too marked a character for two of her Majesty's judges, jealous of the purity of elections, to approve of, and they have declared the seat void, and scheduled the agent for corrupt and illegal practices. It may, perhaps, be advisable for local Primrose Leagues to notice that Mr. Justice WILLIAMS stigmatised political picnics and festivities as pernicious, and expressed a hope that one of the results of that inquiry would be to put an end to them.

ARCHBISHOP WALSH has declared in favour of bi-metallism as a remedy for the difficulties of Irish agriculturalists, and this declaration, follow- ing upon the speech of Mr. BkLFOUR, in Manches- ter, a few weeks ago,will,we are told by some peo- ple,bring the quostion "within the range of practi- cal politics." But when that time comes there will be a good deal more said about bi-metallism than has yet been said. For instance, in what way will bi-metallism improve the position of Irish farm- ers ? By raising the price of agricultural pro- duce of every description. But then comes in the consideration that there are other people to .be taken into account besides farmers, whether Irish or English. If bi-metallism is to raise prices all round, it simply means that those who produce commodities will get more money for what they have to sell, while those who have to live on a fixed income—that is to say, practically the whole body of wage-earners, of annuitants, and of those who derive their income from shares and invest- ments—will have to pay more for what they bay.
There is no magic about bi-metallism, although

some of its advocates appear -to think that we only have to adopt it to get rid of most of the evils of the present commercial system. It is no process of alchemy by which additional wealth is to be created in some facile and mysterious way. All that it can do is to transfer some of the annual wealth of the country from one pocket to another, or rather from the pocket of one person to that of another. Mr. BALFOUR contended that gold had appreciated in value thirty or thirty-five per cent. during the last sixteen years—in other words, that a sovereign will now buy thirty or thirty-five per cent. more than it did in 1876. Supposing then that, by the adoption of bi-metallism, the purchasing power of the sovereign was reduced to the level of 1876, it would no doubt be an excellent thing for the farmer or any other pro- dhcer, for he would get at least four pounds foi that which he now sells for three. But it would be bad for the labourer whose pound a week would go no f.trther than fifteen shillings do at pre- sent, and for the skilled artizan whose two pounds per week would not be equivalent to thirty ; shillings at the present run of prices. TEIDAVES AND SHOPDREAKERS AT W/DNES. At the Widnes Petty Sessions, on Thursday, Eleanor ' Holland, 16 years of age, formerly employed by Mrs. W. G. Bucknall, Victoria-road, as a domestic servant, was charged with stealing a number of articles of clothing I and 17s. 6d. in money.—Mr. Knowles defended.—Mr. Knowles said it was a very sad case. The girl was a native of Nottingham, and came to Liverpool to a home until she got a situation. Mrs. Bucknall told her to pack up her box and be gone, and in the hurry he sug- gested that the articles, which really did belong to Mrs. Bucknall,had been put into defendant's box by mistake. The girl said she had no intention of stealing. If she was sent to prison it would most likely be the means of driving her on the streets.—The Bench said it was a hard case, and they would deal as leniently as possible with her, and fine her 10s. The fine was immediately paid by the girl's sympathizers.—Six boys, named Patrick Kelly (13), Pitt-at. ; Thomas Kelly (14), Peel-st. ; I Patrick Fox (15), Cromwell-st. ; John Fox (14). RECITAL OF " CHRISTMAS CAROL' AT RUNCORN.

Under the auspices of the Runcorn Women's Tempe- rance Society, Mr. John Harwood of Manchester,gave a recital of Dickens' " Christmas Carol," to a large and appreciative company io Bethesda Lecture Hall, on Thursday evening. Mr.E. Wynne Humphreys presided, i and delivered a short introductory speech, n which he mentioned the good work the society was doing, and gave a cordial invitation to any lady desirous of helping them. The Christmas Carol is too well known to need description. The various characters and scenes in the great novelist's gem were pourtrayed with conspicuous ability. There was no striving after effect, yet tke effect was there : the reciter was natural throughout, and he carried with him the sympathies of his auditory. If you want a lusky wedding ring go to 51, Hrou-isr.,wisers yam will get a present with it.—Aost. - A WIDNES PICTURE FRAME DEALER AND HER RAILWAY

TRAVBLLING. Before Mr. G. L. Wigg and Dr. Steele. at Runcorn Petty Sessions, on Monday, Kate Thomas' picture frame dealer, Widnes-road, Widnes, was charged with attempt. leg to defraud the London and North-Western Railway Company be travelling from Northwich to Runcorn without having paid her fare.—Mr. W. J. Bland, solid. tore department,Lime-st.,Station, prosecuted and Mr. J. W. Knowles defended.—ln opening the case Mr. Bland described it as a most deliberate attempt to defraud the Company. On the 21st October Mrs. Thomas and her little daughter attended the market at Northwich, and returned in the evening by the 6.25 train from North- wich. On arrival at Widnes she told the ticket collector "one and a half from Runcorn," and she paid him and left the station. The deteczive.Thomas Goode, who had been set to watch the woman, followed her, and as she was getting into a cab he went up to her and said "Where are your tickets from Northwich to Runcorn ?" She replied "I gave it up at Runcorn." The detective said "not to-night," and she still contended that she had, until pressed further, when she said "I hadn't time to get tickets, but I will pay now." The detective informed her she was then too late, and asked" Why did not you pay the collector when you came out of the gate ?" She replied "I forgot it."—Mr. Knowles for the defence. described the defendant as a poor widow with four chil- dren, and appealed to the Bench to deal leniently with her, as she had no intention of defrauding, but had acted as she had, in a mcment of forgetfulness.—The Bench considered the case a very cleat one,and imposed a fine of 20s. and costs 10s. 6d. DEATH OF MR. JAMES RAY, OF ST. HELENS.

The many friends of Mr. James Ray, the licensee of the Royal Hotel, Westfield-st., St. Helens, will regret to hear of his death, which took place some- what suddenly at an early hour on Sunday Morning. He was a very robust man, and was generally re- garded as being very healthy. In the early part of last week he complained of pains in his stomach, but on Wednesday he became very ill. Dr. Donnel- lan was called in, but despite his every effort he gradually sank, and becoming unconscious, died at one o'clock on Sunday morning, the immediate cause of death being congestion of the brairi. De- ceased, who was 46 yeaiS of age, came from War- rington nine years ago, and became the licensee of the George Hotel, Brook-st. On the death of Mr: J. Ashcroft, three years ago, he became the licensee of the Royal Hotel. He leaves a widow and six young children to mourn his loss. The funeral took plaa-on-Wednesday at Sankey.
