That the meeting of Widnes Town Council on Monday was of the "cut and dried " order, each member had his motion prepared for him and he dutifully moved or seconded as the case might be and business which would otherwise have taken three hours was carried through in a quarter of an hour.

That a short discussion arose on the reappoint- ment of the officials of the Local Board, as corpor- ate servants from which it appeared that 'the Council had two alternatives—either to continue them in their positions or compensate them.
That the officiials are worthy of their positions on the consideration of merit alone.
That now that the qualiacation ot Gaardians is reduced from £25 to £5 we may expect a tine and large crop of candidates at the next election.

That the analysis of the towns water by Dr. Carter Bell requires further explanation. To be described as " good " to one public body and not fit fc.r such a town to another is if not alarming, at all events, far from promoting confidence and the subject should be probed to the bottom.
That it would scarcely do for the -Commissioners to purchase a brine spring for a water supply. That the election of Runcorn School Board will take place at the end of the present month.
That Mr. 11. IV. Deacon has been again unani- mously appoiwed Chairman or the Widnes Free Library Committee and Mr. F. Neil, the vice- chairman. 44.4: s b. 4,1

CO-OPERATION IN WIDNES AND .1 RUNCORN. In connection with the Widnes branch of the Runcorn Co-operative Society a tea party and entertainment was held in Lacey-et., schoolroom, Widnes, on Tuesday evening last. Abovt 350 per- , sons partook of the capital repast provided, their wants being attended to by Mesdames Cooper,Moss Connor, W. Betney, Spencer. Williams, Poole, Plinstone R. Rogerson, Elardman, Dodd, Carter, Brown, and Moores. Misses Hannah Betney, Plinstone, and Roger- son. At the subsequent entertainment the room was crowded, and Mr. T. Riley of Runcorn presided. In his brief address, the chairman advocated the principles of co-operation congratulated the members the local society upon its floursshing condition. During an inter- val in the programme, Mr. Worthington delivered an address in which he urged his hearers not to allow their co-operation to stop at buying their goods at the store and receiving their dividend at the end of the half year but to really live up to the principles of co-operation,and 'to feel that they were members of one brotherhood, combined together to help one another. (Applause.) He mentioned that the share capital of the society was £40,200 made up entirely of the savings of workingpeople and the takings of the society during the last half-year were £40,000. He drew attention to extensions in the business carried out by the directors and concluded by moving a vote of thanks to the ladies who had presided at the tables and to all those who had taken any part in making the gathering a success.—Mr. Rogerson seconded the motion, which was carried by acclamation. The programme was as follows:—" With Is ugh and song," glee party; duet " A B C," Mr. Betney senior and Mrs. Betney junior; song "The white squall," Mr. Price; recitation, "The newsboy's debt," Miss Davies; song and chorus "Clementine," Mr. Withington ; chorus by Messrs. Jno. Betney, W. Roach, and W. Morris (en- cored) ; song "Anchored," Mr. Leathweod ; song "Pil- grim of love," Mr. Lacey; recitation " Jno. Maynard," Miss Harrison; song and chorus "Cookies and mussels," Mr. Withington ; song "The hero of the war," Mr. Price; recitation "Respectable Man," Mr. T. Saunders (encored); song "When the flowing tide comes in," Miss Betney ; songs "The Star of Bethelem " and "The lost chord," Mr. stacey. The accompanist was Miss Palmer. A vote of thanks to the Chairman was accorded on the motion of Mr. Watson' seconded by Mr. Betney, and the proceedings concluded with the national anthem.

div.head: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. 1 RAPHAEL TUCK AND SONS' CHRISTMAS CARDS.
div.p: RUNCORN BOARD OF COMMISSIONERS. 1 RAPHAEL TUCK AND SONS' CHRIST- MAS CARDS.

The monthly meeting was held at the Town Hall, on Thursday morning. Mr. F. ‘'ciswall presided, and there were present Messrs. W.Fisher,J. Meadow- croft. J. W. Lightburn; J. Pritchard, B. Abel, H. Coward, P. Smith, T. Lea, S. Taylor, D. Bisbrown, E. W. Humphreys, W. Leach, W. Hankins-on. F. A. Lake (law clerk), B. Marshall (secretary), and Barker (surveyor).

HEALTH OF THE TOWN. The Medical Officer reported that during November there were 22 deaths,of which one was an inquest case, and of the remaining deaths 4 were due to phthisis, 2 to diart..xa, 2 to pneumonia, 2 to convulsions, 3 to mesen- teric disease, 2 to heart disease, and 1 each to cancer, diabetes, enteric fever, natural decay, meningitis, and disease of the liver. The 22 deaths represented an aver- age death rate for the twelve months of 13.2, and, ex- clusive of the inquest case,of 12.6 of the estimated popu- lation. In view of the prevalence of smallpox in the neighbouring towns, he strongly urged re-vaccination in all cases above the age of ten years.—The Chairman said it was a very satisfactory report.—The Doctor re- marked that it was an exceptionally satisfactory report. AN IMPROVEMENT.

The Highways and Buildings Committee reported that the Surveyor having submitted a plan of a proposed street to be called Balfour-street whereby the junction with the Holloway is considetably improved, and which alteration Mr. J. A. Johnson is prepared to make on condition that the Commissioners relieve him of one half of the expense of making Balfour-street as tar as it is co-extensive with the land of the Railway Company, it is recommended that the amended plan be passed on the above-named terms, subject to the confirmation of such terms by letter. Estimated cost, inclusive of sewering, £l2o.—Mr. Taylor, in moving the adoption of the minute, said the alteration would be a graat public improvemant.—Mr. Fisher seconded.—The Chairman concurred.—After some discussion the minutes were passed. HEALTH COMMITTEE. The Nuisance Inspector had reported a number of nuisances, and notice had been ordered to be served. The General Purposes Committee recommended that an additional lamp be fixed in Picow-st. (bottom of Sails- bury-st.), and one in Pig-lane.—ln moving the adoption of the minutes, Mr. Hankinson said the Committee had had under consideration atar places, but the Gas Co. refused to lay mains.—Mr. Lightburn said any reason- able request of the Board ought to be an obligation on the part of the Gas Co. to fulfil. He protested against anyone making use of a monopoly against the interests of the people.—The Chairman said if the gas service was within 50 yards of the place where the light was re- quired the Gas Co. was compelled to supply its—The minutes were approved.
THE FREE LIBRARY.

The Free Library Committee recommended that 60 volumes be sent to the binders for rebinding ; that the Library be opened for the issue of books every Wed- nesilay afternoon from two o'clock to four o'clock, and that the salary of the librarian be increased by £5 per annum.—Mr. Bristirown moved adoption.—Mr. • Smith aeconded, and suggested that the local printers and bookbinders should ha-ve an opportunity of doing this work. At present the rebinding was done out of the town.—Mr. Humphreys said it was a special and dur- able kind of binding which could only be obtained at one place.—Mr. Smith said the Committee could obtain the same binding from the local tradesmen at the same price.—Mr. Meadowcroft did not think the Committee had gone far enough. The Library was open three nights a week from 7 to 9 p.m., and young girls and grown up i people were to be seen huddled up n the passage, and it was almost impossible t 4 get into the reading room. He suggested that the Library should be open one hour each afternoon and from 6 'o'clock to 8 o'clock each night. This would make very little extra work for Mr. Jones, while it would be a very great convenience to the ratepayers and to the students at the science and art classes. He moved that the minute be referred back to the Committee with a view to affording better facilities to the public.—Mr. Leach seconded the amendment, which was carried.
FINANCE.
The Finance Committee reported that the receipts amounted to £3Bl ss. 9d., and accounts amounting to £466 9s. 3d. were recommended for payment.—Carried.

We are told that this is "The golden age of Christmas cards ", and we may well believe it when the:demand is so vast and varied as to make it worth the while of a firm like that of Messrs. Raphael Tuck and Sons, to turn out so many novel- ties as they have done for the season now so near at hand. The variety of cards and souvenirs of one kind and another is so infinite that it is impossible to partioularize them. They will, we should think, suit every pocket,the poorest as well as the richest, and gratify every taste. They are in every imagin- able style of design, and embellished and repro- duced by every known process of reproduction. The results have been attained only by the employ- ment of precious metals of every shade, and bronzes of every hue, to aid and enrich the effect of the most perfect and artistic colour work. It is a truly " golden collection '' and it is not easy to imagine a more graceful or acceptable Christmas or New Year's souvenir On would be many of those sent out by the eminent firm of art publishers referred to.

div.head: VACANCY ON THE BOARD.
div.p: THE VACANCY ON THE BOARD.

Mr. W. Hankinson moved that Mr. H. J. Grice be ap- pointed to fill the vacancy caused by the resignation of Mr. W. B. Wass. Mr. Grice was highly qualified for the position.—Mr. Taylor seconded.- -They knew the value of Mr; Grice's service on that Board in the past, and lie (Mr. Taylor) would be pleased to see him on the Board again.—Mr. Smith supported the motion, and the Chairman said it would be a very gracious act to Place Mr. Grice in the vacancy. His extreme attention to his duties, particularly while Chairman of tlie Board, called for 'their gratitude, and they had a means now of acknowledging those services.—The motion was carried unanimously.

MISCHLLANEOI79. The agreement with the Runcorn Waterworks Co. was sealed ; the tender of Thomas Rathbone, of Stretford, to supply a new nightsoil. manure boat for £390 was ac- cepted, and communications from the Local Govern- ment Board re the unemployed ana the outworkers under the Factory and Workshops Acts wet° referred to committee.

! ' Mr. James Pritchard sail he understood that vessels ' coming up the Ship Canal with cargoes for Runcorn during neap tides were charged dues, and that they were also charged dues durine; spring tides if they came along the canal without previous arrangement with the Ship Canal Company ; while vessels coming to Weston Point ,with cargoes for the Weaver Trustees and to Ellesmere Port. were allowed to traverse the canal free from dues or tolls. If this were so it was a breach of the I understanding which the commissioners had with the Ship Canal Company, and also contrary to the Ace of ' Parliament. Pcrhaps Mr. Meadowcroft, the local agent to the company, could enlighten them. Mr. Meadow- croft said, so far as his knowledge went, Mr. Pritchard had practically stated what was correct so far as Run- corn was concerned. Whatever might be the practice of the Weaver Trustees or the authorities at Ellesmere Port, he did not know. During neap tides, under the old condition of affairs, vessels would have had to stop at Liverpool several days waiting for tides to bring them up to Runcorn, bat they could now come up the Ship Canal without delay, and that was the reason the charge was made.—Mr. Pritchard argued that Runcorn was entitled to the same exemptions as Ellesmere Port and the Weaver Trustees, or at any other port on that section of the canal. Tnis was an important matter, and had a most serious bearing upon the shipping trade of the port of Runcorn. He moved that a c.smmunica- tion be written to Mr. Collier, the general manager of the Ship Canal at Manchester, drawing attention to this state of affairs, and asking for it to be remedied. —Mr. Lightburn seconded the motion, which was i carried.

div.head: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.
A meeting of this Council will be held on Tues- day evening next, when, amongst other business the following matters will be submitted. CLOSING INSANITARY HOUSES.

The Health Committee have passed the following resolution : —That the Town Clerk be instructed to take the necessary proceedings under the Housing of the Working Classes Act, 1890, for the closing of the follow- ing houses, such houses having been certified by the Medical Offier of Health to be unfit for human habita- tion :-94, 96, 93, 100, 102, 104, 106, 108, 110, 112, 114, 11.6, 118, and 120 Pierpoint-st. THE DEPOTS.

! The Sanitary Works-6-0-m-Mitt-e-e-bave decided that the two intercepting depots be connected by telephone with the depot at Longford. THIS WATER SUPPLY. The Town Clerk of Liverpool having written to say that the Water Committee there are in a position to supply water from the Vyrci/vy Aqueduct, the Warring- ton Town Clerk has been instructed to inform the Cor- poration of Liverpool that a supply of water from the Vyrnwy Aqueduct was not now required, and that there is no prospect of a supply being required.

ALONG HOLIDAY. The General Purposes Committee have passed a resolu- tion that Mr. Charley the borough treasurer (owing to ill-health) be allowed six months' leave of absence from his duties. NVEIAT COUNCILLORS ALLOW THEMSELVES. The General Purposes Committee have also resolved that members of the Council be allowed £2 per day and first-class railway fares when engaged in London on Corporation business, and first-class fares and out of pocket expenses when so engaged elsewhere outside the borough. THE COST OF MARINO STREETS. _

Councillor ROBERTS has given notice that lie will move the following resolution—" That it be an instruction to the Finance Committee as and from March 25th next to declare the expenses incurred in the making of private streets, whenever a majority of the ownnrs of tho pro- perties abutting on such streets may desire it, to be private improvement expenses, and to make such arrangements as may be necessary for allowing to the owners of the property referred to a period not exceed- ing five years for the payment of their apportionments of the cost of such private improvements."

TENDERS ACCRETED. The Health Committee have accepted the tender of Messrs. Manlove, Alliott and Company, Limited, for the supply of a Washington Lyon's patent steam disinfec- tor, at £282; and that of the Grantham Crank and Iron Company, Limited, to supply a vertical boiler, eight h.p., for £45. The Sanitary Works Committee have accepted tender of Mr. T. Stanley Carter for the supply of provender for the next three montps ; and that of Mr. Thomas Pilkington to supply horse-hire for 16 weeks at 7s. per day (man and horse).—The Paving and Sewer- age Committee recommend that, the tender of Messrs. James Barker and Son for 100 gullies and grids, at 13s. each, be accepted ; and also that the tender of the War- rington Slate Company, Limited, to supply 5,000 blue bricks, at 455. 6d. per 1,000 be accepted.—The Town Hall, Park and Baths Committee have accepted the ten- der of Mr. Stephen Moss to supply a patent cylinder boiler for the Town Hall at £l9 10s.

div.head: SHIP CANAL.
div.p: THE SHIP CANAL.
ANOTHER 'FATALITY AT RUNCORN.
LIABILITY ACKNOWLEDGED.

On Monday, a stonemason named Walter Thomas, of Wivern Place, Runcorn, met with his death on the Ship Canal works, at Old Quay docks, Runcorn. Thomas was lying on his stomach, setting a stone in an awkward position, when a bucket which was being swung overhead by a crane became re- leased from the hooks of the chain, and fell upon him, breaking his back, and dislocating his neck. Dr. McDougall was quickly on the spot, and he said death must have been instantaneous. Tlie inquest was held on Wednesday morning, at Runcorn Police Court. Mr. .1. E. Worsley, coroner, conducted the proceedings, and Mr. P. A. Lake appeared on behalf of the Ship Canal Company. At the outset Mr. Lake admitted the Company's liability for compensation to the widow and four children of the deceaseet On the Company's behalf he expressed extreme regret that the accident should have happened. The Coroner and jury visited the scone of the accidont.—Catherine Thomas, 30, Penketh Lane, sister-in-law to the deceased, deposed that he was 43 years of age.—John Kelly, 7, Mill-st., mason's labourer, said he saw the accident. The deceased told him to help to empty " compo " out of the bucket of a travelling crane, and be did so. He saw the bucket drawn up afterwards and he stooped down to clean some " compo " from his shoes. When he turned round he saw the bucket lying on the ground, and the deceased was just falling into the foundations, but he seized hold of his leg and prevented him.-13y the Coroner: The nips were used for lifting the bucket as well as stones ; they did not use a hook.—By. Mr. C. Dutton (Juryman) : So far as he knew the bucket did not strike anything ; the crane was just "jibbing' round. He had never seen a bucket slip from the " clips."-13y Mr. Lake: If they were lifting " compo" alternately they would use the" clips" for both. —Mr. Lake explained that they would lift ten stones to one bucket of " cornpo." John Green, 10 Vine-st., labourer at the crane, said the. cranernan heaved up the bucket, and swung round the jib, when the bucket fell down. He could not say how it was the bucket fell.—By Mr. Dutton : He fastened the clips all right to the bucket. He might as well have been in danger as the deceased, but he supposed "it was not his time."—One of the clips had bees to the blacksmith's to be repaired and it was more square than the other.—By Mr. Lake: He had worked at a crane for years, and he never knew an accident happen before with clips and buckets.—By the Coroner : He thought , clips were as safe as a hook.—Mr. Gregory (juryman) said the bucket had slipped in the clips that morning I when it was lifted. John Phillips, 23 Viaduct-st., Wid- nes, engine driver, said he was in charge of the crane at which the accident occurred. He was reversing the I crane when the bucket left the clips. The deceased I was lying tilt on his stomactionaking good a joint, and 1 the bucket struck him on the side. In answer to the coroner, witne.ss said there was no jerk of the crane whatever ; there was no strain put upon the gearing to 'cause a jerk. He had used these clips for four months 1, and not • a bucket or a stone had slipped from them 1 before. It was the custom to shift buckets with clips. He could not explain why the bucket fell out.—By a jury- man : One clip Was more square than the other was curved.-13y Mr. Lake: There was a hook as well as clips provided. The hook was for lifting buckets.— Evan D. Jones, agent for Runcorn section, said he had examined the clips. One as much straighter than the other. He considered the straight one was not in pro- per form for lifting a bucket. A curved one would be better. A hook was the proper appliance for lifting a bucket,and one was provided ; but it was customary to use clips in the work in which the men were engaged. If the workmen had called the attention of the cfficials to the fact that this clip was dangerous it would have been remedied at once.—Humphrey Richards, foreman, said he had been on public works for 50 years, and had never known a similar accident to occur before. The men never reported to him that anything Was amiss.— The Coroner directed the jury as to the considerations which should guide them in arriving at their verdict, and the jury,after a short canference in private,return- ed a verdict of accidental death, and added that Hwy were under the impression that one of the clips was strained, and that Green ought to have drawn the attention of the foreman to it.—Green said he WAS net aware that it was strained.

div.head: FRODSHA.II,
div.p: FRODSHA.II,

UNION CHURCH SOCIAL AND LITERARY SOCIETY.—OR Thursday evening, Mr. Arthur Rigby read a paper on "The life and times of Oliver Cromwell." TEMPERANCE SUNDAY.—At the several places of wor- ship in Frodsham, reference was made to the great tem- perance question, and total abstinence advocated, elo- quent sermons being preached at the Union Church by the Rev. C. Craddock, and at the Free Church by the Rev. R. Trotter.

Nnw RATES.—At the FrAsharn Petty Sessions, on Wednesday, the maeistratas affixed their signatures to a new poor rate of 101. in the £, estimated to realise £523 18+. 5i.. and a sanitary rate of 4d. in the £, to produce £l4B 16i. 1011., for the township of ',rod- sham.

The rAELSIT CHURCIL—A special service was held in the above church, on Wednesday Peening. in commemo- ration of the tenth anniversary of the opening of the church after restoration, when the Right Reverend the Lord Bishop of S. Asaph preached to a large congrega- tion. The offertory taken at this service was in aid of the fund for the new boys' school, and realised £l9 Os. 11d. SERVICE OF SONG.—A service of song, entitled " Moses," was given in the Methodist Free Church on Sunday afternoon, the musical portions being rendered by the choir, accompanied by the members of Miss Thomas's string hand and the organ, at which latter in- strument Mr. Peter Earlam prosided. The connective readings of Vas history were read by Mr H. Lewis,and altogether the service was a great success. In the even- ing, after a short address by the Rev. R. Trotter, a musical programme of sacred pieces, including sang's, duets, and choruses, were rendered and much enjoyed. ASSAULT ON A SCECOOL ATTENDANCE OFEICER.—At the Petty Sessions On Wednesday Win. Jones, of Newtown, was summoned for assaulting George Jones, school attendance officer and rate collector, on the 19th Nov- ember ; and also for doing damage to his clothing to the amount of 7s. 6d.—Complainant was in Bridge-lane with the rate book, when the defendant met him and used abusive language because he had made complaints respecting his son's irregular attendance at school. Defendant hit him repeatedly, took the rate book from bitn,and threw it into a field. A lad fetched the book,and defendant then jumped upon it. After that complain- ant put defendant on the floor. Whilst there his assail- ant out his thumb into his mouth and tried to tear his cheek.—Defendant expressed his regret for what he had done.—A fine was imposed of 10s. and 103. 6d. costs for the assault, and he was ordered to pay the costs in the second case.

OPENING OE THE NEW ENDOWED Scuocm.—On Wed- nesday afternoon the Bishop of Chester opened the new ' Frodsliam Boys' (Endowed) School. The building is of brick, with Ruabon stone dressings, erected in accor- dance with plans of Messrs. C. Linaker and S. Davies, It is capable of accommodating about 300 scholars, and the estimated cost is £1,300. It occupies the seat of the old school built in 1824. The contractor was Mr. Thos. Davies. At the opening ceremony there was a large attendance. In performing the opening ceremony, the I Bishdp drew attention to the fact that the school hadbeen opened in the faith e f Jesus Christ and in the name of the Holy Trinity,and remarking that the mischief was being done by the effort to obtain undenominational education said the friends of undenominational teaching, he con- sidered, were the enemies of their Lord's divinity, and I therefore should stand their ground very firmly. In that school the members of the Church of England were able to teach the doctrines they themselves believed and he was quite certain that they would be equally zealous to afford fair play tor religious teaching by their Nonconformist brethren who conscientiously differed from them and were willing to have appliances for religious teaching. Fair play on all sides was better than reducing themselves to what was essentially a sham.

The Macclesfield and District Chamberof Agriculture on Tuesday passed a resolution calling the attention of the President of the Board of Agriculture to the present extensive adulteration of cheese and butter, and urging that not only should the law on this matter be more stringently enforced, but that the making up of adulterated cheese and butter in a distinctive form should be made compulsory.

div.head: SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC
div.p: THE SMALLPDX EPIDEMIC
AT WARRINGTON.
We are happy to say that the improved condition of things so far as this epidemic is concerned con- tinues. The following is the report of the Medical Officer of Health up to last night :
Hope Hospital, Dallam-lane, Warrington, Dec. 2, 1892. Cases smallpox since Friday 25th ult 21 Admitted to Hope Hospital Discharged Dead At present in Hospital 139
One death has occurred from the disease outside the hospital. ANOTHER VISIT OF A LOCAL GOVERNMENT BOARD INSPECTOR.

Dr. Saville, the medical gentleman appointed by the Local Government Board, to conduct An In- vestigation on the subject of the epidemic has arrived in the town. We are informed by Dr. Gornall that he is satisfied that all has been done that could be done under the Pre- sent conditions, to cope with the outbreak. During yesterday he not only had a conference with Dr. Gornall, but also visited the Aikin-stree hospital and the Hope hospital, and paid a visit to the Mayor. The Health Committee have resolved to discontinue vaccination at the various stations on and after to-day (Saturday), but the public vaccinator will for the next month, in addition to attending as usual on Tuesday afternoons at Got- borne-street school, attend at the same place every Tuesday night, at 7 p.m. and at the office of Dr. Gornall in the Town Hall every Friday afternoon at 2 o'clock. This arrangement is in accordance with a resolution sanctioned by the Board of Guardians. THE RECOMMENDATIONS OF THE LOCAL

div.head: GOVERNMENT BOARD INSPECTOR. .. .
div.p: GOVERNMENT BOARD INSPECTOR. .. .

- The following are the recommendations which were made by Dr. T. W. Thompson, the inspector of the Local Government Board, who lately visited the town: —l. Further accommodation for the isolation of persons suffering from smallpox should at once be provided, but such accomodatien should be as far as possible removed from any inhabited dwellings—at least a mile, in fact, from any village or other centre of population. 2. Any further additions to the Staff of Inspectors of Nuisances that may be found necessary during the stress of the epidemic, to ensure the prompt disinfec- tion of houses, bedding, &e., should be made without delay. 3. At all times, bt.t especially when epidemic disease is prevalent, it is important that all conditions which may possibly impair general health should be abated. From the Medical Officer of Health I gather, in answer to my question, that the Scavenging Staff 14 n rstroog enough to ensure the removal of exerem.eit .tnd refuse from the neighbourhood of dwellings at sufficiently frequent intervals. Under those circumstances the staff should certainly be increased. 4. Main reliance, however, as rega ris Ow aas. of the epidemic must be placed upon efficient vai.t,ti in and re-vaccination,and on this subject f have addressed a communication to the Guardians. In si far, however as the Sanitary Anthority sae their way to indirectly promote the cause el vaccination and re vaccination they should do so.

div.head: LYMM. PLWARD -A CORitEMON.
div.p: THE LYMM. PLWARD -A CORitEMON.

Sir,—l beg to correct the erroneous impression which seems to be general,that I am the Medical Officer of Health for Lymm, and author of, the famous placard Cr. rn- ing the smallpox epidemic, which has subjected me to various unpleasant attacks and remarks. This confusion of names has occurred frequently before, and I now wish it to be distinctly understood that we are two entirely different medical men, of the same name. lam not, and never have been, Medical Officer of Health of Lymin district, and had nothing whatever to do with the poster prohibiting dealing with Warrington people or their goods. I may also contradict the rumour that I had a smuggled case of smallpox in my household. I have not had any sickness (not even from vaccination) in my family for 18 months. By inserting this in Satur- day's issue, you will oblige yours sincerely,
E. A. FOX. Rylands-st., Warrington, December 2nd, 1892.
EARLESTOWN.

Since our last issue there has been no further out- break of smallpox in Newton or Etrlestown. The three eases which have occurred, and with which prompt measures were taken, are progressing very favourably. The medical men have been kept very busy during the past fortnight, and a large number of the inhabitants have been re-vaccinated. It is felt however, that the action of the authorities in dealing with the cases as they cropped up, has effectually checked the spread of the disease, and it is safe to infer that there is no fur- ther cause for alarm, HAYDOCK.

On Sunday another case of smallpox was reported at Haydock, by Dr. Dowling. On Dr. Hayward, the medical officer of health for Haydock, visiting, the house reported affected, he found the patient was a girl, and on diagnosing the case, he pronounced it one of chicken ' pox only. A peculiar difficulty has now arisen. Dr. Dowling maintains that the case is one of smallpox, but Dr. Watkins, the medical officer of health for Newton agrees with Dr. Hayward that it is only chicken pox, and thus the usual measures in case of smallpox have not been adopted. Dr. Dowling feeling certain that his opinion is the rig,lit one, and that the other medical men are wrong, threatened to report the matter to the Local Government Board, and we understand he has done so. How the difference will be settled remains to be seen. We may state until very recently Dr. Dowling was assistant to Dr. Hayward, and has now opened up a practice u his own account in Ilaydock. SMALLPDX AT LYMM. The smallpox epidemic is still prevalent in Lymm to a large extent, several fresh cases havin,; been reported since last week, but there have beeu no more deaths from this cause.
ST. PAUL'S PAROCHIAL ROOM-, WIDNES.

With the object of raising £l,OOO towards the cost of the new parochial room in Widnes-road, a three days' bazaar was commenced in that building, on Thursday afternoon. The room had been:appropriately decorated, and there were six stalls well filled with an assortment of useful and ornamental articles. The stalls were pre- sided over as follows :—Mrs. Deacon's stall : Mrs. Deacon, Mrs. Brock, Miss Carey, Miss Nun, Miss Smart, Miss I Nolan, Miss Deacon, Miss H. J. Deacon ; Mrs. Garett's stall - s. Garrett, Mrs. Edaards, Mrs. J. Williams, Mrs. Wharton, Mrs. G. Davies, Mrs. MacLennan, Miss Kate Garrett, Miss Timmins ; Mrs. F. Neil's stall : Mrs. Neil, Mrs. Mitchell, Mrs. Paliu, Mrs. Hughes, Miss Gill, Miss Wilkinson, Miss Gibson, Miss Baker, Miss White ; Mrs. Irnison's stall : Mrs. Imison, Mrs. Dwerryhouse, Mrs. Brookes, Miss Maggie Jones, Miss Marion Jones, Miss Robertson, Miss Moore ; Miss Purver's s'all : Miss Purver. Miss Statham, Miss A. Cross, Miss M. Huat,Miss E. Goff, Miss M. E. Large ; refreshment stall : Mrs. Crawford, Mrs. R. Vs. Roberts, Mrs. Jones, Mrs. Ireland, Mrs. Upward, Mrs. Hunt, Mrs. Beesley, Miss Raw. There was a large company present at the °peeing cere- mony. The vicar (the Rev. G. 11. Garrett) welcomed them all to the new parochial room. He felt deeply grateful that the desire of his heart and of so many others was almost accomplished in seeing the school erected. The building would cost about £3,000, of which £2,000 had already hen received, and it was for Wpm to raise the other thousand during the progress of the bazaar. He was sure he object they all had in promoting the bazaar was to help on the work of God iii Widnes, and he trusted that the building would be the means of carrying on their Church work more efficiently. Mr. Gilliat after an appropriate speech, said he could well understand in a populous parish like St. Paul's , presided over by the earnest zeal and effiziencv of their Vicar, that of all things needed there was nothing more imperative than accommodation, such as was provided in the building which they were in. It was impossible to recommend from the pulpit, still less to carry out all those auxiliary things connected with religious educa- tion, which would be what that room would be used for. He had taken a deep interest in the recent School Board election, and he was pleased to see on that Board represedtatives of the voluntary system, both Boman Catholics, and members of the Church of England working together with Nonconformists, and he hoped the work would be carried on in future as it had been in the past. He was pleased to see brotherly love exist- ing amongst the members of the various churches al- ' though working in whatever way it had pleased God to reveal the truth to them. He was bold to prophesy that they would look back with satisfaction, congratul- I ation, and thanksgiving upon the opening of that- room. He had great pleasure in declaring the bazaar open. (Applause.) Mr. Stuart Deacon moved a vote of thanks to Mr. Gilliat and this was seconded by Councillor F. Neil and agreed to. There was another opening ceremony yesterday, when the Vicar announced the result of the past days efforts was £2OO. In complimentary terms the Vicar intro- duced Mr. C. B. Toiler to announce the bazaar open.— In doing so Mr. Toiler referred to the great influence of such a building, and expressed the hope that many would have reason to bless it in the future. He was eordially thanked for his services on the motion of Councillor G. I. Neil, seconded by Mr. J. C. Crawford, who remarked that although Mr. and Mrs. 'foller were not well-known to the middle classes, their names were blessed in many houses of the poor.
THINGS HEARD AND SEEN
AT WA RRINGTON.

Sometimes, when I have been in the Warrington Police Court, and heard the ridiculous long-winded rigmarole of legal terminology with which a defend- ant is charged with committing even the most or- dinary every-day offence, I have been strongly in- clined to express in a cacchinatory outburst that contempt of court which—so far as this foolish rhodomontade is concerned—l have certainly felt. The poor prisoner, sometimes, must feel perfectly terrlted when he hears read the portmtously wor ly indictment against hiri,and feel that if he is proved guilty of anything half so awful as all this verbiage seems to express, he is lost. This hocus-focus jargon is only a portion of that system with which it is supposed a wholesome terror of the law is struck into the breasts of the community, and does serve to inspire respect for it in weak and ignorant minds, but only excites con- tempt and an inclination towards derision in educated minds. Indeed it is not long since, at the borough police court, the magistrates' clerk him- self—who, of course,is not to blame in the matter— gave vent, in a sudden revulsion of the old lay Adam, no, doubt, at sight of one of these pompously bombastic documents in which some simple charge against a prisoner was laboriously embodied. "It is hardly necessary to read all this rigmarole I suppose " he remarked, amidst an approving titter in court. I really am occasionally disposed when I think of the inane and tedious folly of some of our forms of jurisprudence to agree with honest Dg- berry's sententiously expressed opinion that " the law is an ass."

Why, in heaven's name,cannot a man charged with say stealing a coat on the Bth of October be in- indicted on that charge in plain common-sense diction, without being grandiloquently dumb- foundered by the information that he " did on the eighth day of October instant feloniously steal,take and carry away, and appropriate to his own use a certain article of wearing apparel to wit a coat; perhaps a long string of other superfluities besides? But we are oppressed almost to mental suffocation with the fossilized and fusty folly of the middle ages ; and the worst of it all is that there are a lot ot tiresome and dreary fogies who have a sneaking regard for, and linger with fatuous reverence over, this kind of thing, just because it is old, though it is utterly out of place in these more enlightened dap. Sweep it all into the limbo of old-world foolery, say 1, and there let it rest.

It is reported that Mr. Byrne the Irish labour candidate, said at the meeting of his Irish support- ers on Sunday, that" he should stand in the Coun- cil chamber on his back irrespective of political parties:" What did Mr. Byrne mean by advertis- ing his pertormauce in the Council of such a piece ot municipal acrobatism as standing on his back. lie is on his back now certainly, electorally speak- ing, though I should like to see him and a few more labour representatives in the Council, but standing on his back when he got there would be a representation of labour indeed. IV hen Benjamin Disraeli was about to put up for a certain constituency, he was asked by someone Who was desirous to sound him as to his Par- liamentary principles,on what he proposed to stand in his political campaign. "On my head," was the reply of the witty future Premier. What Mr. Byrne means about standing on his back I cannot tell ; but his 59 supporters evidently believe that stand- ing on his head in the sense that Disraeli meant is a feat that. he could accomplish in the Council with- out toppling over.

We are not perfect. It is a singular thing that we can be gulled into a fraud by the most impu- dent trickster, if he be clothed in respectable garb, as easy as a mouse can be entrapped with cheese. And tile whole time we flatter ourselves upon being "knowing." We have an appreciation for "res- pectable" frauds there is no doubt. If a poor down-trodden ragged tramp sneaks up our back- yards, with the object of pushing a lace or pin trade he receives no encou• agement. The good house- wife thinks she knows his little game, and bangs the door in his face with an emphatic "No," and then flatters herself upon frustrating his fraudu- lent designs. But when the respectable swindler comes to the front door why, he take her in. She earn% resist him. This is an instance of it.

Last week a gentlemanly-looking young fellow drove up to a small shop in Latchford. The establishment is kept by a mechanic, whose name we will not mention. 'He was out at work, and consequently his wife stood behind the counter to attend to the gentlemanly visitor. After a few preliminary remarks, of an affable character, the latter got to business. He said he represented a new tobacco manufactory in Liverpool, whose speciality was cigaretts. He knew they did a good business at that shop and he wished them take an agency for the " pipes brand," as he called it. And after a long and polite conversation he per- suaded the good woman to take on trial four five shilling boxes, which he generously let her have at three shillings each. She paid the money down and received the boxes. Then he promised to call again, and raised his hat and drove away.

That evening the enterprising lady told her lord and master of the transaction. And by and by she brought him a box, just to look at. The cigarettes looked nice, as he saw them arranged in tight little rows. He took one out to look at the tobacco. Then his wife saw him take several out rapidly, and the next moment he threw them to the ground in a rage. He had discovered that they were all empty. He probably thought they were a " selling brand," because he told his wife rather angrily that they had" been sold."

But the male gender is not infallible in this direction. Only last week I was told of how a young married man well known in Warrington Friendl3 Society circles succumbed—not altogether to fraud. He went to a certain draper's shop in town to purchase a singlet. As the pretty young lady behind the counter fixed her tender, languish- ing eyes upon him, his face became suffused with a purple blush. He tried to look her in the face but couldn't. So he fixed his eye on the floor, and in a confused manner muttered that he wanted a "sin— sin—singlet." And in a while she came tripping along, and placing an item of baby's apparel before him asked if that size would do.

The beads of perspiration stood on his forehead and then they tricirled down his face. Her smiling eyes met his again, and then he couldn't explain a bit. Ile planked the money down and hurried out. And now, would you credit it,,when that gentleman reached home he offered his wife the parcel and un- blushingly said it was a birthday present for the baby, notwithstanding the fact that that important individual is only six months old ! And yet we are said to be perl,ect,

I am told that the Burton chainless cycles, as illustrated in the" Graphic" of November 21, was 80 to speak, " the cynosure of all eyes' at the Stanley Show held in the Royal Agricultural Hall, Islington, London, and orders from big agents, sbippers,and some of the fastest riders in the States, Belguim. Denmark, France and England have been booked by Mr. Burton. We understand, too, that Mr. Burton's labour saving machinery, as manufac- tured by an eminent firm is likely to be used by many firms of engineers, tool makers, aad gun manufacturers.

In view of the agri-c—ult—u;a-rdepression, the following. important rent reductions have been made in Choshire Sir John Stanley Erringtun,Bart.,lo per cent.on the Pud- dington and Ledsham estates ; Captain Congreve. 25 per cent, on the Burton estate ; Mr. Birkenhead Glegg, 10 per cent, on the Backford estate ; and Mr. R. C. Xaylor, 15 per cent, on the Houton estate. Mr. Naylor. • has reduced his rent for the last ten years.
FATAL TRAP ACCIDENT AT EATON,

CHESHIRE FARMER KILLED. On Thursday night, as Mr. Mullock, of Poulton, near Chester, a prominent Cheshire farmer and cheese.- maker, was driving through the Eaton-hall approach with his wife, Ins horse shied, and both were thrown from the trap. Mr. Mullock sustained serious injuries, and died shortly afterwards, whilst his wife escaped without serious injury.

div.head: GREAT COAL STACK ON FIRE.
div.p: GREAT COAL STACK ON FIRE.

Sr. ETIENNE, TIIIIISday.—A serious fire occurred last night at the coal mine known as the Piuts des Hosiers. The flames, which broke out among a large quantity of stacked coal, spread rapidly, extending over an ared of nearly one thousand square yards. The firemen were quite unable to cope with the conflagration. All the mining officials were on the spot and there was ark enormous crowd of spectators.

div.head: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
div.p: BEFORE THE MAGISTRATES.
IN QUEST OF CVERDLET MARSH WITH A. GUN.

At the Daresbury Petty Sessions on Tuesday Arthur Brannard, signalman, employed at Arpley Station and living at 20 Nicholson-st., Warringtcn, was charged with trespassing in pursuit of game on October 27th, on land in the occupation and possession of George Dodd, at Walton Superior. A gamekeeper employed by Sir Gilbert Greeisall deposed t. seeing the defendant crossing the land with a gun, and, on his asking him where he was going, replying "You have spoiled my sport:"—The defendant said he had only been at Arpley Station about three weeks, and he took out a gun license and started for Cuerdley Marsh where he understood there was some shooting to he had. fie was directed, through Walton, but missed his way and found himself in a field where on going up to the keeper, whom he observed, he was charged by him with trespassing in pursuit of game.— The Bench fined the defendant the cost of the summons only, 4s. ed.

div.head: MINOR CASES.
div.p: MINOR CASES.
NEWTON PETTY SESSIONS.
SATURDIT.—Before Messrs. T. J. Gillespie (cbairman),
W. F. Gooch, and T. H. Personi

THE SECENTiIIY OF A FRIENDLY SOCIETY IN THODBLII.— Horatio Seddon, secretary of the Golborne District Branch of the Loyal Order of Aneient Shepherds, was charged with a breach of the Friendly Societies' Act, by anlawfully with-holding a contribution book, the pro- perty of the Order, after having been duly requested to deliver up the same.—Mr H. J. Wichlows (Manchester), appeared for the prosecution, and the defendant WAS re- presented by Mr.H.L.Riley,of St.Helens. Mr. Widdoovs,l Id intro lucing his case said that the defendants' officiall duty was to keep several books of the Branch. Amongst those books was the contribution book, in which the centributions of the members were entered by him. Last September there was a question raised respecting the accuracy with which the book was kept. A meeting was called at the Queen Anne Inn, Got- borne, and it was then decided that the books should undergo an official audit. Defendant appeared to be troubled about the examina- tion, and on the following day (September 25th), he re- quested two members of the Committee of Management to call at his house. This they did. He then asked them to assist him to get out of the necessity of the matter being reported at headquarters. He admitted in the conversation which took place that his boaks were not correct, hut offered to allow tw,, gentlemen te in- spect them, for which office he would pay them. The gentlemen referred to were sorry for his position, and they did all they could on his behalf, but at a meeting held the same evening it was finally decided to let the matter take its own course. On the following day Messrs. Dowries and Hirst met again and informed defendant of the result of the deliberations of the previous evening. The defendant was told that the matter would be re- ported to the district official. The defendant replied " All right." On the followiag Friday, Mr. Healy, the Provincial Deputy Chief Shepherd, together with two other officials, met at the defendant's house, and de- mended the books in accordance with the order of the lodge. The defendant at first refused to hand them over, but finally surrendered all the books, with the exceptionl of the contribution book. In reply to the demand for that, the defendant said that on the previous Tues- day a boy brought a letter to his house from Mr. C. ' Downes, which ran as follows:—" Mr. Sodden, would ' you please let me have the loan o 7 your contribution book to-night and oblige—Yours truly, GRA lILES Dowlaes." That letter, so far as Mr. Downes was con- cerned, was a forgery. Mr. Dowries would tell the Court that he never wrote the letter, or authorized any- one to write such a note. The defendant said that he gave the boy the book, and not having received it back, he was consequently unable to deliver it up. The de- fendant admitted, on further questioning, that he was aware that the handwriting of the letter purporting to come from Mr. Dowries was not that person's writing, but bethought that he might have instructed his son to pen the letter. The defendant, said Mr. Widdows had no right to trust the book out of his keeping, especially in the face of the examination which was pending. Mr. Widdows then detailed the various communications which were forwarded to the defendant, insisting on the delivery of the books, or in default threatening legal proceeaings. The book not being delivered by October 31, it was decided to take proceedings.—Mr. Riley said that he could prove that the contribution book could have no relation to any possible defalcations. He could also bring several witneases to prove the correctness of the accounts, as audited by them for the past six years. Moreover, that was not the court in which to bring such an action. The charge ought to be tried in a civil court whine the mouth of the defendant would not be closed. Continuing, he said he could produce a witness who was present in the house on the night when the defendant gave the contribution book to a bey on receipt of a note. After careful consideration the Bench decided to dismis:. the case.

WARRINGTON BOROUGH POLICE COURT. Ilidowoa.v.—Before Mr. F. Monks (chairman), Alderman Harrison, and Messrs. T. Birchall, and S. Wright. WIFE DESERTION.—Richard Lowe, labourer, last from Leigh, was charged by Mr. B. Shearer, on behalf of the Guardians, with leaving his wife and three children chargeable to the Union. He was sent to prison for three months. BREAKINGA WINDOW,—Ann Thomas, 4 Florence-at., was charged with breaking the window of the Bear's Paw Inn,Buttermarket-st-on Saturday night. lie did the damage because,he being drunk, the landlord would not serve him with drink. He had to pay the damage and costs.—Martin Bart, drunk and disorderly on the 19th November, on Friar's Green, ss. and costs.—Henry Jones, in Powell-sreet, on the 19th November, bad to pay costs.—Maria Edwards, in Dial court on the 20th Nov. had to pay costs.—Catherine Gerrard, in Hopwood-St.. on November 21st. She had thrown a bucket of water into a woman's house and wet the constable who proved the case, also smashed the win- dows. It was stated that she had had over 30 pints of beer that day. A witness for the defence said the window was broken through the defendant being knocked against it. 10s. and costs. Daum( IN CO4WIE OF HORSES. —Richard Griffiths carter, 74 Wellington-street, was charged with beim, drunk in charge of a horse and cart.— The 'defendant said he had been a teetotaller for a long time, but had two glasses of whisky because a house he had been in was in such a filthy condition that he felt ill after coming out of it.—Mr. Norman, inspector of nuisances, said he had employed him in removing bedding which was practically disinfected. He bad no occasion to take drink. He himself had not, though he had to gis into premises where there was smallpox.-55. and costs.—David Manning, Cow-lane, Sankey, for a similar offence, 53. including costs.—Thos. Whitley, carter, 86 Wellington-st., drunk while in charge of two horses and a lurry, was fined ss, and costs. AN Ass ASTRAN.-.—Fienry Ellison, 20, Percy-street, was charged with allowing an ass to stray on November 18th. A witness said the donkey kicked his son as be was running out at night, and cut his head in two places. The defendant was also charged with allowing the ass to be astray on November 20th. A police- constable said he had received several complaints about the animal biting and kicking people. The defendant was fined ss. and costs in each case.—The Chief Con-

stable said a man had been laid up a fortnight through the donkey biting his arm. CHIMNEYS ON Fran.—James Daley, Scotland-road, for allowing his chimney to be on fire on the previous Fri- day.—Sergeant Taylor said the defendant put paraffin on the fire to get it to light quickly, and set the chimney alight. They remarked that they were disinfecting the town of smallpox.-2s. 6d. and costs.—Alfred Hazle- hurst,Church-st., for a like orence, is. AN HOTEL NnisaNcs.—Samuel Wilson, Feathers Hotel, Bridge-st., was charged with having on November 28th an accumulation of filth in a midden in the hotel yard, thereby causing a nuisance. Mr. Norman, inspector of nuisances, proved the ease. The Chairman said Mr. Wilson's sense ought to teach him better in the face of an epidemic like the present. The defendant was fined 10s. and costs, and informed that he must pay 10s. per day as long as the nuisance lasted.

TUESDAY—Before Messrs. R. Garnett (in the chair) E.J. Guest, and Dr. Starkey Smith. A DESERTER.—John Herd was charged with deserting from the 3rd South Lancashire Regiment. The case against him was proved, and defendant was fined 40s. and costs or seven days' imprisonment. HE SNATCHED THE COATS.—Japnes McDonald, a Ship Canal navvy of Rose and Crown-st., was eharged with stealing two men's coats value 43. 6d. from the shot of Catherine Gibbons, second-hand clothes dealer, Mersey- st.—The evidence adduced showed that about seven o'clock on Monday night he purchased a pocket knife,for which he paid 3d. Be left the shop, and presently re- turned, when he was seen by Ann Hayes, a neighbour, and Clara Gibbons, complainant's little girl, to take a blue serge jacket and a new linen jacket from the nails on which they were hung near the door. The little girl ran in and told her mother, and someone gave informa- tion to P.C. Baxendale, who was near at hand. Mrs. Gibbons hastened from her shop, and followed prisoner into Academy-st., and saw him take ofT his own jacket and put on the linen jacket. He then tried to put the blue serge one on, and at this moment P.C. Baxendale came up and saw that he was drunk. Be took him to the police station, and prisoner, when charged with the stealing the jackets, said he got them from a man at the corner of the street for half-a-crown. Mrs. Gibbons came to the police station and identified the articles.— Prisoner, who pleaded guilty, was fined 10s. and costs, or 14 days in default.

THURSDAY.—Before Alderman Chandley in the chair), Alderman Sutton and Captain Ridgway. Ma. RILEY'S PATIENTS —The following cases were dealt with at the instance of Mr. Riley, school attend- ance officer :—James Spencer, Tilley-st. • Thomas Row- lands, School Brow ; Elizabeth Moores. ; Wm. Finch, Pierpoint-at. ; John Jones, Gladstone-st. ; Edwin Stacey, Refuge Square ; Leah Briars, Back Williain-st. ; Win. Baines, Back William-st. FRlDAY.—Before Alderman Harrison (in the chair), Councillors J. H. Fleming and H. Roberts, and Messrs. Win. Pierpoint and S. Wright. . .

A LAME HORSH.—Cabal Pearse, milk dealer, Knuts- ford-road, was summoned for working a horse in an unfit state, on the 23rd November. Inspector Dowty, of the R.S.P.D.A., prosecuted, and said that the defendant was in the habit of working an old brown pony, which was lame in the hind leg, in consequence of the stoifold joint being broken. The defendant said she had "pro- fessional" evidence to prove that the horse did not suffer from a broken stoifold, and she asked for an ad- journment.—The case was accordingly adjourned for a fortnight.
WARRINGTON COUNTY COURT. TUORSDAY.—Before His Honour Judge Ffoulkes.

DISPUTE BETWEEN A BROTHER AND SISTER.—F. W. Massey, formerly a coal merchant in Dallam-lane, claimed £2 18s. 9d. from Wren Thomson, White-street, his brorher-in-law, for coal. The defendant admitted the claim, and put in a counter-claim for £6, for board and lodging. Mr. Arthur Browpe appeared for the plain- tiff.— rhe defendant said he claimed £6 from the plain- tiff for board and lodgings, from August 29th, to Oct. 24th of last year, eight weeks at 15s. a week.—Cross- examined by Mr. Browne, he denied that Massey was ever asked to stay with him. It was true that Mr. Massey's father made them presents from time to time, but not on behalf of his son. He did not press the plaintiff for the money as long as be was just commenc- ing business. On 26th September he sent in an account to Mr. Williams, an accountant, the plaintiff having failed, and his affairs being placed in Mr. Williams hands.—Leuisa Thompson. the defendant's wifb, and sister to plaintiff, said her brother Came to her house on the 29th August, and asked her to take him in. She did so, and he remained eight weeks, paying nothing during that time. They did not ask him for anything. —His Honour gave judgement for the plaintiff, both on the claim and counter-claim.

EXECUTORS OF STEPHEN MOSS v. LATCHFORD.—The executors of Stephen Moss, blacksmith, Academy-st., Warrington, claimed £1 9s. balance of an account for ironwork done, from James Latchford, butcher, 104 Orford-lane. Mr. Browne appeared for the plaintiff,and Mr. Longton for the defendant. For the plaintiff it was stated that the defendant ordered a pair of wheels to be made by plaintiff for which he had had £4 Ws. but had had tires made for the wheels there being extras and for which £2 93., was charged, the defendant pay- ing on account.—For the defence it was stated that it was understood that the £4 103. was to include tyres. He paid £1 for bolts and a spring as extras, but not on account of the tyres, and id not re cognisethat £l9s., remained due.—His Honour thought it was idle on the defendant's part to say that the £1 was not paid on account, and gave a verdict for the plaintiff. HUDSON T. BLaxs.—ln this case Thomas Hudson of Stockport, assignee of C. J. Dim m, official receiver, trustee of the estate of Samuel Green, bankrupt, late furniture and general dealer, Mersey-st., sued Robert Blake, labourer, 119 Mersey-st., for recovery of 30s. Mr. Rylands, of the firm of Rylands and Son, Man- chester, appeared for the plaintiff.—The defendLnt said he owed the money but disputed his liability for court costs. He admitted that he had had proper notice of the bankruptcy, but said he had promised to pay Mr. Green if he called to collect the weekly payments as usual but he did not call. A written application for payment was made by Mr. Hudson a month since, but he did not state where the money was to be paid. He dared say half of Stockport would receive money from him if it got the chance. Be had never had a chance of paving.—The plaintiff's application was handed up to the judge, who pointed out that there was no notice in it as to where the defendant was to pay the money, and on this account gave a verdict for the plaintiff for 30s. only, disallowing court costs. DARESB
IURY PETTY SESSIONS.
TUZSDAY.—Before Mr. W. Long (chairman), the Hon H. Talbot, and Mr. J..Neild.

ISLEEPY DniyEns.—Joseph Taylor was charged with riding asleep on a dray, on the 22nd of October, at Kechewick, was fined 53.—Harry Long, of Bridge-st., Warrington, asleep on his cab, on the sarne date, at Moore, was fined the costs, 3s. 6d.—Peter Bramhall and Ernest Moreton, of Hartford, asleep on their carts at Stretton on the 7th of November, 2s. 6d. each including costs. DRUNIL AND DISORDNRLY.—Jane Young, married woman, of Stockton Heath, on the 9th of November, 10s. No NsivE ON A CART.—A. 0. Grange, of Warrington, was charged with using on the 18th November a cart without having his name painted thereon. The ease was dismissed.

Poecrniel.—Peter Rowson,labourer at Dallam Forge,was charged with trespassing, on November 12th, in pursuit of game, on land in the occupation of Mr. Collin Mclver and Mr. Wm. Mortimer, at Grappenhall. He was with another man, and they had six rabbits upon them, and had ferrets and nets in their possession. Both men gave their wrong naines and addresses. P.C. Millington took Howson to Warrington, and the first policeman they met told him who he was. The other man got away. The defendant was fined 40s. and costs.—George Groom, of Stockton Heath, was charged with trespassing on the 20th of November, in search of game, on land in the occupation of William Barber, at Grappenhall, also with a like trespass on the 20th of Sep- tember, on land occupied by Mr. Joseph Charleton Parr. Mr. Browne appeared for the prosecution. —lsaac Braithwaite, head gamekeeper to Mr. J. C. Parr, said on the 20th of September, about half-past two p.m., he saw the defendant coming across a field on Mr. Parr's estate. He watched him and saw him cutting nets down, and with a ferret and a net endeavouring to catch rabbits. Witness went up to him and got hold of him, and had a struggle with him. He said he came I from Acton Grange, but would not give his name. He said witness had made a "fair cop," and he would go quietly, but while witness was picking up a stick he got away, and threw a stone the size of ahalf brick at 'him. The defendant had a stick with him with a socket to fit a spade for digging rabbit burrows. Witness picked up I a pocket book in one of the burrows, which Contained the defendant's name and address, and certain entries of money, and on the 20th of November. Witness then gave evidence as to the further poaching by the defen- dant, who was then in company with two men, they having two dogs on the 20th of November. He was then apprehended by P.C. Millington, and witness produced to him the pocket book, and asked him if the hand- writing in it was his, and he said it was.—The defen- dant said he could not have said this, as he could not write, and stated that the entries as to money payments referred to his dealings in his works on the canal, his wife and others having entered the items. He denied the charge of trespassing in pursuit of game on the 20th of September, and asked why he was not charged with what he had really done. The charges was then amended to one of trespassing in pursuit of rabbits, and the de- fendant promply pleaded guilty to this. He was fined 20s. and costs in each case. . _

CHARGES OF ASSAULT.—Lizzie Holden was charged with assaulting and beating Elizabeth Forgen, at Stockton Heath, on November 23rd, and Forgen was cross-summoned by Bolden on a charge of assault. For- gen said Holden who was a perfect stranger to her, came to her lodgings and asked for her, and on her answering the door, witness told the defendant she did not know her and was closing it when Bolden pushed it open, tore a handful of hair out of her head, now pro- duced, and knocked her against the wall.—John Rolls-

brook said Holden came complaining with an oath that Forgen had been calling her names, and he corroborated as to Holden assaulting her, upon which, be said, Forgen kicked her and got loose.—Holden said Forgen would not give her an answer and kicked her, and got hold of her by the hair. She did not pull Forgen's out.---The Bench bound Holden over to keep the peace, and the case against Forgen was dismissed .—Stephen Cork, plate- layer, No. 7 Het, Norton, was charged with assaulting Mrs. Ann Kirk, also with assaulting Mrs. Elizabeth Chater, both on November 20th. Mr. Jenkins appeared for the prosecution and Mr. Browne for the defence.. Ha said all the parties lived at the huts, and there appeared to have been some heartburnings among them. He said on the date in question Mrs. Kirk's little boy, about six in the evening, took some food to the defendant's horns for a fireman who lodged there, and his hands being full, kicked at the door. The door was opened, and he left the food on the table, and before he came out, the defendant kicked him. Mrs. Kirk came for an explanattion, and he assaulted her, and also Mrs. Chater who interfered.—George Kirk, the boy, corroborated the statement as to himself, and said in answer to Mr. Brown that Cork did not complain of his kicking at his door before siz in the morning. He had been with his brother when the latter had done this, and they had both run away, but witness had never kicked the door in the morning.—Ann Kirk, deposed that on her complaining to the defendant about his kicking her boy, he spat in her face and threw her down; and he knocked down Mrs. Charter who came out and remon- strated with him for using very foul language.—Mrs. Charter and Robert Russel her lodger, and others corroborated..—For the defence Janus Wilson was called, and declared that Cork had not kicked the boy, but qply threatened to do so if the lad kicked at his door in The morning. Witness denied that any assaults were com- mitted on the women, though he said Mrs. Kirk came using very vile language to Cork.—Frederick Taylor and Charles Smout, lodgers of Cork also gave evidence that there were no assaults.—Abram Bebbington a lodger at another hut said the women were worse than the man, and John Wilson, Mrs. Kirk's lodger, said the defendant never struck either woman.—The Bench dismissed the cases' the Chairman expressing the opinion that they were too paltry to be brought there. div.head: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSSONS.
div.p: WESLEYAN FOREIGN MISSSONS.
MEETING AT RUNCORN.

The annual services in aid of the Wesleyan Foreign Missions were held in St. Faure Chapel, Runcorn, on Sunday last. There were large con- gregations at both the morning and evening ser- vices. The Rev. Conrad S. Sargisson, of Bur:dem, preached two eloquent sermons. Specially selected music was rendered by the choir and scholars at each service, Mr. W. B. Grice being at tbe organ. The collections realised .813, 118. we. The annual public meeting was held on Monday evening in the same place of worship, and there was a numerous audience. Mr. T. Simister ptesided and there were present the Revs. T. Wilkes, W. Arrowsmitb,.J. Hanby, R. Posnett, Conrad S.. Sargisson and Wm. Goudie (missionary from India', Messrs. J. Simp- son, S. Pope, J. R. Frith,.F. J. Norman, A. R. Nor- man B. Rniveton, J. Rawlinson,.R. Poanett, and E. Taylor (secretary). The Rev. W. Arrowsmith gave extracts from the seventy-eighth report of the Wesleyan Methodist Mis- sionary Society. The return of the year showed an in- crease under almost every head. The number of mis- sionaries in the service of the society showed a slight reduction, directly due to their present financial condi- tion. This particular item indicated the Church's sup- port of her Missions, and not the SWIMS or no success of missionary labour. Of other workers, themselves the growth and product of Christian life in many lands, there had been an encouraging increase. The number of paid agents, evangelists, . catechists, native teachers. kc.. had increased by 70, and of unpaid agents, local preachers, Sunday School toachers,.&e..., by 325. Of full and accredited Church members the increase was in round numbers 1500, while the number on trial for mem- bership was about I,ooo.lnore than. it was a year ago. The principal work of the society in .the heathen world lay in Africa, in India, and in China. The missions formerly carried on by their society in South Africa continued to flourish under the fostering care of the South African Conference. The interest attaching to India, as a mission field, was all but over- widow:Lg. During the last decade alone the population had increased by nearly 28,000,009: In this vast coun- try there were now 288,000,01)0J people the great majority of them under direct, the remainder under indirect, British rule. Whatever apathy or scepticism with regard to Indian missions might be found in this country, those who were engaged its the work-English, American, and German missioearies of every grade and type-were full of confidence and hope. Of the six dis- tricts in Continental India, all showed an increase of membership except one, in which there was practically no change. Their European missions had long consti- tuted an important branch of the society's operations. France, Germany, Italy,. e +eh, presented its own features of moral and spiritual interest. In recent years the Society's income had not, as was well known, kept pace with the requirements of its work. Twelve months ago they were obliged to report a defi- ciency in the year of £lO,BOO, which, added to a previ- ous deficiency of £8,500, made a total deficiency on the Ist January, 1891, of a little over £1.9,370. That amount was lessened by £2,080 special donations re- ceived during the year through Miss Farrar and Mrs. Chubb. The total income from all sources at home and abroad was £125,129, being an increase of £.3,057 on the previous year. The total expenditure for 1891 was £129.197, being £3,568 less than in the previous year, but £4,068 more than the income. There was, therefore, in spite of an increase of £3,000 in receipts and a de- crease of nearly £3,700 in the expenditure, a deficiency on the year of a little over 24,000. That was to say, the income of the year just closed was insufficient by £4,000 to meet an expenditure which had been reduced as far as practicable. But the society's expenditure could only be kept down to last year's level by the arrest of their work at a stage of great fruitfulness and pro- mite. It would mean the resolute refusal of opportunity in its most inviting and commanding forms. The com- mittee commended the figures to the candid considera- tion of their friends, and'asked from the connexion "a ten per cent. increase" upon last year's returns. The receipts from the Liverpool district from all sources I were :-Legacies, &c. £7,964 Bs. 9d., being an apparent ' decrease of £99 153. 41. ;but as the legacy part of the whole showed a decrease of £366, there was really an increase in the ordinary income of £250. The Runcorn circuit had contributed £296 9s. 2d.. against £255 . 16s. 9d. last year; or an increase of £4O 12s. 7d. The sum given by St. Paul's congregation and Brunswick Sunday School was £166 4s. 2d. Mr. E. Taylor submitted the local report, showing that in the present year the receipts were :- Collected by Mrs. Soulby, £6 165.; Mrs. Speakman and Mrs. A. R. Norman,£s 195.; Miss Simister, La 125.6 d.; Miss Crosby, I£s Os. 6d.; Miss Norman, £ll 2s. 6d.; Brunswick 'Sunday School, £76 4s. 7d. (against £64 17s. 4d. last year) ; collections in chapel, £llls. 10d ; total, £127. 6s. 11d., compared with £ll4 We. Bd., twelve months ago, or a net increase of £l2 103. 3d. The collections at the public meeting a year ago realised £5l 7s. 6d. It was explained with regard to the Sunday school that the amount was made up as follows :-Collections, boys, £l2 19s. Id. . - girls, £6 Is. 9d. ; books, boys. £14.125.;. girls, £29. 1334 collections, spring meeting, £6.115. 2d.; and at annual meeting £7' 7s. 7d. In conclusion, he made a touching reference to those workers in connec- tion with the missionary cause who had been removed by the hand of death. The Chairman, in the course of his address, said that !tr. Newton Davies, who had been asked to preside over, those proceedings, had generously contributed a dona- tion of £lO. He thought they had every reason to be satisfied with the grand results of the labours of those -in their Sunday school, for they had obtained a splbndid The Rev. Conrad S. Sargisson, in an interesting address, spoke of the comparatively small part of the the world which was professedly Christian, and of the large proportion that was heathen. Notwithstanding the depth to which the people had fallen, bethought that recent history gave them every reason to have their faith considerably strengthened. The people had been generally improved through the gospel of Christ. Be referred to their duties in view of their possession of the blessed Word, and urged all present to thought- fully, lovingly, and intelligently continua in their efforts.
The Rev. W. Goudie gave a most interesting account of his work in connection with the outcasts of India.
Votes of thanks were accorded—io--tiCe—depait-lon",-the Chairman, and others who had taken an active part in the anniversary. The collection taken during the pro- gress of the meeting realized £5O.

div.head: SWEATING SYSTEM_ --- EVIDENCE BY MR. CHARLES BOOM.
div.p: THE SWEATING SYSTEM_ --- EVIDENCE BY MR. CHARLES BOOM.

At Wednesday's .sitting of the CaTou-r—dr-o-ra—m- ission Mr. Charles Booth gave evidence on the swesti rig sys- tem. He recommended that the scope of the factories and workshops acts should be extended, and that land- lords should be made responsible for structural and sanitary defects of workplaces, and the occupiers for misuse of the premises, such as overcrowding or the working of illegal hours. Be proposed to make the occupier liable for fines for defects in structure, but with power to recover from the landlord, and, on the other hand, the landlord should be liable ,as well as the occupier, for fines on account of misuse of premises. The occupier, if fined for structural defects, should be entitled to stop the amount out of the rent, and the landlord, if fined for misuse, should be entitled to col- lect the amount with his rent from the occupier, or recover it by summary process. He did not think the existing evil was due to any great extent to the inhu- manity of employers. There was the competition [ between workers themselves, and there was also the I competition of rarious small masters with each other, which caused them to press hardly on those they employed. Be did not think that a law to check the immigration, of pauper aliens would have any important effect.

div.head: BAD MEAT PROSECUTION AT ST HELENS. CONFLICT OF EVIDENCE. HEAVY FINE.
div.p: BAD MEAT PROSECUTION AT ST HELENS. CONFLICT OF EVIDENCE. HEAVY FINE.

The adjourned case of the St. Helens Corporation against George Wrigley, butcher, 51, Parr-st., for depositing unsound meat for sale was before Mr. Thomas Pilkington and Mr. W.J. Thomson on Tues- day, The Town-clerk (Mr. Jeeves) appeared for the prosecution, and Mr. H. L. Riley defended. The case put before the court on Tuesday last waS that on the 17th inst. Police-constable Smirthwaite, the meat inspector, found a porti.,n of the shoulder and the ribs of a carcase which was in a state of putrificatioia on defendant's premises, and that such premises were in a filthy condition. Mr. Riley opened for the defence, and contended that the condition of the premises ought to be excluded from the case. As a matter of fact the Least was killed in the middle of the previous week at the Liverpool Abattoir,. and this forequarter was sold to defendant on thy Friday in Liverpool. It was then brought with other ferequarters to defendant's shop at St. Helens Junction,. and was afterwathe entrusted to a butcher named Matthew Lowe. His place was in a perfectly sanitary condition, and was a well-arranged establishment, and it was- only on the day before it was, seized that it was brought from Lowe's place, and deposited in the shop in Parr-at., where it was seistd.—William liamsden, naazia- ger anddirector Liverpool Abbatoir Company, and vice- president of the National Federation of Butchers, who sold the meat in question to Wrigley,said the beasts were exceedingly sound and perfectly healthy. On the 18th inst. he visited the stables at the Town. Hall, and recognised the meat as portion he had sold. Ha had it taken down off the hook, and applied every test which he knew for determining whether it was whole- s-.me. On that night the meat was wholesome and perfectly sound.—By the Town-clerk There was a little sourness from spinal marrow or pith, but no necomposition had set in in the meat. He had never said to anyone that the meat was not sound.—Thomas C. Hewlett, wholesale butcher, and treasurer of the Liverpool Butchers' Association, then. gave evidence. On Friday, the 18th inst., he accom- panied Mr. Ramsden to examine the meat, and corrobor- ated what the previous witness said. Having regard to his past experience, the meat was perfectly good.— Hewlett, in answer to the Town Clerk, said it was not the practice of the association to defend all butchers brought before the magistrates. Wrigley was not a member of the association, and they were not defending him.—Daniel Gilvray„ butcher, St. Helens; Thomas Williams, salesman for Nelson and Sons, Liverpool ; and Robert Getty, manager of the Liverpool Abattoir, and formerly meat inspector for the Liverpool Corporation, all of whom had seen the meat on Friday, the 18th inst., said it was wholesome.—This closed the defendant's case.—Chief Cohstable Wood said in August, 1883, Wrigley was fined £5 and costs for preparing unsound meat for sale.—The magistrates decided to convict, and the Town Clerk asked for the expenses of the prosecu- tion witnesses.—The magistrates inflicted a fine of Eta, with ordinary court costs amounting to one guinea.

div.head: ALLEGED ROUGH TREATMEZIT OF A LUNATIC.
div.p: ALLEGED ROUGH TREATMEZIT OF A LUNATIC.

The CHAIRMAN asked for an explanation as to an account of Mr. Willace,relieving officer,for the removal of a lunatic named John Houghton,which had been charg- ed against the Board.—Mr.Wallace explained that it was in consequence of his c‘insiderir'“, the charges too much and having had to have the bill reduced, also in conse- quence of delay in getting accounts in. It was mentioned that the lunatic had broken the window of the cab in which he was removed, which had involved another charge,and Mr. Wallace stated that the man was urged by the pace into the cab in too rough a manner. —ln reply to questions,, Mr. Shearer stated that they used unnecessary pressure.—The Chairman said the only question was whether the police officers, having more experience than the Board's own officer, used their discretion in, the matter. There was no com- plaint that the man was abused.—Mr. SHEARER : I beg your pardon. There is a very strong complaint. I got a certificate from the asylum at Rainhill, and he had • been abused by someone shamefully.—Mr. Shaw : In that case I should like further discussion on the matter. —Mr. SHEARER, in reply to a question, said the man was very much marked indeed.—Mr. WALLACE said there was no force used in taking the man to the asy- lum.—lt was stated that the matter would come before the Lunacy Commissioners.—The subject then dropped.

PADGATH SCHOOLS.COMMITTEH. This Committee recommended that the usual Christ- mas dinner be supplied to the officers and children as in- previous years, but considered it undesirable, by reason of the present epidemic, to have the usual Christmas 'treat for the children. The Committee recommended that the superintendent be instructed to issue a circular to all the customary subscribers explanatory of the case, and saying that their subscriptions wouid be applied for the use and entertainment of the children on a more favourable opportunity. The doctor's report stated that the children were healthy.—Mr. W. FloootrroN moved the adoption of the report. He observed that they did not want the cow to get dry for want )f milking, so the Committee thought the best) plan would be to issue the circular to the subscribers, because, though they had to forego the usual Christmas treat, there would be some- thing provided later on for the amusement and edifica- tion of the children at a later period of the year.-4f.r.
