div.head: WARRINGTON AMATEUR PHOTOGRAPHERS SOCIETY.
div.p: WARRINGTON AMATEUR PHOTO- GRAPHERS SOCIETY.

AN INTERESTING LECTURE. The usual monthly meeting of this Society was held in the Committee Room of the Museum, Bold- et„ on Tuesday evening, The President, Air. T. J. Down took the chair, and there was a very large attendance, who were there to see Mr. S., J. Bucha- nan Wollstozn of the Platinotype Company, gave a practical demonstration on the working of Platino- type. Mr. Down, on introducing Mr. Wollaston to the meeting,said it gave him very great pleasure to be present that evening to witness the fineet, best finished, and most permanent process •in photo- graphy, and in the name of the Society to give the lecturer a hearty welcome. Mr. Wollaston, on rising, said it was necessary to say a few words before going into the practical work, res- pecting the hot bath which was now practically a thing of the past, being superseded by the new cold bath pro-' tees, claiming for the latter several advantages, among which were superior keeping qualities, greater simpli- city of manipulation, and more control orer the result. Unlike the hot bathprocess, a good print could be made frorn almost any negative, by modifying the method of printing, the developer, and its application,, and excel- lent results could be ontained from a negative that would net give a passable print by any other process. Great stress was laid upon the abeniute necessity of keep- ing the' paper "bone" chy,before,charing,and after print- ing,if brilliant results were required. Should the paper have absorbed moisture, there woold be a correspond- ing tendency to mealiness. *Mr.Wollaston said that very thin negatives might, with advantage, be printed under blue ;:and hard ones, under signal green glass,. The prints could be developed by immersion, floating,, or by brush; the lecturer preferring the latter as having more command,thereby obtaining a fuller scope for the artistic treatment of the subject. Detailtand transperancy in the shadows can be retained by first covering those parts of the print with a thin layer of glycerine,robbed on evenly with the finger,. the development being afterwards pro- ceeded with in the usual way. During the dismission which Mowed the demonstra.- tion Mr. Wellastou passed round some beautiful spec-i- -mens of platinum prints and also kindly criticised tier work of Mr. Aylward and Mr. warding who bad pre- pared some prints-for the occasiors. Mr. H. N. Dough- ton in proposing a hearty vote of thanks to Mr. Wollaston for his•able and very interesting lecture and de:nonstration,,said that what they- had seen that even- leg was a pleasant revelation to them, and taking into consideration the•absolute permancy of the prints, the ease of manipulation,.the perfect control under develop- ment, they as serious wnrkers, would, give the process a thorough trial.—Mr. Aylward in seconding the vote of thanks, said that having tried the paper nothing gave him better satisfaction,, and he knew of no other that lends itself so readily to individual artistic treatment than it.—The following gentlemen were duly elected members of the society :—Mr. Thomas Prince, 4- Herse- markert-st., Mr. George (grounds, 88 Winwick-st., Mr. Alfred Sutton, 20 Bold-st., Mr. W. H. Dell, 38 Bewsey- st., Mr. Orton, Arley Green, and Mr. Chas. A. Timmins, ROckfield, Runcorn.

LADIES' GUILD OF NEEDLEWORK AT WABRINGTON. At the invitation of the Mayoress (Mrs. Edward (Ireenell), a meeting of ladies was held in the Mayor's Parlour, at the Town Hall, on Tuesday afiernoon' "for the purpose of forming a Ladies' Guild of Needlework,.to provide clothing for the poor during the winter months, as it is feared that much distress has already been caused by the pre-- sent epidemic, and that there will be a hard win- ter."' The Mayoress presided, and the other ladies pre- sent were—Mesdames Witlis,,Broadbent, Milling, Litton, Gornall, Long, Pickmere, Pigot, J. L. Tunstall,. Madeley, Monks, Coates, SmethurSt, Armitage, S. Reynolds,Cross- ley, H. Woods, George Venn,Harding,James Fairclough, R. T. Fairclough, John Fatirclough, It. Smith, A. Edels- ten, Clare, J. Reynolds, W. H. Robinson. and Fox; the Misses Gornall, Long, Massey, Smith, Milling, Atkinson, White, Westwell, B. Detton, Pierpoinl., (St. Austin's), Taylor, Kendrick, C. Harvey,and Rimmer. Mr. Stanley Wilson (Assistant Town Clerk) was also present. TheMeroaess, in opening the proceedings, said : We meet to-day to discuss two subjects, which we will con- sider separately, the first the forming of a Guild of Needlework in Warrington for the poor of our own town. These guilds have been formed in many towns around, and have been found most successful. The rules are very simple. All that is required is that each member undertakes to send two new garments yearly,, by a specified date, with a nominal subscription. Gentlemen members are in great request as, well as ladies, as in ad- dition to wearing apparel, blankets, boots, and men's clothing are valuable. The articles subscribed by the mem- bers will be distributed to the clergy of all -denomina- tions,for the use of the poor in our town,by members of a committee formed to-day. If possible, I propose that all contributions be sent to me by January Ist, as the poverty, owing to the epidemic, is great. As the date only gives a short time in which. to make garments, I would remind all that there are • many sales of work earning on, at which garments oan be bought most ressonably, namely--Christ Church,. Latchford; st. Jaßa..'s ; Cairo-st., and the Charity Investigation Society. It is necessary to • form a tadies' committee who will be willing to undertake to find a certain num- ber of associates, to procure two articles each and to dis- tribute the articles ;.also a secretary. (Applause.) It was resolved—" That this meeting forms itself into a Guild e a Needlework, for the purpose of providing clothing for , the borough of Warrington and neighbourhood, and that each member pay a subscription of is., and pro- vide two garments." ' It was further • agreed that the Mayoress be appointed president, , Mee. Harrison vice- aresident, and Mn. Edlesten secretary and treasurer, ' with the following Executive Committee—Mesdames Greenall, Harrison, James Fairclougb, Pickinere, Armit— age, Monks, J. L. Tunstall„ Smethurst,. Long, FAN and the Misses B. Dutton and Pierpoint. LADIHS SEWING PARTY;

The Mayoress then— Sei-eest-e-ti- the formation. of a working party in connection with, the society well known and well organised,.. namely, the Charity Investigation Society. After con- sulting with Mrs. Harrison, .she suggested that any ladies who felt inclined to help in. that cause shmaid meet at the Town Hall once a weeltfor the purpose of. sewing garments for the poor. The amount of good that society did was well-known, and extra help this year would be most acceptable owing to the epidemic: The committse had kindly undertaken to make all necessary arrangements as to work, cutting-out, &a. She would feel most grateful to any ladies who would join her working party in connection with the society to be held in the Town Hall weekly. (Applause.) The first'sewingiparty will be held on Tuesdan, next elt two o'clock.

div.head: Mc IRISH SEAT DECLARED VOID.
div.p: Mc IRISH SEAT DECLARED VOID.

At Trim,. on Wednesday, Mr. Justice O'Brienliand Mr. Alttice Andrews delivered judgment in the South Meath election pstition. Mr. Justice O'Brien said as to the allegations of bribery no evidence had been given, and as far as ths allegation of treatirg was concerned the evidence respecting Father Tynan did not support it. On the question of physical violence and intimidation he should say that though there had been a good deal of violent conduct at Clonard and Sumnsorhill, the violence was not of such a general character as would void the electierr.. The principal matter as regavded intimidation was the action of the priests. First and foremost was the pastoral of Dr. Nulty. which contaftied most start- ling propositions. He could not see what occasion there was for the discression of the delicate 3nd dangerous question of personal purity in that pastoral, and for the terrible warnings and imputati sns that wen levelled irrthe document against men3bers of a certain party..l he pastoralL was so written as to inflame and excite the deepest and, strongest feeling of the Irish population. In the election the Church became a vast political agency, and all the priests were canvassers for Mr. Fullam. In Aact, it al- most seemed as though the priests were the candidate. , and Mr. Fullatn only their agent. On account of that.' action the seat must be declared void. Mr. Jhstice. Andrews concurred, and said that in his opinion the. Bishop's pastoral alone would have been suffic-knt to void the election.

div.head: Lettere to the Orator.
div.p: Lettere to the Orator.
RELIGIOUS EDUCATION.

Sfr,—l should like to say how cordially I agree with the Very Rev. the Dean of Manchester as to the need of an education based upon tho principles of religion. Un- doubtedly this is highly desirable. But what are the principles of religion the absence of which the Rev. Dean so much deplores? Can any one man give us a list of these principles, and would any ten men be found to agree to them? It is mere absurdity to talk of the "principles of religion" in connection with British schools supported and governed by men of all shades of religious opinions—and none. My agreement with the rev.speaker would involve the definition of the principles of righteousness—teaching the children to be kind and considerate one to the ether, to be truthful, honest, and helpful—to be, in fact, the raw material for the manu- facture of good citizen.. No sane person could quarrel with such "religious principles" as these.

But in the absence of definition of the term we are not sure that what the very rev, speaker had in mind was not a priestly education—a clerically conceived and con- trolled education. This to many religious and worthy people would be the abomination of desolation. A reli- gious education might very well mean an educa- tion according to the strict tenets of Mohammed. The Mollahs would be apt to say this was the only form of religious education. But in the alphabetical list of reli- gions we have Methodists and Mormons ; they too would cry out for religious education. Which among all these is the religious education ? Let these conflicting reli- gionists decide which and what has to be taught as a religious education, and then they may have some chance of its adoption. But an education based upon any one of these will not satisfy the rest, and has no chance of adoption. The very rev, spoke of the "hands of the educational dial" being turned backward. Many laymen think the best means of preventing this is to keep the hands of the clergy off the education dial as much as possible. The South American States and our nearer neighbour Russia are sufficient examples of what the clerics can do in this direction. Let us then by all means have an education based upon righteousness; but let us not introduce de- bateable matter into so important a business. The maxim "Do unto others as ye would that others should do unto you" is one recognized from Indus to the Pole.— Yours,
JOHN PEERS.

div.head: VACCINATION.
div.p: VACCINATION.

Sir,—Referring to the value of vaccination and re-vac- cination as a "protective " for small-pox, Professor Alfred R. Wallace, in his little work entitled " Vaccina- tion useless and dangerous," Part 11., p. 38, says : While . . . . utterly powerless tor good, vaccin- ation is a certain cause of disease and death in many cases, and is the probable cause of about 10,000 deaths annually by five inoculable diseases of the most terrible and disgusting character, which have increased to this extent steadily, year by year, since vaccination has been enforced by penal laws !" and from forty-five years of registration statistics he further proves. (2)—" That the diminution of small-pox mortality coincides with a diminished [italics not mine] instead of an increased effici- ency o. official vaccination." (3)—" That one of the most severe epidemics of small-pox on record, within the period of accurate statistics, incurred after 33 years of official compulsory and penal vaccination." Professor Wallace is an eminent and highly respected authority on vaccination, and at the present critical juncture I would advise people to read the Professor's work mentioned above. In vaccination there lies a real danger, not an imaginary one. Thousands of people have had filthy and dangerous diseases communicated to them by the vac- cinator's lancet, and hundreds have been its victims by death. _ . .

I was rather surprised to read under the heading of " How to stop the small-poix " a letter in your issue of the 19th inst. from a correspondent who I now mark signs himself Thomas Fletcher,the direct purpose of which is ta try to rebuild the crumbling Jennerian nostrum. Mr. Fletcher, I notice, has discovered a novelty, vize— pure vaccine lymph—the use of which guarantees the non-transmission of other diseases such as syphilis, scrofula, Ste. Well all I can say is that I should not like to be held responsible for the irreparable injury likely to result from such a system. Mr. Fletcher is Indeed very dogmatic, but his reasons for being so are not of a very reliable and substantial kind. That the calf lymph apology for all the past mischief does not prove decidedly advantageous, but that it proves decidedly the opposite, will be fully borne out by the following illustration :—ln the " Lancet " page 948, we , read: " In a herd of choice Jersey cattle kept near Philadelphia, one cow died, and, on examination, she was found to have had tuberculosis. I veterinary surgeon examined the herd, but could detect no evidence of the disease in the other cattle. But, as an aid to diagnosis, he employed tuberculin, and found reaction in six cases. These animals were slaughtered, and all but one were found to be suffering from tuberculosis. The exceptional case was not fully determined. This herd had been selected with the greatest care, &c." In commenting on this on a former occasion I wrote in the " English Mechanic," July 22nd, 1892, what may well be quoted here. " Now, the lesson that this example conveys, perhaps not to all, but at least to those who possess an unbiassed mina, is that experts have proved themselves unable to guarantee whether cattle are suffer- ing frost tuberculosis or not. Therefore, does not this one fact alone dispose of the whole case for calf lympk ? ' If no expert can tell whether a calf is healthy or not, the use of it is to create a healthy disease-product is absurd—as absurd as the healthy disease itself.'" It is the same old story. The wolf cunningly dressed up in sheep's clothing, that even those who have been bitten by the devouring monster cannot but believe him to be their benefactor.—l am, yours faithfully, JOSEPH COLLINSON.

div.head: Trout-street, Wolsingham, County Durham, November 25th, 1892.
div.p: Trout-street, Wolsingham, County Durham, November 25th, 1892.

"A LEARNER ON THE BRIDGE OF ASSES.' Sir.—Our Learner your Learner everybody's Learner—for at this rate he offers to become a clessic— will in future ages be known as the" Examiner's" Mala- prop. His reference to the shillelagh was not needed to convince me that lie is not an Irishman. His entire innocence of mother wit proves that. He is Irish in nothing except his bulls! But Scotch he may be— Sydney Smith's typical Scotchman, into whose head it required a surgical operation to get a joke. If the diffi- culty of extracting one be commensurate, well may our Learner hug the one jocular bantling to which he stands Godfather! Some antiquarian at some period of the XXI. century may haply stumble over a mossgrown slab bearing, in appropriate wood and lead, this legend : Hie jacet Malaproprium Exameris Warringtonensis Cum blunderhusticus Solus . .

If the latinity is somewhat shady—well so is the sub- ject. I note with alarm that our Learner is casting anxious eves around as though seeking aid in his distress. I doubt not he would feel it a great relief if some one— even a vivisector—would step into his shoes and the arena. It is much pleasanter to be a spectator than the recipient of a shillelagh mauling. When our Learner descends from the serene heights of jovial jocularity and 'condescends to " solid argument "—then "ye Gods and littlefishes " what a sight it is to see this Titan making chaos of system, and confusion worse confounded! As an example of his " solid "—that is dense, not to say feaden—argument take his fourth paragraph. Here we .hay. again our old friend the savage who, by "working off" his effete old father, precludes the cultured man of the XIX. century from the study of nature. Albeit in a changed garb—clothed in more elaborate ambiguities— this is still the conclusion he draws from the premises which lie says are "according to Mr. Peers." If this be so the state of the moon must have had to do with it, and my friends had better provide for me an efficient keeper. This statement of mine as the savage's assumption of nature's prerogative to deter- mine our lives is a veritable " Pons Asinorum " to "A Learner." Is it possible to project into the cephalic impenetralla of our poor Learner that here there is no :question of the study of nature by the savage, but of his unwarranted and unwarrantable interference in a matter which ought to be left to her. She, in her good time, will give us notice to quit; but the savage takes upon himself t* act as " chucker out." Being only a Sage and not a wizard I cannot see how this" precludes the cultured man of the 19th century from the study of nature In the manufacture of this amusing conclu- sion this precious sentence occurs :—" They (natural laws) are the seat and home of all truth and reality." ! ! This beats Agnosticism. Is there no truth outside the limits of physical science ? Can the laws of morality be weighed—their atomicity determined along with the . combining proportion of murder ? Now is not the

shillelagh amply justified ? A Learner has not always a surgeon handy to introduce a" solid argument "into his other wise impervious cranium. I am particularly interested in his postscript, and hasten to assure him that my studies of his unique mentality, have not been disturbed by any thoughts of what he thought as to my personality. As to his,l hays never even had the curios'ty to inquire. Why should I? Is he not mine, and can I not taake him dance and fling his arms about by pulling at the proper strings? Have we not fortnightly the pleasure of seeing him " take more line with the inevitable result of getting the hook still further into his unfortunate gills ? Who has not seen a kitten with a ball of wool and the resulting 'entanglement, the fettered limbs, and the start of fear at the self imposed fetters ? " Give some men rope enough and they will hang themselves" is an old adage well illustrated by this modern instance. There is more rope left.—Truly yours, JOHN PEERS. Penketh, 27 Nov., 1892.

div.head: RE-VACCINATION.
div.p: RE-VACCINATION.

Sir,—The subject is of such great and permanent im- portance that I trust you will kindly grant me space to reply to Mr. Thomas Fletcher's letter, which appeared under the above heading in your last issue. If he will acquaint himself with the literature of the subject, he will find that an adroit system of figure-cooking has for years past been the chief element in the official pro- vaccinist case. Sir Lyon (now Lord) Playfair's tactics in this way were some years ago publicly exposed by a London physician in a pamphlet entitled "Sir Lyon Playfair's logic," and, about the same time, the late Mr. Wm. White, in a shilling booklet, entitled "Sir Lyon Playfair taken to pieces," completely eviscerated that distinguished political chemist's speech in the House of Commons in 1883,in support of compulsory vaccination Neither Sir Lyon, nor any one on his behalf, has at- tempted to refute this crushing exposure by Mr. White.

Mr. Thomas Fletcher must have some very extraordi- nary ideas to suppose that poor private anti-vaccinists can afford to re-print and to re-publish " the whol report" of the Sheffield epidemic. The first issue of that official blue book was priced at 245. Subsequently, owing, I believe, to the blunders discovered in it, the book was withdrawn, and another edition, revised, was circulated at about half the price. Ask any bookseller, in however large a way of business, how many copies of such a book he would be able to sell ? As to the alleged report of the German Government on re-vaccination, published, as said, on the 15th November, in the London "Standard," I think Mr. Fletcher is confounding such a document with the telegrams or letters of the " Stan- dard's" own correspondent at Berlin. I may, however, say in passing, that the GermaN Imperial Commission on Vaccination, in 1884—a body mainly composed of pro-vaccinists--placed, inter alia, on record their delibe- rate opinion that there are real and serious and unavoid- able risks in vaccination, and, in consequence, to lessen these risks, they advised the abandonment of the arm- te-arm system throughout the German empire, and the substitution of calf lymph. Thus,at a blow, this learned body gave a flat contradiction to the persistent and almost shameless ass ertions of the whole pre-vaccinist body in England, who have stubbornly asserted, in the face of clear evidence to the contrary, that vaccination r is perfectly harmless, and is,moreover,a sure protection, or a certain mitigator, of smallpox. But here is a very ;bort and logical method of bring- ing all these statistical manufacturers to the test. It has been proved to demonstration before the present Royal Commission on vaccination (and the evidence is to be found in the three reports of that body already published) that, on an average, the number of deaths to cases in smallpox is almost exactly the sane as it was before Jenner's time. This demonstrated truth at once sweeps away all the fanciful arguments raised about the so-called " protection " given by one, two, three, four, or more vaccination " marks." Broadly stated, the average fatality rate in the disease is about 18 per cent. of the cases. And it may safely be said, that even if a person has been vaccinated repeatedly, and afterwards takes malignant smallpox, it is a hundred chances to one that he or she will die. Per contra, if he has never been vaccinated at all, and takes mild smallpox, it is a hundred chances to one that he will recover. These are elementary facts to all who have carefully looked into the literature of the subject; though, of course, vested interests cannot see such very plain things. In this matter the medical profession is somewhat like the clerical. Half a generation ago the learned repre- sentatives of the church met in council, and revised the New Testament. These representative pundits all agreed unanimously, that the passage in one of the epistles (St. John's) relating to the three heavenly witnesses is spurious, and is an interpolation. On it mainly rests the orthodox doctrine of the Trinity. But has the church accepted the decision of its own appointed experts? .Not a bit of it ! So these medical fossilised orthodox. The Marson tables and that entire school of argument, has been absolutely discredited,and no professional man with a shred of reputation to lose dare publicly stand forward to defend them. But are they officially abandoned? Not a bit of it ! Directly smallpox threatens this well- vaccinated land, out come these old and foolish bogeys from the Local Government Board ; and the obedient local medical officers of health, like lay figures manipu- lated with wires, mechanically repeat the cackle—not one in 500 of them having probably more than the merest smattering of the subject—that extremely superficial and traditional teaching derived from the hospital medical schools.

Mr. Fletcher says he has "personally a very strong objection to vaccination," but that he has submitted to it three times, not only for his own safety, but for the safety of those around him. If those around him were vaccinated, and therefore " protected," how could he endanger them ? And how could he himself be in dan- ger after his second vaccination ? Apologising for the length of this letter, I am, &c., Nov. 29.
J. H.

div.head: ANIMAL TORTURE AND ANCESTHETICS.
div.p: ANIMAL TORTURE AND ANCESTHETICS.

Sir,—You will, I am sure, with your usual liberality and love of fairplay, allow me through your valuable columns, the opportunity of addressing your readers on an aspect of the vivisection question but too little under- stood in its entirety by the laity, although we are still in the midst of a protracted discussion of the question in general. I refer to the administration of ancesthetics to animals which are about to be subjected to the cutting and slashing process of experimentatiomand of the capital which is made out of the use of ancesthetics by the vivisector and his abettors. . .

There are many reasons advanced by the vivisector in the defence of his craft—all bad, none good, and the one in particular of the bad order, because of the apolo- getic uses to which it is put, is that of ancesthetics ; framed, no doubt, by an industrious body of experienced hyper-scientists, for the purpose of making their op- ponents eat humble pie, as they generally have to do themselves. Nor in this case will they be exempt, and if those of your readers who have followed my remarks thus far, will bear me out to the finish, they will see that I make no vain boast, and, what is more, they will mark that I expose the vivisectional clique with their Own weapons. My first illustration is one of a series of experiments by an English physiologist of acknowledged reputation, Dr. Watson Cheyne, on rabbits, as described in the 1" British Medical Journal," of the 4th October, 1885, p. 645, by Dr. Watson Cheyne himself, whose words read thus ; "February 11th, 1882. Incisions were made antiseptically into the lumbar muscles on each side of a large rabbit. A croton-oil tube was introduced on each side, the muscles and skin were stretched over them with catgut. . . . ths wounds healed . . . . on April 6th (fifty-four days later), the tubes were burst by pressure, swelling formed on each side, and on May 3rl the rabbit was killed ; on making incisions through the skin and muscles, large abscesses contain- ing cheesy pus were found deeply seated." The nar- rative of the experiment adduced, stripped of its technicalities,and reduced to ordinary language,amounts to this : First of all the animal's loins were cut open sufficient to allow the insertion of thin glass tubes filled with irritating liquid, after which they were carefully sewed up; secondly, and ultimately, the tubes contain- ing the liquid were broken, and the liquid allowed to escape and diffuse itself among the lacerated tissues of the animal, producing, as a matter of course, violent in- flammation,and extensive abscesses. . . " The whole became a putrid mass, full of organisms," was the re- result of a similar experiment, and in this and ether forms, experiments were carried out on many other rabbits. Now, these experiments were made not for any practi- cal purpose, nor were they of any real utility ; but because, as I would have subsequently proved, had space permitted, they were scientificaily interesting. It is very evident too, that as some of the experiments occupied a period of nearly three months, the animals must have suffered in a fearful manner, and endured great pain. Of course no ancesthetics were used for Dr. Cheyne's experiment, and, indeed had an ancesthetic been used its action would have frustrated the vivisec- tor's desire to obtain a result scientifically interesting. My second illustration is taken from the report of the Royal Commission on Vivisection, 1878. The question was asked: "Then may I take it there are a great num- ber of experiments which, supposing a frog to be a sensitive animal, must cause a vast deal of pain, which are not done under chloroform ?" To this question Edward Albert Schafer, M.R.C.S., F.R.S., replied : There is no doubt of it. And there is no precaution taken to diminish pain, if it suffers pain. I think [may say no special precaution." My third and concluding illus- tration is taken from the Royal Commission evidence also :—" I suppose with rabbits you would not use chloroform ?"—I use chloral hydrate ; but as a general rule, for my scientific investigations, I do not use chloroform, or any other ancesthetic, except for conven- ience' sake, in dogs and cats, and for no other animals as a general rule. 'I here may be exceptions, perhaps; but, as a general rule, I think I am safe in saying I do not use it.—You gave it as your opinion, that your views on the subject, although not shared by the British public generally, were the views of the British physiolo- gists would not say that distinctly, but I know a few of them, and I think that is the view hekl by them." Emmanuel Klein, M.D.,F.R S., &c.

div.head: 111 E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 3, 11492
div.p: 111 E EXAMINER, SATURDAY, DECEMBER 3, 11492

Thus it appears that those who at e qualified to know, hold that anesthetics would frustrate the object of many experiments, if applied ; that is to say, that there are innumerable operations which involve extreme tor- ture, that cannot be performed under complete and genuine ancesthetics, of which we may count the fol- lowing :—(1). Those experiments which are coneerned with the reflex action from the sensory nerves ; (2), those which are connected with the glandular secretions, the liver, etc; (3,, those on the digestion ; (4), those on the heart and circulation ; (5), toxicological experiments —poisons; (81, all pathological experiments (consisting of the artificial induction of disease.) Dr. George Hog- gan. The truth is, as Dr. Hoggan emphatically told the Royal Commission so long ago as 1876, " Ancesthetics have proved rather a curse than a benefit to the subjects of experiment." As far as I can see their only use has been, and is, to lull the public—at least ancesthetics are seldom administered even in the most excruciating of cases, such as taking a number of dogs, and scalding them to death by pouring boiling water over them several times in succession, or of soaking them in tur- pentine and setting fire to it. Such is my case against the vivisector, and his plea that the animals suffer little pain, since ancesthetic precautions were observed. —lam,
JOSEPH COLLINSON.
Wolsingham, Co. Durham, _. Nov. 25th, 1892.

div.head: MIL J. PRICE'S "SCHOOL CASE."
div.p: MIL J. PRICE'S "SCHOOL CASE."
HE THRENTEINED TO APPEAL.

Mr. John Price, of the Temperance Hotel, Win- wick-street, and formerly president of the Warring- ton Trades and Labour Council, waa again brought before the magistrates at the Borough Court this morning, charged with not providing sufficient elementary education for his son Thomas. The magistrates present were Alderman Chandley (in the chair), Alderman Sutton, Councillor James Fair- dough, and Captain Ridgway. The defendant pleaded not guilty.—Mr. Riley (school attendance officer) said this was a case from Wycliffe School. The defendant's lad was over 13 years of age, but he had not passed the fourth standard. He should, therefore, attend school. Boys who had passed standard IV., and were over 13 years of age, were allowed to leave school. He asked the Bench that morning to make an order on the defend- ant ti send his boy to school until he was 14 years of age.—Alderman Sutton : But children are allowed to go to school half-time.— Mr. Riley replied that that was so in certain cases.— Defendant : There is an error in this summons. The last summons was admitted to be wrong, but there is a still greater mistake in this one. The summons says I have habitually neglected to'send my boy to school for the last six months. If that be the case, I want to know how it is that Mr. Riley has allowed my son to pass his standard P—Defendant said he had three sons older than this one in Manchesier, but when they were 13 years of age they were at liberty to leave school, provided they did not work amongst machinery.—The Chairman: That remains to be proved. If you wish to argue that point you will have to do so in another court. Still, setting aside technicalities, what is your reason for set- ting your back up and trying to argue in this Court in justification of the neglect of your children's education ? Don't you think it is very unwise as a father to act in this manner ? The law is made for the purpose of get- ting children well educated to enable them to fulfil their positions in life. To make these legal quibbles is a very great weakness on your part; it is like what is commonly called "cutting off your nose to be revenged on your face."—Defendant (warmly) : Not at all.—The Chair- man : What is your reason for setting up your back ? Why not allow the child to finish his education ? Defendant : The lad wants to get away from school, and I consider lam justified under the act in allowing him to do so. He has passed the second standard three times. Each schoolmaster he goes to puts him back a standard, but I suppose it is a matter of business on their part. There is not a lad in the school who can read better than he can. Alderman Chandley (firmly) : We have been arguing on a moral point of view, now we go on to a legal point of view, and make an order for the child to go to Wycliffe School.

div.head: CAIRO-STREET CHAPEL
div.p: CAIRO-STREET CHAPEL
REV. R. A. ARMSTRONG ON "UNITARIAN-
ISM AND MODERN THOUGHT."

At Cairo-st. Chapel, on Sunday, the Rev. Frank R. Freeston preached in the morning on "Temper- ance Reform." Recommended the. -observance of "Temperance Sunday" and reviewed the various methods suggested for reducing the evils of tem- perance, amongst which he placed first total abstinence.

At the evening service an address was delivered by the Rev. R. A. Armstrong, of Liverpool, on " Unitarianism and Modern Thought." There was a large congregation.. The preacher said that the interval between the landing of Columbus on transatlantic soil and the burial of Tennyson on the 400th anniversary of that event marked a tremendous revolution in the condition of the human mind. The new world of plain arid forest revealed by the great discoverer was but the symbol of the new in- tellectual world, of which mankind h3d since entered into possession. To realise this, let them but select 12 greatest names in literature and science of the interven- ing time, and imagine that never yet had those names been spoken nor the thoughts of those men been thought. In literature, bhrkespeare, Milton' Wordsworth, Tenny- son; in astronomy, Copernicus, Galileo, Kepler, New- ton; in various sciences, Dalton, Herschel!, Lyell, Darwin. Let them try to empty thought of all that these names stood for; in what a mental desert, what an intellectual chaos they would find themselves. There I had been in these four centuries an absolute revolution in the presentation df the universe—of the sum of things Iknown—to the scientific imagination. They had on the I one hand this complete revolution in the sum of know- ledge ; yet on the other hand the very formularies cry- stallised in the intellectual atmosphere he had endeav- oured to sketch were still presented to them as contain- ing the sum and substance of religion. Was it possible Ito conceive that, coming from an age of such restricted thought and knowledge, they could contain the largest, best, and truest that could now be thought and known of the relation of God to man. He believed that if they rapidly reviewed the contents of modern knowledge of the universe, they would find help towards an expan- sion and elevation of religious thought of the very high- est helpfulness and value. Be should divide this review of knowledge into sketches of what now was known of the birth and growth of worlds, of man, and of Bibles. He then proceeded to discuss the nature and the growth of the solar system as described by recent astronomers, passing on to the larger universe of boundless expanse which is revealed beyond. Even yet in the distant galleries of space fresh worlds are coming into being. The teeming womb of space is not yet delivered of all her brood. The hand of God tquches to life ever new clusters of lustrous worlds. We can think no bound, no beginning,no end to the process of the birth and growth of worlds. Then as for the birth and growth of man, instead of man ready-made but six thousand years ago, they now knew that seven thousand years ago there were already great cities in Asia and Africa, employing an age-long development of civilisation behind them. And the palceentologist traced the implements or the bones of man away right through the vast glacial period to a quarter of a million of years back; while the , biologist taught them that even then primitive man was himself the product of an endless evolution, stagting from the first cell of protoplasm washed by the sea-lime on the shore. And as words and man were the slow product of of evolution, so also were Bibles themselves. In various centres of the human race there came a time when men, touched with the spirit of God, began to write down their thoughts and emotions concerning holy things, and in a later and less inspired age their descendants collected these writings into Bibles, and , declared them miraculously authoritative over intellect and conscience. All these facts in the birth and growth of worlds, of man, and of Bibles, were now absolutely assured by the safe ways of scientific investigation. But four hundred years ago they had never been con- ceived. The whole structure of the orthodox theology rested on a universe six thousand years old, of whim the earth was centre, a human race six thousand years old, originally innocent and subsequently fallen, a Bible unique and superhuman, absolutely authoritative over , thought and conduct. These three pillars, the breaking ' of any one of which involved the toppling to the ground of the theology superimposed upon them were all three pulverised by modern knowledge, and the current theo- logy was left utterly without support. Let them con- sider rather whether religion had not its truer basis in the very nature of man. They would then find that from the primeval savage up to the Christian theist of to-day there had been a slow, sure, largening, deepen- ing, spiritualising of the idea of God, step by step and stage by stage, till from the fetichism of the earliest human worship, they had reached the sublime concep- tion of a universal unseen power, permeating and pene- trating every shred and fibre of the colossal universe, manifested in the force of gravity or the thrill of the electric shock, in the darting of light and the flash of flame, manifested no less in every movement of love in the heart of a little child,and in the great historic move- ments of nations and of races. This was the living God, the Heavenly Father, whom the prophet of Nazareth declared. All men and women were His children, and he was Father to them every one.

div.head: COLCHESTER INSUBORDINATION
div.p: THE COLCHESTER INSUBORDINATION
CASE.
SEVERE SENTENCE.

The sentence of Private Gooch. 4th Hussars, was read out on the Barrack-square, on Thursday, in the presence of a full muster of the squadron. He was declared guilty of cutting harness, sentenced to two years' imprisonment, and dismissed the service with ignominy. Colonel Brabazon, addressing the men, said he could not gee what could make any man discontented except fatigue duty, and this must be done. He hoped the sentence would be a lesson to others.

div.head: AT THE WARRINGTON FAIR.
div.p: AT THE WARRINGTON FAIR.
SOME SPECIAL FACTS.
By LUKE BLUNT.

Saturday night last was the inaugural occasion of the December fair for this year, notwithstanding the fact the, the date was the 26th of November. The fair is the sole reviving remnant of an ancient and a once popular institution. In the good old days when we couldn't boast a theatre in Warrington, the half- yearly lairs came as a boon and a blessing. For did they not bring with "them the old schools of most of our best actors—the penny " gaffs." Peo- ple are won; to treat those " gaffs with withering blasts ot supercilious contempt, now. Thay won't remember that Irvin, and Toole, Sheridan, and dozens of leading actors were reared—in their histronic lives—in the cradle of the "gaff." It was there that they imbibed from Mother Art their irrepressible powers of infusing into the drama and comedy, tinges, and aspects of life-like realism. In those days, too, many other enjoyable things came with the fair, for, indeed such things as artistically worked baby linen and real birch twig rods could only be obtained from the travelling vendors who occasionally made a temporary home of the fairground. There is no doubt the fair was then considerably appreciated, but somehow a breach arose between the public who lived near the fair, and the persons who brought the remnant of the old institution to the town. I have been told—in secret—that the cause of the disruption was the oft recurring way in which hens and other fowl became permanently absent from the hen coops when the fair was about. They used to go out quietly at night and forget to come back. Whatever the primary cause of the illfeeling might have been, it has been handed down to the present generation, who declare that the row and rabble associated with the fair is intolerable. The whole time the fair is in town they complain of getting barrel organ for breakfast, dinner, tea, and supper, with the additional use of it as a nightmare when in bed.

On Saturday night, as the crowds of people surged from out of the market and down Bewsey- street, to the fair ground, the scene was interest- ing. The people jostled and pushed, and laughed and shouted. In the glare ana blaze of the dozens of oil lamps, the swing boats could be seen ascend- ing and descending, the hobby-horses swirling round and round. The whirr of the stall man's rattle, the crack of the rifle at the shooting gallery, and the shouts and yells of vendors, lent a slight feature of confusion to the occasion. But the last word seems only to fit when the organs are men- tioned. The cadence of the word just slides in when you stand half breathless, listening to the mad mix- ing medley of" Maggie Murphey's Home" "Down by the old mill stream," and "Little Annie Rooney" "Your Brother Willie's Dead," or "Put me in my little cot" "My black-eyed Susan Jane." One of the organs possessed the accompaniment of a bell, and one of the roundabouts possesses a shrieking kind of instrument, which you can hear for almost half a mile around, as it emits nerve-splitting shrieks, like demonical laughter. It is then that you think of the people who live about the fairground, and wonder why they do not petition the corporation for the abolition of the carnival.

As you approach nearer the scene you come to one of many canvass covered stalls, whereon, in all the glory of a battered silk hat, stands a man. This is the lucky-bag gentleman. He is excitedly harangu- ing the crowd upon the contents of his mysterious wares. The flaring lamp by his side lights up his face, and those of the bystanders, as he bawls "Now then, heres yer chawnce. I leave here to-night. This is the only chance you'l have of getting the most valuable and highest quality jewellery for the insignificant sum of one penny. Its your own I fault if you miss it." Sometimes a precocious individual will recommend the generous, benevol- ent vendor, in tones of inhospitable cruelty to "goo whoam wi thi," or ironcally inquire what he takes them for. Occasionally this leads to exchanges of repartee ; but the vendor's time is more or less occupied in exchanging his packets for pennies. Close by, is one of those interesting fixtures where people with a greater possession of money than discrimination, spend a shilling in trying to throw rings upon sticks for sixpenny knives, which they mostly don't win. Boys anxious to unburden them- selves of their pocket money usually go there. The man in charge has the most implicit belief in their abilities to win, and he encourageingly invites them to "go on me boy. Have another try—keep your pecker up, your the sett as will win, you are. You young fox—ha-ha." The boys industriously "try, try, try again," but either fiom the want of con- fidence or the ultimate lack of pennies, they don't manage to succeed. You advance into the thick of the crush. Behind you are being rushed off your feet by small boys, to your right a stout old matron with her market- ing basket is jamming you on to the next stall ; whilst in front you are charged down by some young fellows who rush for a body who is behind you. Hard by are the popular " dobby-horses." Those are universal favourites. There is always a crowd round them—people looking on with open- mouthed pleasure, others enthusiastically recognis- ing friends upon the wooden steeds, whilst others view the scene with a kind of meditative melan- choly. It is a sight calculated to stir your feelings. Here you see a little chap sitting scientifically upon the gilded horse of wood, and he holds the reins with as much care as though he was guiding a fiery charger. Behind him comes a full-grown man, in a condition known as "half seas over." His legs are dangling all over the place, one arm clasps the horse's neck, and with the hand of the other he is waving his hat. He generally thinks he's doing Dick Turpin's ride to York, and with excited cries of "go it Bess—one more mile," he goads his horse over an imaginary nine-barred gate. The next character, generally to be seen, is the 14-stone lady, in all the pomp of her Sunday clothes. As a rule, &e &ant get excited, and childish, and fanciful, like her beery lord. Oh, no. he mostly sits erect, with a Queen Elizabeth style of serenity and state- liness. She holds the reins in tier right hand,whilst her left is placed effectively on her waist. As she speeds along at an exhilerating pace, her only care is to appear refined and becoming. She gazes upon the crowd, as she swirls around, with a calm and superior air, and if she isn't a particular friend who calls out " Ow're yer enjyin' it, Mary Hann she won't deign even to smile, let alone speak. Round about here there is plenty of life. People of all ages are engaged in an earnest endeavour to spend money against time; except those who didn't have any money, and they just crowded round and looked on.

_ Hard by is the boxing booth. A great number of men repaired here for enjoyment. Before the booth on a platform stood three men wearing box- ing gloves, and inviting the large crowd to "come inside and have a try." Some went in and had a try; and you could see them coming out, after a while, with bleeding noses and coloured eyes. Sometimes an intoxicated man would come and commence a discussion. One came round to the back of the crowd. He was only a little man, but a look of in- domitable courage glistened in his eyes. He had his hat squashed in his hand, and anon he jumped up and made clutches at the air. Then he dropped down solidly, like a keg of butter. But they knew' what he meant, and one of the boxers threw a pair of gloves to him, and asked him to go inside. "Who yer (hic) throwin at, you (hic), ign'rant thing," said be throwing the gloves back. He was beginning to make quite an impression, when by- and-by, a big strapping woman came around. She had a large cabbage in one hand, and some celery in the other. She stole up quietly on her toes. Then she peered gently inte his face and said "You want to fight again do you—you cantankerous little cur. You will fight will you? Now just go 'long —garn, run! jump! skoot !" He turned round with a fierce stare, and opened his mouth to speak. But the same moment the celery sticks fell upon his head with a thud, and the cabbage collided with much force with his countenance. His hair came out by the roots next, and she layed she would " ilea him," too; and when he picked himself up from the ground she lead him out like a shepherd leading a lamb, only more so, because she dragged him more than led him. There was a menagere close by, and round the entrance of this place dozens of people flocked,and enjoyed an average kind of entertainment from the illustrations of the show, and the sight of a Spanish looking gentleman with long hair and short pants, and of whom people whispered" He's the lion tamer, look at him." As the night wears on the place be- comes more thronged. Navvies, labouring men, factory girls and ethers all flock there. And when the night nears to its close the sight seers go in for fried fish, chip potatoes, ginger-breads, winkles, penny cigars, clams, and other things. Whilst the people living in the neighbourhood offer ap thanks for small mercies—for two or even three hours of peace and quietness dosen't come amiss sometimes. It is towards the close of the fair, too, that most of the fun commences—just when many of the visitors are beginning to receive the exhilerating 'sviv # armaymmarassaa

div.head: NOTES ON GAMES AND it ATHLETICS.
div.p: NOTES ON GAMES AND it ATHLETICS.
FOOTBALL.

That modern descriptive phrase" its all orf " was very much applicable to Warrington football last week, The task of announcing the death of one of the most popular sections of "ye goods old English sporte " has become such a regular and common matter with the writer of these notes that he was beginning to despair of seeing the announcement of another match with War- rington. But this distressing doubt was removed from his mind when he saw the posted placards announcing that the match with Wigan will positively take place on the causeway ground on Saturday.

There is no doubt that this arrangement for the re-ap- pearance of one local leather manipulation, has been made on account of the almost complete disappearance of the smallpox epidemic in town. And there is still less doubt that many hundreds of people in Warrington will greet this re-opening of the season with pleasant approval. But for all that, one cannot hide behind the fact that the smallpox has been efficacious in snatching from us the most enjoyable portion of the year's foot- ball season.

The match between Lancashire and Yorkshire at Fallowfield was of course a source of attraction to the majority of Warrington football lovers, and they left by special trains for Fallowfield in hundreds. The match, there, however, was,to a great extent,a disappointment, for the condition of the ground rendered a legitimate and enjoyable game of football impossible. .The scoring showed that plainly enough, and the fact of each team only scoring a try was sufficien: to, prove that play was not of a favourable character.

When the Lancashire forwards went off with such, dash in the big match the Yorkshire spectators were fairly astonished, and when M'Cutcheon made his britliant run in there were many long faces in that reserved. enclosure ; but all were smiles again when Lockwood, scrambled over to score the equalising point, and from, that time forward the Yorkshire sympathisers—and there were plenty of them at Fallowfield—had very little. cause for anxiety.

Valentine, if rumoum is to be believed (says the " Athletic News "), was not too well pleased at being left out of the Yorkshire match. He had already played nine times against the Yorkists for Lancashire, and he was anxious to create a record by playing in a tenth game.

There is one thing about the county match at Man- chester on Saturday which rather pmizles me. For three parts of the time the Lancashire team were on the de- fensive, their forwards being altogether unable to cope• with their burly opponents. In spite of this the game ended in a draw, and,it is said, the try that was given to Yorkshire was of a very flukey description. Yet we are told with a auspicious amount of unanimity by the Manchester press, that Boscow, the Warrington full- back, was a failure.

Everybody admits that the. Lancashire full-back had no end of work to do, and surely he must have dome it in a remarkably successful manner to make a draw of a game, when the forwards in front of him were practi- cally beaten almost from the commencement. We are told that Boscow didn't always gather the ball so smartly as he might have done, but I notice the same complaint is made against such experts as, Lockwood and Dyson. The fact is smartness was. almost out of the question, considering the state of the field, the condition of the leather," and that a lot of forwards like those of Yorkshire were" playing up," as they did do ; and we all know that the methods of, the Yorkshire forwards are not always of the gentlest.

The committee of selection for the North team will have a very awkward task before them this season. Hitherto Yorkshire and Lancashire have provided the bulk of the players, but now Dtsrham, Northumberland, Cheshire, Westmorland,. and Chroberland all have very strong claims to be represented in the important game against the South.

Salford and St. Helens, Recreation meet for the first time next Saturday, and as the match is in connection with the Lancashire Cup,Competition it sitl N. interest- ing to note how the "'rejected of next season'i com- petition will show up against the New Barns cracks. I suppose the Salford team will have to don white jerseys for this match on account of the Recs' usual attire being of the same ruddy hueasSalford's.

There was nothing more, curious in Saturday's matches than the performances of Oldham and Broughton Rangers, who each scored their first win in the Lanca- shire Cup competition over opponents who up to that time stood without & defeat registered against them in the list. Both winning clubs, too, were playing away from home.

The Rangers could hardly have hoped to be successful against Rochdale Hornets, and in the early part of the game the superior forward play of the home team seemed to put the visitors kuite in the shade. Playing up bravely, however, the Rangers were doing as well as their opponents before half-time, and in the second portion of the game held the upper hand. With the Oldham win, which was a fairly easy one, Pennington's goal-kicking bad something to do. After changing ends with the score one goal each, Tyldesley managed to beat Broughton by adding two tries.

Members of the • Gym." are preparing themselves, or at least the “ eight "are, for the coming contests in the shield competition. Vaccination has been, interfering with thepraetices recently, and bar exercises have been left aeverdy alone, until within the past few days. High jumping is being well attended to by several of the members, and we hear that Benien. is. "coming out strong_

Oh, how " the mighty are fallen !” Thom ha already been some figurative weeping and gna,thing of teeth at the Liberal club, over the Christmas-BiNiard Handicap. The novices have been proving themselves adepts, whilst the alleged adepts have been, so to speak, knocked into cocked hats. All the best players in the club have been beaten, including the winnte of last year's best prize.

Samuel Meadowcroft, engine fitter, was placed on Nis trial at Manchester Assizes on Thursday, for the murder of his wife at Gorton. rho crime of which the prisoner was accused was one ot an exceedingly shocking char- acter, and there does not seem to have been any material difference between it and the murder for which the man Mellor, of Oldham, now lies under sentence of death. The evidence of the surgeon as to the condition in winch the body of Mrs. Meadowcroft was found is appalling, showing as it does that the most savage and long-con- tinued violence must have been used. The jury, how- , ever,thought the offence cnly amounted to manslaughter, ' and Mr. Justice Gainsford Bruce, after gently admonish- ing the convict, sentenced him to penal servitude for ten years. div.head: COUNTY FOOTBALL MATCH.
div.p: THE COUNTY FOOTBALL MATCH.

AN INTERVIEW WITH H. ASHTON. The one topic of interest in Warrington during the week amongst all who interest themselves in football, was Joe Boscow's performance last Satur- day as fell hack for Lancashire, in the match against Yorkshire. Most of the Manchester sport- ing papers criticised RJscow's play in an exceed- ingly keen, and not too unbiassed style, and this, together with the fact that a great portion of the " field," hooted the full back in an ungenerous, not to say uugenatmanly, fashion,. has caused the sub- ject to be well discussed in Warrington. With a view Do getting a clear and honest account of BOSCONVB behaviour, our representative called upon Mr. Harry Ashton, the popular captain ot the War- rington first team, who witnessed, the match at Fallowfleid.

" What do you think of the treatment which Boscow has received in connection, with hia play on Saturday our repreaentative naked. " Well," said Mr. Ashton "1 most say thatTl think Boscow has Seen dealt with somewhat unfairly. Of course it cannot be said that he played a brilliant ;game—or a game equal to what we have been ac- customed to seeing him', play. But he most cer- tainly was not to blame for that. 1 consider he is linkable a fall-back as any in Lancashire, and I con- ; eider his play on Saturday was entirely mamed by his surroundings. In the first place the field was in such a condition that no man couid have played a faultless game. In addition to the. field being in a generally swampy condition,Bose cow was constantly compelled to save the rushes- of the Yorkshire forwards,and on .one such, occasion the ball actually floated about in the water. Then.' again, he was compelled to devote his attention to the work of Jimmy Marsh (three-quarters) ,w-ho. was devoting his attention to "Marking Gold- thorpe,.and on several occasions he was interfered with by Marsh and M'Cutchon taking his play. But taking Boscow's play all round, it was cer- tainly good, with the exception of his kicking, and when onewas aware that he was paddling about in , two inches of water, it does-not require mach e2o• planation. For my part, considering that he was playing behind a beaten set of forwards, I think. Boscow did exceedingly well in not allowing his opponents to get over the line."
.4 Was he responsible for the try which they scored against him?"

" Certainly not. Ile stopped a dangerous rush of, the Yorkshire forwards, and before he was given a • chance to play, the ball he was lifted off the ground and the leather carried over the line, his forwards being to blame for not coming to his assistance, and, indeed, when the score was made it was mach disputed, and rightly too." "It is rumoured that a great amount of the shout- ing and hooting from the spectators had been organised by souse one,for a purpose. Do you think there is any truth, in it ? " " I don't think, so. My opinion is that the shout- ing and discouraging cries you allude to emanated chiefly from representatives of—and people in- terested in—other teams,all of whom felt a natural amount of jealousy at not having had a man selected from their own particular team." "Do you think thecommittee of the Lancashire team are dissatisfied with Boscow ? " "I don't know. I consider he has not had a fair trial owing on both occasions to the unfavourable condition of the elements, and also to the fact that the forwards in both opposing teams were smarter than the Lancashire forwards. In the match against timberland he is admitted to have been the saviour of the game..

div.head: ME STORY OF GLASTONBURY ABBEY.
div.p: ME STORY OF GLASTONBURY ABBEY.

LECTURE AT WARRINGTON: 'There does not appear to be anything particularly inviting about the announcement of a lecture upon ,t-Glastonbury Abbey." Yet it had the effect of drawing together an exceedingly large audience in the Cairo-street Co-operative Hall, on Thursday. night. Perhaps this was because the Rev. C. C. Mourn, of Liverpool,was down to deliver the lecture and" something good 'was expected of him. The meeting was under the auspices of the English Church Union, and there were consequently many leading church people present. The lecturer was detained on his way to Warrington and while the audience were waiting the Rector (the Rev. W. F. Willis), indulged in a few hum- °mous remarks, and. then the Rev. Morley Stevenson spoke about the English Chureh Union. It hgd been said he remarked, that the society was Ef political one, but he could assure them that it was not. They didn't care anything about politics in their organivition, it did not pre- tend to take any part..or hold any views upon any politics. What they wished to do was to act as a 1 safeguard to the Church of England, and it did not matter whether the members were Conservatives or Home Rulers, so that they were good Church- men. Then he impressed upon them the necessity of learning as much as possible about the Church, and he recommended several works to them which he said would effectively solve many problems ot Church history. About half-past eiglit the Rev. C. L. Elcum arrived and was greeted with an out- buret of applause. He immediately set towork, and in a few moments bad launched upon his subject. And it was one which was generally Considered to be the most entertaining,interesting. and educating lecture givon in the Hall for many months. Out of a subject which strikes one as be- ing simple and prosey, the lecturer worked out and :elaborated something,., which deserves a more ex, pressive name than "-a lecture." It was a kind of ,descriptive history of Glastonbury Abbey, in which was interwoven with considerable skill and taste, many of the worthless deeds of Henry VIII. in his 'destruction of the old monastries, and contrasting. 'acts of piety and devotion amongst the monks of that time. The line taken by the lecturer was a combination of tine rhetorical and literary craft. He commenced by telling the simple story , —or fable—of Aremathea the early Christian, and . the founder of Glostonbury Abbey. He spoke of the tale told of that good man, marching up .the bill where the abbey was built, and planting his. staff in the earth, and seeing it burst forth into a rose tree which blossomed afterwards in winter only. He believed that was merely a figurative illustration of how Aremathea himself burst forth into a plant of Christianity and thrived in the wintry season of Briton's paganism. From this the lecture went on to the erection of the abbey, and showed how in construction it became even a finer structure than Westminster Abbey, and how in importance it was so great and renowned that: St. Patrick of Ireland and Ring Arthur and and many other notable men visited it. Indeed it became a second Rome so many were the Sainte buried there. In material riches it boasted some of St. Dunstan's grandest pieces of handicroft. Then tte speaker continued and portrayed, the peaceful, holy, quiet lives of the monks of the abbey, and the good and hospital work which they , did. From.this he gradually worked on and on until he reached the period of the reformation—the reign of Henry VIII. At this time the Abbey possessed an annual revenne of .£120,000 which it was said toleave tibed solely in promoting educa- tion—keeping with one or two other monastortee,, , the light; of learning burning in England; and also in assisting to feed and house the poor. The abbot was then Richard Witting, a very gentle and holy man. The king, prompted by, ' Cardinal. Wolsey, had commenced the deadly work, of abolishing the monasteries, and filching their revenues. He kept a body of examiners,who visited the monasteries and reported upon their condition to the. king. The chief of these examiners-was Richard Cromwell, once a barber, a baker, and upon. his own confession,," once a beast." This man swooped down upon unsusperting Witting,and find- ing a book in his library coudemning—accordingto. ' the Pupal creed—the king's divorce, he reported it to. Henry VIII. Witting was taken to the Tower , of kondon,through the Traitor's Gate,and compelled :to sign a document agreeing with the king's meta- ;m.onial enterprise. He was released, but almost 'directly he reached his abbey, he was re-taken by some of the royal retainers, dragged through the :streets of Glastonbury, hung, and then drawn and quartered. The abbey and its revenue was con s- eated by the royal vulture, and soon fell into rum and decay.

That application be made to Parliament in the Session of 1893 for a Bill to provide for the purchase by the Runcorn Improvement Commissioners, compulsorily or by agreement of the undertaking of the Runcorn, Weston and Halton Waterworks Company, the winding up and dissolution of the Company, the extension of powers for the Loeal Govern- ment of the District, the amendment of Acta, and for other purposes. LIVERPOOL WINTER ASSIZES DECEMBER. 1892. 'T'he Commissions for holding these Assizes will be opened at Liverpool, on MONDAY. the sth December.
